acton-lectures-modern-history-1906:
Lord Acton lectured on modern history, and the 1906 volume gathers his survey from the Renaissance to the nineteenth century. Power, liberty, and conscience drive his account of how the modern world arose. Acton, a liberal Catholic, judged rulers by a strict moral code.

Famed for the line that power tends to corrupt, he weighs kings and churches alike. Nations rise, in his telling, as freedom gains or loses ground. The lectures show deep learning worn with clarity and force. Readers meet history as moral reasoning, taught by a master who believed the past must answer to conscience, not merely to success.
andreyev-savva-and-life-of-man-1906:
Savva and the Life of Man, two plays by Leonid Andreyev, came to English in Thomas Seltzer's translation of 1920. Savva, written in 1906, follows a young anarchist who plots to blow up a famous icon. He hopes the blast will free the crowd from what he sees as false faith.

The Life of Man stages a whole human life as allegory, from birth to death in five scenes. A gray figure with a candle watches, marking how fast the flame burns down. Andreyev's theater mixes symbol, crowd scenes, and stark ideas. These two plays show his stage work at its boldest. Both ask what, if anything, gives a human life its meaning.
antonina-or-the-fall-of-rome-pg3606: Wilkie Collins's Antonina dramatizes the fall of Rome in vivid scenes. Goths besiege the city while love blooms amid the ruin. The young novelist paints history in bold and stirring colors. A thrilling tale of an empire's end.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-06:
Burton's sixth volume of the Nights, issued in 1885, presses Shahrazad's long narration onward. Romance, farce, and moral fable alternate in her telling, often nested three tales deep. A listener who loses the thread finds signposts in Burton's careful headings and summaries.

The translator's aim was the whole Arabic book, not a nursery selection. What Galland had smoothed for French salons, Burton restored with notes and plain speech. His wife Isabel helped see the volumes through the press in Benares and Trieste. The work's scale is part of its meaning: a world told night by night. Volume six keeps that world turning at full richness.
arabian-nights-burton-supplemental-1886-:
The sixth supplemental volume, issued by 1888, concludes Burton's Arabian Nights in sixteen books in all. Burton closes his gathering of further tales from the side manuscripts of the tradition. With this volume the English reader at last holds the fullest Nights that the nineteenth century could build.

Burton's learning, gathered across a lifetime in the East, stands behind every page of the set. His versions of Aladdin and Ali Baba, his Terminal Essay, and his thousands of notes all live in these sixteen volumes. No later English Nights has replaced his as the scholar's standard. The Gutenberg text here is ebook 3450. Shahrazad's long bargain with death ends, in Burton, in abundance.
arbois-jubainville-druides-1906:
Henri d'Arbois de Jubainville, the head of the French school of Celtic studies, wrote this work in French in 1906. His theme is the druids and the gods of the Celts. The Celts once spread from Ireland to the lands of the Danube.

The book looks hard at Celtic gods who take the shape of beasts. Bulls, boars, horses, and birds each play a part in rite and myth. He set the druids at the heart of that faith, as its priests and wise men. French in tongue, it stays a lead text of its school.
arxiv-2511-20106:
Li, Shi, Li, and colleagues build a speech corpus where emotions come mixed, not single. Their 2025 paper introduces EM2LDL for speech emotion recognition. Most emotion datasets use one language and one label. Real feelings blend several emotions at once. Multilingual speakers also switch languages mid-sentence often.

The corpus spans English, Mandarin, and Cantonese speech. Utterances were harvested from online platforms for realism. Code-switching within single utterances is included deliberately. Each clip carries a distribution over thirty-two emotion categories. Two hundred thirty-one unique speakers contributed recordings. Gender and age are fairly balanced across speakers. MBTI personality traits accompany a subset of voices. Baseline models used self-supervised speech encoders. HuBERT-large-EN scored best among the baselines tested. Young-to-older transfer beat the reverse direction clearly. State-of-the-art models still struggle with the fine detail. Dataset, annotations, and code are publicly released.
arxiv-2511-20206:
Markova, Larsen, von Neumann-Cosel, and a large team probe the inner statistics of indium-109. Their 2025 paper extracts nuclear level density and gamma strength. The isotope is neutron-deficient and hard to study. Data came from a cadmium-106 alpha reaction. Proton-gamma coincidences fed the Oslo method analysis.

Level density and gamma strength were obtained together. A shape method cross-checked the extraction carefully. Both quantities resemble neighboring cadmium and tin nuclei. Model predictions disagree with the data substantially though. One surprise stood out near the neutron threshold. No dipole strength bump appears in indium-109 there. Neighbors show that pygmy enhancement clearly. Theory calculations with tin isotopes framed the contrast. Capture cross sections were estimated from the new data. Proton capture matched direct measurements excellently. Neutron capture rates strayed from a standard library. Star-process simulations inherit less uncertainty now. Astrophysical p-process models gain firmer inputs.
arxiv-2511-20406:
Mishayev, Sverdlov, Amir, and Dym show a graph learning flaw strikes close to home. Their 2025 paper concerns message passing neural networks on graphs. Such networks pass information between neighboring nodes layer by layer. Oversquashing means distant information gets squeezed through bottlenecks. It was blamed for failures on long-range tasks only.

A test problem called Two-Radius exposes the flaw nearby. Solving it with message passing demands huge feature dimensions. Those dimensions grow with the size of the graph. The authors split oversquashing into two distinct mechanisms. One is the bottleneck effect, possible even at short range. The other is vanishing gradients, tied to long-range tasks. Adding virtual nodes did not fix the short-range bottleneck. Graph transformers succeeded on the same task, though. Existing connectivity measures fail to predict this failure mode. The benchmark is offered for future architecture studies.
arxiv-2511-20506:
Varughese and a large team let machines discover readable laws for atomic forces. Their 2025 paper derives interatomic potentials through symbolic regression. Molecular simulations need formulas for how atoms push and pull. Hand-designed forms often miss charge transfer and far-from-balance behavior. Their search instead grows equations from data directly.

Equation learner networks propose candidate interaction formulas. A reinforcement learning engine steers the search through function space. Tree search pairs with gradient descent to explore options. Training data came from quantum calculations across many atomic states. Crystal through highly disordered setups were sampled. Copper served as the test metal. The best found models beat fixed-form Sutton-Chen potentials. Lattice constants, elastic constants, and phonon spectra all matched better. Two-phase melting tests confirmed physical realism at interfaces. The resulting equations stay fast and human-readable. Modeling gains accuracy without losing physical meaning.
arxiv-2511-20806:
Elisa A. Tau and colleagues dissect in 2025 dwarf galaxies and their stellar halos in 17 Auriga Project simulations spanning 300 million to 20 billion solar masses. Metallicity falls with radius everywhere, gradients running from minus 0.18 to minus 0.07 dex, and the centres of dwarfs below 6.3 billion solar masses are poorer in metals than those of heavier dwarfs. Gradient strength correlates with nothing obvious, neither mass nor accreted mass.

The scatter in halo metallicity does have an explanation: timing. At fixed halo mass, dwarfs that swallowed their dominant satellite later host richer halos. Late arrivals had longer to enrich themselves before disruption. Age profiles bend into a U in about 65 percent of the galaxies, driven by in-situ stars, as star formation stops in the outskirts and mergers fling stars outward. Accreted halos show a link between age and metallicity, the richer ones being younger. The authors stress that galaxy outskirts carry half the story.
arxiv-2511-21206:
Wind energy researchers Francisco de Oliveira, Martin Bourhis, Zahra Sharif Khodaei, and Oliver Buxton report a new kind of wind tunnel study from Imperial College London in 2025. Turbines inside wind farms face choppy air from upstream wakes, which bends their blades and shortens their working lives. The team wanted to watch blade bending and the wake behind the rotor at the same time, under controlled turbulence and spin settings.

Their model rotor, one meter across with three blades, carried fibre-optic strain sensors along its blades while wire probes mapped the wake four rotor widths downstream, across 21 test cases in all. Air-driven strain peaked at a tip-speed ratio near 3.5, close to the design value of 4, and at the blade tip it supplied up to 75 percent of all strain fluctuation at design settings. The matched records give engineers real data for checking fatigue models.
arxiv-2511-21406:
Shahar Hod defends his decades-old results against a recent retelling in a 2025 comment on gravitational collapse physics. Three decades ago, Hod and Piran showed that collapsing charged scalar fields fade with oscillatory inverse power-law tails that decay more slowly than the tails of neutral fields. A 2025 numerical study by Álvares and Vaño-Viñuales revisited the same model with modern hyperboloidal methods, agreeing with most of the classic findings.

Hod argues that the new paper also carries inaccurate claims and critical errors worth correcting. His comment restates the precise classic results, including the conditions attached to them. In particular, the slower decay law holds only when the field starts out static. That law falls like time to the power minus twice l plus two, and it needs the relevant multipole present before collapse begins. Neutral fields, by contrast, decay with the steeper Price-law exponent.
arxiv-2511-21706:
Hui Wang, Fafa Zhang, Xiaoyu Zhang, and Chao Mu plan goal-oriented dialogues by letting a language model rehearse both sides, in 2025. Steering a conversation to a goal within limited turns is a planning problem. Prompt engineering depends on human craft, while trained policy models adapt poorly to new scenarios and cost much to build. Their method, NRPA-GD, needs no task-specific training at all.

A language model simulates user and system simultaneously, generating candidate conversation trajectories. A nested Monte Carlo rollout scheme evaluates those trajectories, while a policy adaptation step updates the strategy from real-time feedback as the dialogue unfolds. On four standard goal-oriented dialogue datasets, NRPA-GD outperformed both prompt-engineered systems and specially pretrained policy models, beating the previous best system overall. Most strikingly, it surpassed ChatGPT while running on a model of only 0.6 billion parameters, showing planning can substitute for scale.
arxiv-2511-21806:
Schäfer and colleagues study a Heisenberg antiferromagnet, a standard model of magnetic spins that prefer to point opposite their neighbours, placed on a maple-leaf lattice. That lattice is a two-dimensional pattern with five neighbours per site and three kinds of bonds, and its geometry frustrates the spins so no simple ordered pattern satisfies everyone. The team focuses on heat and magnetic behaviour across temperatures.

Their main tool is a numerical linked-cluster expansion, a method that builds answers from small clusters, checked against three other simulation techniques. The expansion kept working down to zero temperature, which is unusual, and the heat capacity showed two peaks, near 0.479 and 0.131 in units of the spin coupling, at the higher and lower temperatures respectively. The results point to a ground state with only short-range magnetic correlations, built from resonating hexagonal motifs, rather than a conventionally ordered magnet.
arxiv-2512-00006:
Yuqin Zhao and co-authors present VeriPy, a Python-based route to hardware accelerators for software-defined radio. Software-defined radio performs communication processing in software, making systems flexible and customizable. Hardware accelerators are widely added to boost performance where software alone is too slow.

Their approach generates pipelined or unrolled accelerator designs from Python descriptions. A higher-level design flow shortens the path from algorithm to working radio hardware. Flexible, fast radios serve research testbeds and evolving communication standards alike. Pipelined and unrolled generation are the two hardware styles offered, letting designers trade speed against resource use.
arxiv-2512-00506:
In online facility assignment, customers arrive one by one and must be served immediately, with no knowledge of who comes next. Rawha Siddiqi Riad and Manzurul Hasan analyze the expected cost of this problem on a regular polygon in 2025. Facilities with unit capacity sit at the polygon's vertices.

Customers arrive at uniformly random positions along the edges and go to the nearest available facility, with ties broken by coin toss. Expected cost analysis shows how much the online rule loses against perfect foresight. Such geometric assignment problems model dispatch and load balancing, where decisions cannot wait for full information. Regular polygons give the problem a symmetry that cleaner analysis can exploit.
arxiv-2512-00906:
M Özgün Güleç and Koray Şafak design a movable scaffold in a 2025 engineering paper. Their system is a platform that can move across the outer face of a building, reaching spots workers need for cleaning, repair, or inspection. The platform has three degrees of freedom, so it can shift in three independent ways.

Cords wound on pulleys hold and drive the platform. Servo-controlled motors at the four corners of the building face turn the pulleys. The paper covers the mechatronic design, a dynamic model of how the platform moves, simulations, and real-time control experiments. Safer, steadier scaffolds could cut risk in facade work.
arxiv-2512-01006:
Wilten Nicola reports a clean negative result about reservoir computing in a 2025 paper. In reservoir computing, a fixed random recurrent network does the heavy lifting, and only a simple readout is trained. The coupling strength of that reservoir is a key dial set before training.

A common heuristic sets the dial near the edge of chaos, where the network almost turns chaotic. Nicola shows that, for threshold power-law reservoirs, coupling strength is really a scale parameter. It rescales the system without changing training accuracy. That finding frees users from careful tuning of a dial that, in this setting, does not matter.
arxiv-2512-01606:
Rom and co-authors measure the mass spread of faint objects in the Trumpler 14 cluster. Young massive clusters are prime sites to study brown dwarf birth. Trumpler 14 is about a million years old and rich in hot giant stars. Its harsh light may shape how small objects form.

The team counts objects below star mass in the cluster. Their mass function shows how counts fall as mass drops. That shape tests if brown dwarfs form like stars or like planets there. Harsh clusters give a stress test for birth theories.
arxiv-2512-02006:
Tracking a single point as it moves through a scene is a basic vision skill, and multiple cameras make it both richer and harder. Jahyeok Koo and co-authors present MV-TAP in 2025, a point tracker that follows points across multi-view videos of dynamic scenes by sharing information between views.

Multi-camera rigs observe complex real-world action from several angles at once, and understanding moving objects in that footage is central to many applications. A point hidden in one view may be plainly visible in another, and cross-view information lets the tracker exploit that. The method aims at steadier, longer tracks through crowded, changing scenes.
arxiv-2512-02106:
The interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS is a visitor from another planetary system, and its chemistry records the conditions where it formed. Jason Hinkle and six co-authors report 2025 observations from the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope, targeting its early emissions of hydrogen cyanide and carbon monoxide.

Submillimeter observations measure parent molecules directly as they leave the comet's nucleus and enter its coma. Tracking how the hydrogen cyanide output changed over time adds a clock to the chemical snapshot. Together, the measurements help astronomers compare this foreign comet's makeup with the comets born around our own Sun.
arxiv-2512-02306:
New omni-modal language models read text, images, video, and audio together, and each new sense opens new ways for conversations to go wrong. Boyu Zhu and six co-authors present OmniGuard in 2025, a guardrail system for these models that reasons deliberately before judging content.

Earlier guardrails mostly handled one modality at a time and framed safety as a simple yes-or-no classification. OmniGuard instead deliberates, which should make its judgments more robust across modalities and tasks. As models absorb more of the sensory world, safety systems that think before they rule become essential infrastructure.
arxiv-2512-02506:
A. Riotto computes how an extreme kind of black hole flexes under outside gravity. The objects are extremal Reissner-Nordström black holes, charged holes at the edge of what physics allows. Their tidal response is summed up by Love numbers, values that say how much the hole deforms.

Working with one symmetric shape of such a hole, Riotto solves the full nonlinear Einstein equations exactly. The static Love number for this case turns out not to vanish. That result feeds the wider debate on whether black holes respond to tides like ordinary stars do, or resist in a special way. The case is rare, but rare cases are the ones that test the rules the most.
arxiv-2512-03106:
A diamond sensor that reads magnetic fields can now run on an LED. This 2025 work presents a small, low-cost version of that sensor for teaching. The sensor uses flaws in diamond, called NV centers, that glow red when lit.

In place of the usual green laser, the team uses a strong LED. That swap makes the device safer and cheaper, and lets viewers see the glow at once. The parts are simple to put together. Schools and outreach events could use it to show quantum sensing in a hands-on way. Teachers can build a class demo around it, since the parts are cheap and the glow is visible to the eye.
arxiv-2512-03406:
People weigh AI tools against human therapists in new ways. Junsang Park, Sarah Brown, and Sharon Lynn Chu study that choice in this 2025 work. As generative AI enters mental health care, beliefs may drive who seeks which help.

Using the Health Belief Model, they surveyed a university sample and a national adult sample. They measured belief-based predictors of intent to use AI or therapists. Knowing those predictors helps services design support people will accept. It also flags where AI help may be trusted too much or too little. Belief data can guide outreach, showing which groups need human contact first.
arxiv-2512-03606:
Marine wind forecasts guide ships and energy work, yet data are sparse. This 2025 work reframes wind forecasting as correction of a global weather model. Observations over the ocean are sparse, mixed in type, and variable in time.

The authors use incoming observations to correct numerical weather prediction output for marine winds. Accurate winds are essential for safe navigation, ship routing, and offshore operations. Observation-driven correction could sharpen forecasts where buoys and ships are few. That helps both safety and fuel savings at sea. Correction, rather than replacement, keeps the physics of the global model in play, while local observations nudge winds toward what ships report.
arxiv-2512-03706:
Running a molecule atom by atom is exact but slow, so teams often compress the system into a coarse-grained version with fewer moving parts. Vahid Nateghi and five co-authors examine how to do that squeeze without losing the physics that matters. Their 2025 preprint treats underdamped Langevin dynamics, a standard model of motion buffeted by random kicks.

Following the Zwanzig projection approach, the authors derive a closed formula for how the compressed system moves. They then show how a data-driven technique called generator extended dynamic mode decomposition can model that reduced motion and recover timing properties such as transition timescales. A further step, thermodynamic interpolation, carries samples from one set of conditions to another without fresh simulations. On a two-dimensional test system, the combined method reproduced both the energy behaviour and the kinetics of the full model.
arxiv-2512-04006:
Cross-entropy loss runs nearly all of deep learning, yet theory usually swaps it for squared error or studies only convex models, missing how it truly behaves. Connall Garrod, Jonathan P. Keating, and Christos Thrampoulidis close part of that gap in a 2025 machine learning preprint. Their testbed is the simplest non-convex case: a two-layer linear network fed standard basis inputs.

A quiet discovery powers the analysis. Initialising the network with a Hadamard pattern diagonalises the softmax operator. The weight matrices keep their singular vectors fixed, so only singular values evolve. With that reduction, the authors build a Lyapunov function and prove global convergence, despite spurious critical points in the landscape. The endpoint is the neural collapse geometry, the first proof that gradient flow on cross-entropy reaches it. The authors suggest the trick can unlock analyses well beyond their model.
arxiv-2512-04106:
Hunting security flaws in code with a language model raises a training question: fine-tune the model, or just show it good examples in the prompt? Fouad Trad and Ali Chehab compare those routes for code vulnerability detection in a 2025 software engineering preprint. Their twist is retrieval: instead of random examples, the prompt is stocked with past code that resembles the snippet under review.

Using a Gemini Flash model, they test random few-shot prompting, retrieval-augmented prompting, and labelling by retrieval alone. Retrieval-augmented prompting beat the other prompting strategies and roughly doubled the zero-shot score. It also outperformed a fine-tuned Gemini, though at twenty examples it trailed a fine-tuned CodeBERT, which scored highest overall. That specialist's lead comes with training costs the prompting route avoids.
arxiv-2512-04206:
Bao-Jun Cai, Bao-An Li, and Yu-Gang Ma review how tight pairings between nucleons shape dense nuclear matter. Inside a nucleus, two nucleons can lock into a short-range pair and fly apart with high momentum. These pairings leave a long tail in the momentum spread of each nucleon. Their 2025 arXiv review gathers what is known and ties it to the equation of state, the rule that links pressure and density in dense matter.

Neutron-proton pairs dominate the effect, driven by the tensor force between them. The minority kind in a lopsided mix gains the larger high-momentum share. The review shows how these tails shift both the motion energy and the binding energy of dense matter. They soften one part of the symmetry energy and bend the usual smooth rules for mixed matter. Such shifts matter for neutron star models and heavy-ion collision studies.
arxiv-2512-04406:
Jie Wang, Liangbing Hu, and Bican Xia present ManiDSDP, a solver for a class of hard optimization problems called semidefinite programs. These programs show up in control, sensing, and machine learning, often with a low-rank answer and ones fixed along the diagonal. Direct solvers strain as size grows. Their 2025 arXiv paper reshapes the dual problem so it can be solved on a curved space of matrices.

The method first removes the free variable by projection. It then factors the matrix variable, turning the task into optimization on the oblique manifold. A Riemannian trust-region method solves each subproblem, with rank adjusted on the fly. A curvature hint from each finished step feeds the next, speeding the climb. The authors prove every limit point of the method meets the standard optimality tests. Such solvers widen the reach of semidefinite tools in engineering.
arxiv-2512-04606:
M. Pinamonti, A. Sozzetti, D. Barbato, and the GAPS team report a long-period brown dwarf circling the star HD 128717, also catalogued as Gaia-6. Brown dwarfs sit between giant planets and stars, and the border zone between them stays poorly mapped. Gaia's third data release flagged this star for a wobbling companion. Their 2025 arXiv paper, the seventieth in the GAPS series at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo, confirms the companion with ground-based data.

The team gathered a dense series of radial velocity readings with the HARPS-N spectrograph. Those readings trace the star's sway as the companion tugs it. Combined with Gaia astrometry, they pin down a wide, eccentric orbit and a low mass in the brown dwarf range. The program also hunts for smaller inner planets in such systems. Each weighed long-period companion sharpens the census of the planet-to-brown-dwarf frontier.
arxiv-2512-05406:
Rhys Evans and Primož Potočnik take a census of Cayley graphs, the networks built directly from a group's own multiplication table. Given bounds on size and degree, they present methods to construct every group up to a given order that admits a Cayley generating set of a fixed size. They also list those generating sets within a group, counting duplicates up to the group's own symmetries only once.

With those methods they generate complete lists, up to isomorphism, of the three-regular Cayley graphs on at most five thousand vertices and the four-regular ones on at most about a thousand vertices. Complete censuses like this are reference infrastructure for graph theory: they let conjectures be tested against every small example rather than a sample, and they reveal which symmetric networks actually occur. The methods themselves — exhaustive yet symmetry-aware — are the paper's engine.
arxiv-2512-05506:
Junho Myung and eight co-authors report what happened when a language model was let loose as a writing tutor in real middle-school English classes. Model-based scaffolding — step-by-step hints that support learners as they compose — promises much, but real classrooms impose mixed proficiency and tight time. The team deployed their system for six weeks with eighth-graders in a South Korean school, watching benefits and side effects in the wild rather than the lab.

Scaffolding did improve students' ability to compose grammatically correct sentences. But the step-by-step style demotivated weaker students and deepened their reliance on the system. Classroom dynamics suffered too: confident students monopolized the teacher's attention, while the tool's constant help masked which students were quietly struggling. The authors distill design guidelines for writing support that includes rather than sidelines — a cautionary field report for educational technology.
arxiv-2512-05806:
Martino Gulisano and Marco Gabiccini compute safe regions for a car and its driver, treated as one dynamical system. The model has seven states and mimics human driving through a delayed preview controller: the driver watches the road ahead and reacts late, as people do. The question is global stability: from which starting states will the car settle safely, without leaving its operating envelope?

Their method optimizes Lyapunov functions, the energy-like certificates of stability, using sum-of-squares programming. An iterative procedure grows the certified safe set. On a two state benchmark the method recovers a prescribed safe region accurately. Applied to the full vehicle model it maps safe sets for understeering and oversteering cars. The sets agree well with exhaustive simulation, at far lower cost. Such certificates could run as a live safety layer in future cars.
arxiv-2512-05906:
Lennart Landsmeer, Amirreza Movahedin, Said Hamdioui, and Christos Strydis build the plumbing that lets spiking neural networks train on modern AI chips. These networks communicate in sparse, delayed spikes. Simulators usually force sparse traffic into dense, memory hungry structures. Gradient training must respect the event structure too. The team's framework, ADSEQ, computes gradients through queues of spike events, delays included.

The queues are autodifferentiable, so standard training tools can push gradients through them, and they are designed to sip memory. Benchmarks ran across four hardware families: ordinary processors, graphics chips, Google tensor processors, and a low power unit. Design lessons differed sharply by platform. Classic queue shapes suit processors; ring buffers win on graphics chips until memory pressure favors sparser structures; tensor processors like an approach based on their sorting hardware. Such plumbing decides whether big spiking models can be trained at all.
arxiv-2512-06106:
Constanze Albrecht and nine co-authors let ninety two people meet their older selves, and measured what changed. Future You builds digital twins decades ahead, with cloned voices and aged faces. Participants met theirs as text, voice, or avatar, against a control. The target is future self-continuity, a known lever on long term choices.

Every personalized format strengthened that connection, plus emotional well-being and motivation, against control. The avatar produced the most vividness, yet no format significantly beat another; what predicted the outcomes was interaction quality, how persuasive, realistic, and engaging the encounter felt, not its medium. Text drifted to careers; voice and avatar to reflection. One model beat three rivals at moving outcomes. Invest in conversation quality; the avatar is optional.
arxiv-2512-06206:
Akis Linardos, Spyridon Bakas, and many partners report the results of the FeTS Challenge for the year twenty twenty four. The contest tests ways to train AI on brain scans held at many hospitals, without moving patient data to one place. Teams had to outline the parts of a brain tumor on MRI scans, while the shared training had to stay fast and robust across sites.

Six teams took part, each judged on scan scores and on how much data their method had to send. The top place went to a method that uses a control rule, much like a thermostat, to weight each site's update when the shared model is built. That method scored best overall and also settled fastest. The report shows how careful joining of site updates can lift both accuracy and speed in joint medical training.
arxiv-2512-06406:
Xianzong Wu, Xiaohong Li, Lili Quan, and Qiang Hu build UncertaintyZoo, a shared toolkit for measuring how unsure a deep learning model is about its own answers. Models that guess wrong with confidence can do real harm in fields like driving or medical care, so knowing when a model is on shaky ground matters. Many gauges for this doubt exist, but each ships in its own format, blocking fair comparison.

The toolkit gathers close to thirty gauges across five families under one standard interface. To show it in action, the team used it on the task of spotting flaws in code, running two language models of code through the full set of gauges. The gauges did surface real doubt where the models were likely to err. The toolkit ships with a demo video, aiming to make doubt a routine part of model testing.
arxiv-2512-06506:
Junhui Jeff Cai, Linda Zhao, Wu Zhu, and their co authors ask whether generative AI has acted as a co founder for new businesses. They treat the release of ChatGPT in late twenty twenty two as a sudden drop in the cost of starting a firm. Places in China with more AI skilled people should feel that drop most, so the team compares firm registrations across map grids with differing stocks of such skill.

Grids rich in AI skill saw a sharp surge in new firms, driven wholly by small firms, which added up to a clear slice of all national entry. Large firm entry fell, matching a shift toward leaner ventures. The new firms were smaller in capital, owners, and teams, strongest for first time founders and firms with clear AI uses. The authors read generative AI as a pro competitive force favoring the small.
arxiv-2512-06906:
Wenjie Zhang and co-authors build MINES, a system that spots abnormal behavior in web applications by learning the rules those applications should obey. Modern services run through web APIs, and attacks or illegal visits leave log traces that often look nearly normal. Worse, the logs are noisy and miss key facts kept in databases, so models trained on raw logs learn the wrong lessons.

MINES works at the level of structure instead. It folds API signatures into the database schema, then infers the hidden constraints linking the two. A language model proposes candidate links, and normal logs are used to accept or reject each one. Accepted constraints become small programs that check live logs for violations. Tested on tamper attacks against five real applications, MINES caught anomalies with high recall and almost no false alarms, beating the log-based systems it faced.
arxiv-2512-07006:
Xuanyu Liang and co-authors try to cut the energy bill of next-generation mobile networks without cutting service. In open radio access networks, the radio units that talk to phones draw heavy power yet stay fully awake even when traffic is thin. Smarter control could sleep those units in step with demand. Earlier learning controllers chose from a fixed menu of actions, which grows unwieldy as networks get dense.

The team instead uses a controller, called TD3, that turns a continuous dial rather than picking menu items. That gives finer control over sleep modes across large radio environments. In simulations, their approach saved more than half the energy of an always-on baseline. It also beat menu-based controllers by a small margin, while settling faster and behaving more steadily.
arxiv-2512-07306:
Thierry Petit and Arnault Pachot build fake populations that are exact, not approximate. Modelers of societies and markets need artificial citizens who match official statistics while making sense one by one: no toddlers with jobs, no households that contradict themselves. Data-driven generators infer such groups from samples and drift. This constraint-programming framework instead encodes the target statistics and structural rules directly, producing populations that hit the numbers precisely, without needing any private raw records at all.

The approach is checked against official records, and the authors study how small departures from the targets would ripple into downstream conclusions. The work sits inside a project where the synthetic people can be questioned through large language models, letting analysts rehearse policy and market scenarios and receive steady, decision-grade answers.
arxiv-2512-07506:
Yuzhen Qin, Zonglin Liu, and Marcel van Gerven wrote this 2025 control theory paper. Electrical stimulation can steer brain activity, but safety rules cap how it may be delivered. Each stimulation cycle must be charge-balanced, injecting zero net charge into tissue.

What such balanced inputs can and cannot achieve was poorly understood. The authors study discrete-time linear systems driven only by charge-balanced signals. They ask which states those signals can reach and steer between. Two practical signal styles get separate treatment in the analysis. One repeats the same balanced pattern in a periodic rhythm. The other uses balanced inputs that never repeat in that fixed way. For each style, they derive fresh reachability and controllability conditions. Numerical tests then design the lowest-energy input that does the job. The results matter for both fixed and adaptive brain stimulation protocols.
arxiv-2512-07706:
Yu-tin Huang and Justinas Rumbutis wrote this 2025 theoretical physics paper with Shao-Cheng Lee and Henry Liao. Conformal field theories are pinned down by a method called the bootstrap. The bootstrap usually leans on unitarity, a rule that many interesting theories break.

The authors design a bootstrap strategy that works without that rule. For a trial spectrum, crossing equations at several points fix the coupling data. If the data still drift with the chosen point, the trial is off. That drift becomes a single score measuring truncation error. Searching over spectra then means driving that score down. No convexity or unitarity assumption is needed along the way. Applied to two-dimensional building blocks, the method recovers known minimal models. Non-unitary examples come back correctly. Beyond those, it finds candidate solutions in a harder regime.  A practical route beyond the unitary world results.
arxiv-2512-07806:
Gyeongjin Kang and Eunbyung Park wrote this 2025 computer vision paper with Seungkwon Yang, Seungtae Nam, Younggeun Lee, and Jungwoo Kim. Rebuilding a large three-dimensional scene from many photos is slow work. Their transformer does it in a single forward pass, from dozens to hundreds of images.

The design follows a motto: look broader for the whole, finer for the details. Two hierarchies carry that motto through the architecture. Between views, the model's perspective widens from local shots to groups to the full scene. Within each view, detail starts fine and gathers into compact, dense tokens. The pairing buys both speed and a rich final representation. Coupled with three-dimensional Gaussian splatting, the system renders its scenes. Tests across diverse datasets show top generalizable reconstruction quality. Efficiency and scalability hold across many view counts and layouts.  The work targets scene-hungry tools.
arxiv-2512-08206:
Duo Zhang, Junshan Huang, and Jingjin Yu, roboticists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about two robot arms tidying a tabletop together. In their planner, called SDAR, two arms with two finger grippers must rearrange objects whose start and goal layouts are strongly tangled. Working so close together, the arms need task plans and motion plans that truly fit each other.

SDAR joins a task planner and a motion planner in one loop that sifts through many candidate plans. The task side breaks down a graph of object dependencies to find dual arm plans better than adapted single arm ones. The motion side uses graphics processor tools in a layered search for the best synchronized motions. In tests, it solved every complex, long horizon task given to it, with quality far above earlier methods. Trials on two real robot arms confirmed the plans transfer directly and reliably to hardware.
arxiv-2512-08306:
Sarwesh Rauniyar, a machine learning researcher, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about random forests. Ordinary decision trees split on one feature at a time: fast and stable, but clumsy when the true boundary is rotated or depends on feature combinations. Oblique forests split on combinations instead, at real cost in speed and complexity.

His method, JARF, keeps the simple forest and fixes the data instead. A first forest estimates outputs, and finite difference gradients of those estimates are averaged into a matrix that captures which feature directions matter. That matrix defines one global rotation of the feature space, applied to every input before a standard forest trains. On tabular classification and regression benchmarks, the rotation consistently improved plain forests. It often matched or beat oblique forests while training faster. One supervised twist of the input space, he argues, recovers much of what oblique splits buy.
arxiv-2512-08706:
Leon Kogler and coauthors introduce RESTifAI, a tool that uses large language models to generate tests for REST application interfaces. Such tests need to be reusable in automated delivery pipelines, not just run once. Many existing tools focus mainly on server errors, which leaves normal use and rule breaking inputs less well covered.

RESTifAI first builds valid test cases that follow the happy path of correct use. From those, it derives negative cases that check proper success responses and also proper client error responses for bad inputs or broken business rules. The authors compare the tool with two recent language model based tools and find similar performance, with gains in reuse and pipeline fit. Trial use in industrial services is also reported, and the tool is publicly available.
arxiv-2512-08806:
Daniel Freeman and Mitchell Taylor solve a problem on stable phase retrieval posed by Cahill, Casazza, and Daubechies. Phase retrieval seeks to recover a signal from the magnitudes of its measurements. With a frame in finite dimensions, the process is always stable in a strong Lipschitz sense. In infinite dimensions, it is always unstable, leaving a gap between the two regimes.

To bridge that gap, the earlier authors built nonlinear subsets of an infinite dimensional space where retrieval works with a weaker Holder stability estimate. They asked whether those subsets also enjoy the stronger Lipschitz stability. Freeman and Taylor answer the question in both directions. They give examples that fail Lipschitz stability and other examples that satisfy it. That split answer clarifies exactly where the stronger property can and cannot be expected in this intermediate setting.
arxiv-2512-09006:
Dyna Soumhane Ouchebara and Stephane Dupont study whether large language models can detect vulnerabilities in source code, comparing prompt engineering with fine tuning. Software production has grown fast, and reported vulnerabilities rise each year, so automated detection has become essential. Prior methods range from classic program analysis to recent artificial intelligence approaches.

The study uses an open Llama model and code samples from two public vulnerability data sets. Many fine tuning and prompting settings are explored. A novel double fine tuning approach is suggested, and a less studied test time fine tuning approach is also tested. Results highlight that fine tuning is important to solve the task well, and double tuning performs strongly. Prompting alone proves ineffective, while retrieval augmented generation works relatively well for selecting examples. The authors conclude that Llama models hold real potential for this task, with several questions left for future work.
arxiv-2512-09106:
Metod Jazbec and coauthors propose training the sampling procedure of diffusion language models with reinforcement learning. Diffusion language models now match autoregressive models on many tasks and promise faster inference. A critical design choice is which tokens to unmask at each diffusion step, since that order shapes both quality and throughput.

Common heuristics, such as confidence thresholding, beat random unmasking but need manual tuning. Their performance also degrades as block sizes grow. The authors formalize masked diffusion sampling as a Markov decision process, with the language model as the environment. A lightweight policy, based on a single layer transformer, maps token confidences to unmasking decisions and is trained directly. Learned policies match leading heuristics when paired with block generation. In the full diffusion setting, they outperform those heuristics, giving a more robust path to efficient sampling.
arxiv-2512-09206:
Christopher Carter and four co-authors write a short note on how to design experiments when some participants will not follow the treatment they are assigned. This problem, called partial compliance, weakens many field trials. The authors ask whether screening people before random assignment can help, and what the best screening rule would be.

Their theory gives a clean answer. Keep everyone who would comply, and screen out everyone who would not. That rule leaves the measured treatment effect for compliers unchanged, cuts the typical bias, and gives the most statistical power at the same time. In practice nobody can see in advance who will comply, so the note discusses workable screening strategies and offers a simple test of whether screening is doing its job. The authors plan a real experiment to show the design in action.
arxiv-2512-09406:
Hai Ci and colleagues present H2R-Grounder, a system that turns videos of people handling objects into videos of robots doing the actions. Robots could learn manipulation from everyday human video, avoiding robot data collection. The hard part is the embodiment gap: human hands and robot grippers look and move differently.

Their video-to-video framework needs no paired human-robot examples, just unpaired robot videos. The key is a shared cue. In training videos they paint out the robot arm to get a clean background. They then overlay a marker and arrow showing the gripper's position and orientation, and teach a generative model to insert the arm. At test time the same trick is applied to human videos, painting out the person and overlaying pose cues. A fine-tuned video diffusion model generates robot videos that mimic the human's actions, with more realistic motion than baseline methods.
arxiv-2512-09706:
Kaichen He leads a team presenting CrossHA, an agent model that can act through several kinds of interfaces at once: high-level application programming interfaces, graphical user interface events, or low-level commands. Agents are confined to one action space, which is rigid when the best granularity of interaction changes from step to step. CrossHA instead chooses the most effective interface for each step of a task on its own.

Training combines cold-start supervised fine-tuning with a multi-turn version of group relative policy optimization, a reinforcement learning method. The agent learns adaptive action switching without human-written rules, balancing high-level efficiency against low-level precision. Experiments on more than eight hundred tasks in the open-world Minecraft environment gave state-of-the-art performance, beating fixed-action baselines and showing generalization and efficiency on long-horizon reasoning. Code and models are publicly released.
arxiv-2512-10106:
Gaurav Koley and Sanika Digrajkar build a simulator to watch recommendation algorithms and social networks reshape each other. On live platforms the two evolve together, but controlled tests risk harming real users. Their agent based simulator closes the loop: agents produce content, form ties, and get picks from a graph attention network. Settings are fit on Mastodon data, and the simulator is checked out of sample against Bluesky, matching structural measures closely and time patterns reasonably. The headline tests vary when recommendations switch on.

Turning the recommender on earlier versus later changed network transitivity and content diversity in clear ways, while engagement barely moved. Delaying activation increased diversity and reduced modularity. Scaling the simulation to thousands of agents kept the effect, though weaker, and a Jacobian analysis confirmed local stability under bounded user reactance. The authors release setup schemas and reproduction scripts.
arxiv-2512-10506:
Tomohiko Mizutani works on endmember extraction, the task of pulling the pure material signatures out of a hyperspectral image, where each pixel mixes light from several materials. Self-dictionary methods are accurate but slow, because they treat every pixel as a candidate pure signature, which breaks down on large images. His idea is to shrink the data first.

He assumes the standard linear mixing model, with pure pixels present. On that basis he designs a reduction step that discards pixels made of mixtures. It keeps the pixels near the true endmembers, and he proves that property formally. The reduced set then feeds a self-dictionary method built on linear programming. In experiments, the combined method cut computing time substantially while holding extraction accuracy. And the code is public, which makes the thirty-seven page study easy to test on new images.
arxiv-2512-10706:
Chuanlong Ma and a large team replace copper with light for controlling a superconducting quantum processor. Scaling such machines is throttled by the bulky, heat-leaking electronic cables between room-temperature controllers and the cold chip. Optical fibres carry signals without the heat, but until now they had only driven simple two-level qubits over short distances.

The team demonstrates optical control of a bosonic processor, running universal operations on the combined space of a transmon qubit and a storage cavity. With an array of cryogenic fibre-integrated photodiodes they prepared Fock states holding up to ten photons. They also controlled bosonic modes remotely over fifteen kilometres of fibre with fidelities above ninety-five percent. High-dimensional control, many channels at once, and long reach together address what distributed quantum data centres would need.
arxiv-2512-10906:
Feras Al Taha and Eilyan Bitar design controllers that stay good when the statistics of the noise are only roughly known. Their setting is a finite-horizon linear-quadratic stochastic control problem, where the noise distribution is not given but confined to an ambiguity set. All distributions whose mean and covariance sit within norm balls around nominal values. They ask for causal affine policies that minimise the worst-case expected regret over that whole set.

The minimax problem, forbidding as it looks, admits an exact reformulation as a tractable convex program, interpretable as a regularised version of the ordinary nominal control problem. Working from the dual of that program, the authors build a projected subgradient method that scales and computes optimal controllers to any desired accuracy. Experiments compare the approach against leading data-driven control methods. The paper appears in the proceedings of the Learning for Dynamics and Control conference.
arxiv-2512-11406:
Madeline Shelley, Chiara Boetti, Marina Knight, and Matthew Nunes estimate the hidden network of dependencies inside high in extent time series, where many related quantities evolve jointly. Knowing which series directly influence which others supports forecasting and scientific analysis. Temporal dependence makes the conditional independence graph hard to recover with standard tools.

Their method moves the problem into the wavelet domain, where signals are decomposed by time scale and location. Within a locally stationary wavelet setup, the network estimation becomes a principled sparse graphical model problem solvable with established penalised techniques. Theory confirms the estimator recovers sparse dependence structure consistently. Extensive model runs show the method performing well, and an application to hospitalisations of COVID-19 patients shows its use on real data. The approach gives analysts a statistically grounded way to map dependencies in complex evolving systems.
arxiv-2512-11506:
Georgios Kaoukis and colleagues build EmeraldMind, a system that checks corporate sustainability claims against evidence to catch greenwashing. Companies can mislead the public with vague or false environmental claims, and general purpose chatbots often lack the verifiable facts to judge them. EmeraldMind instead centres everything on a purpose built knowledge graph.

The graph, EmeraldGraph, is assembled from corporate environmental, social, and governance reports, surfacing checkable evidence that generic knowledge bases miss. A retrieval augmented language model then assesses each claim against that evidence and returns a verdict with its justification, openly abstaining when a claim cannot be verified. On a new dataset of greenwashing claims, the system matched strong accuracy while covering more claims and explaining itself better than plain language models. No fine tuning was needed, which keeps the approach easy to update as new reports appear.
arxiv-2601-07106:
Jeremy Mould and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers more power on large scales. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The high value of the cosmic microwave dipole may be telling us that dark matter is macroscopic rather than a fundamental particle.

The possible presence of a significant dark matter component in. The form of primordial black holes (PBHs) sug gests that dark halo formation simulations should be commenced well before redshift z = 100. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07206:
Research by Hao Li and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with LLMRouterBench. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Large language model (LLM) routing assigns each query to the most suitable model from an ensemble. The authors introduce LLMRouterBench, a large-scale benchmark and unified framework for LLM routing.

It comprises over 400K instances from 21 datasets and 33 models. Moreover, it provides comprehensive metrics for both performance-oriented and performance-cost trade-off routing, and integrates 10 representative routing baselines. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07306: Nesar Ramachandra and co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how the cosmos builds its large shapes. Gravity rules that build at the grand scale. Gas and stars add a push at scales near one megaparsec. To catch that push, a model must track gas flow and star-based steps. Those steps are too fine to run in full, so models pack them into short-cut rules called subgrid models. The authors use a fast stand-in, called an emulator, to test many subgrid picks at low cost.
arxiv-2601-07506:
Dongryeol Lee and colleagues probe a weak spot in using language models as graders. Many teams now let an LLM judge answers to questions against a given reference. Lee's team asks whether judges actually follow that reference. Their 2026 preprint reports a critical failure mode in reference-based evaluation.

When the reference conflicts with what the judge model already believes, scores turn unreliable. The model leans on its own stored knowledge instead of the text it was given. That drift substantially lowers evaluation fidelity, the authors report. The finding matters wherever LLM judges score question answering at scale. It warns builders to test judges against references that deliberately contradict common knowledge.
arxiv-2601-07606:
Bingyang Ye and colleagues ask how anyone can grade a model's judgment of new research ideas. Large language models now assess and forecast scientific ideas, yet checking those judgments is hard. Their 2026 preprint introduces Proof of Time, a benchmarking framework that is semi-verifiable. It ties judgments made today to signals that only become visible later.

An idea judged promising can later be tested by what actually happens in science. That delay is the point: time itself supplies the ground truth. The framework aims to scale, so many judgments can be scored without endless expert review. Better benchmarks for idea judgment matter as labs use models to pick research directions. The paper speaks to AI evaluators and science funders alike.
arxiv-2601-07706:
Andy Haverly, Shahram Rahimi, and Mark A. Novotny map classical computer instructions into a quantum computing form. Their 2026 preprint transforms ARM assembly instructions for use in quantum algorithms. ARM assembly is a staple low-level language in classical computing. The core achievement is a direct mapping from that language to quantum paradigms. The team shows the method by computing the Fibonacci sequence.

A worked example matters because it proves the mapping can run a real algorithm. Bridging classical assembly and quantum circuits could lower the entry barrier for programmers. It also raises questions about which classical patterns translate usefully. The paper speaks to quantum software scholars exploring new compilation paths. It treats assembly as a possible front end for quantum programs, not just a hardware detail.
arxiv-2601-08106:
Sergio Cabello, Timothy Chan, and Panos Giannopoulos study Delaunay triangulations with help from predictions. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats a basic task in computational geometry. Given points in the plane, the Delaunay triangulation is a standard mesh with strong shape properties.

The setting adds a predicted triangulation G, a guess at the correct answer. When G lies close to the true triangulation, an algorithm should finish faster than starting cold. The authors ask how to use a good guess without being hurt by a bad one. Their work joins a growing line on algorithms that learn from predictions while keeping firm guarantees.
arxiv-2601-08206:
Vedad Dzanic and three co-authors review lattice Boltzmann methods for non-Newtonian fluids. Their 2026 arXiv review appeared in the Journal of Non-Newtonian Fluid Mechanics. Such fluids break the single constant viscosity rule that simple flow models assume.

Common traits include shear-thinning, shear-thickening, viscoplasticity, and viscoelasticity. Everyday examples range over ketchup, blood, toothpaste, and mud. Lattice Boltzmann methods simulate flow on a grid of particle distributions, which suits complex behavior. The review gathers how these methods handle each non-Newtonian trait. Engineers and researchers get one reference for simulating fluids that refuse to act like water.
arxiv-2601-08806:
Abhi Kottamasu and seven co-authors set up a test of AI on real paid code work. Many tests ask a model to fix a small bug in a toy task. Paid work is broader. It can mean new features, long files, and talks with a client brief. The team wants a test that fits that real scope.

Their test is called APEX-SWE. It grades top models on tasks with real cash value in code work. Each task asks for a full piece of work, not a lone code line. Scores show if a model can do work a firm would pay for. A reader who hires or builds code AI gets a hard, fair scale for that claim.
arxiv-2601-09206:
Song-lin Zhao, Xiao-gang Mu, and Da-jun Zhang turn a smooth model into a step form that a PC can run. The model is the Mikhailov model, a pair of linked wave rules. A step form swaps smooth change for hops on a grid. Done with care, the step form keeps the deep traits of the smooth one, such as its set of saved counts.

They use a matrix sum path to build the step form. They also build a pair of step Miura maps, which tie the model to a known wave chain. One rule of the pair comes from how those maps fit. A reader in wave math gets a step twin for a classic model.
arxiv-2601-09306:
Xin Xia, Hongzhi Yin, and Shane Culpepper bring large chat models to pick work that runs on the phone itself. On phone picks have clear gains. They are fast, they keep user data on the phone, and they work with no net. But chat models are vast. Their RAM and power needs can swamp a phone, so a plain port is a high risk bet.

The team gives ways to shrink and speed such models for step by step picks. Each pick rests on the user's past picks in a row. The model has to scan that row and call the next item, all on the phone. A reader in phone AI gets a path to private, fast picks with no host in the loop.
arxiv-2601-09606:
Manning Gao and five co-authors rethink how machines judge the mood of a clip. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents GRCF, a two-stage framework for multimodal sentiment analysis. Most past work used pointwise regression, predicting one score per clip.

A single score is fragile under label noise and ignores whether one clip is more positive than another. Pairwise methods learn from comparisons instead. GRCF adds group-wise ranking with a calibration stage. Judging relative order first, then calibrating the scores, should steady predictions across text, audio, and video used together. It also makes the final scores easier to compare across datasets.
arxiv-2601-09706:
Andreea Dutulescu, Stefan Ruseti, and Mihai Dascalu target a blind spot of transformer language models: numbers. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes value-aware representations for numbers. Models often ace hard math benchmarks yet slip on basic arithmetic.

The root cause, the authors argue, is that numbers enter as symbols. Their embeddings do not state the value the number stands for. That gap produces systematic errors in simple tasks. Teaching the representation to carry value could firm up everyday calculation. It is a small, targeted fix aimed at a surprisingly common and costly failure.
arxiv-2601-10406:
Weiping Fu and co authors grade quiz items by their flaws, not by one score. Auto quiz makers can write items with deep flaws. A fact may be false. The marked answer may not fit the ask. Past grade tools give one whole score. That can hide a flaw and rate a bad item high.

The team built ErrEval, a grade tool that names flaws. It lists each flaw it finds in plain tags. The score then rests on those tags. Labs can see why an item lost marks. The work aims for grades that match how a human pro would fault an item.
arxiv-2601-10606:
Peng Chen, Xiaobao Wei, Yi Yang, Naiming Yao, Hui Chen, and Feng Tian build RSATalker, a system that animates talking heads for conversation. Such avatars matter more as virtual reality grows, above all in social scenes with turns of talk. Older methods split into two camps. Mesh-based 3D methods handle two-person dialogue but look fake.

Large 2D models look natural yet cost too much compute to run smoothly. RSATalker aims for realistic, socially aware faces across multi-turn exchanges. A good avatar must react to a partner, not just recite lines. The work speaks to teams building virtual meeting and social spaces where faces carry the interaction.
arxiv-2601-10706:
Quinten De Man, Atharva Sharma, Kishen N Gowda, and Laxman Dhulipala present UFO Trees, a data structure for dynamic forests. The dynamic trees problem asks software to keep a tree current as edges come and go. Queries ask whether two nodes are linked, or what lies on a path. The classic link-cut tree has led this field for forty years.

The authors' tests show link-cut trees are still the fastest sequential option. UFO Trees target parallel batch updates instead, where many changes land at once. The design claims both practical speed and proven efficiency bounds. Such structures sit inside graph analytics and network tools that must track changing connections at scale.
arxiv-2601-10906:
Mark Van Raamsdonk and Alejandro Vilar López build a menagerie of exact solutions in three-dimensional gravity. The solutions carry heavy matter particles. They generalize a construction by Antonini, Sasieta, and Swingle, known as AS2. That construction was argued to define states in a conformal field theory that are dual to a spacetime holding a closed baby universe.

A baby universe is a small cosmos pinched off from the main one. Having many exact examples lets theorists test claims about how such states behave. Holography, the duality between gravity and field theory, is the frame. The zoo of solutions gives the community concrete cases for debates about entropy and the interior of black holes.
arxiv-2601-11306:
Dimitry Gurevich studies quantum matrices of GL type in this 2026 preprint. The work sits in reflection equation algebras, a quantum algebra field. Such algebras are tied to even skew-invertible Hecke symmetries. A generating matrix, called L, holds the algebra's core data.

The main result computes characters of the spectral values of L. Those values live in finite-dimensional representations of the algebra. Each representation is labeled by a partition of an integer. Characters sum the weights of a representation in one number. Knowing them maps how the quantum matrix acts across cases. That map helps classify the representations of these algebras. The work is pure algebra with roots in quantum physics.
arxiv-2601-11506:
R. Vukelich and seven coauthors build a terahertz spectrometer for deep cold. Their 2026 preprint puts the system in a dilution refrigerator. Terahertz time-domain spectroscopy probes quantum materials with light. A dilution refrigerator reaches temperatures far below 1 K.

The fridge is a Bluefors unit with a 7 T split-coil magnet. The team measured waveforms at 145 mK in the setup. Fields ran from 0 to 6 Tesla during the runs. The test sample was a gallium arsenide quantum well. Cyclotron resonance was the target signal in the well. Cold, high-field terahertz tools open new states to study. Quantum materials often hide their traits at just such extremes.
arxiv-2601-11606:
Farzana Islam Adiba and five coauthors build a pipeline for the MIMIC-IV dataset. Their 2026 preprint handles the resource's many data kinds at once. MIMIC-IV is a large public electronic health record set. Clinical machine learning research uses it widely today.

The set holds structured data and clinical notes together. Waveforms and imaging data add two more kinds. These modalities sit disjointed in the raw release. Preprocessing and aligning them takes heavy manual effort. The team's pipeline automates that join across modalities. Aligned data can then feed downstream clinical studies. A shared pipeline saves each lab from redoing the grind.
arxiv-2601-12006: Rami Luisto asks if the shape of a road network can show how rural a place is. The work starts from a personal watch on Finnish roads and their shapes. City grids and country lanes form quite unlike graph shapes. He treats this as a qualitative study, not a strict count. Figures match road shapes from city and country sites with shapes from group theory. The aim is to see what geometry alone can tell.
arxiv-2601-12106:
Rodrigo Moreira, Larissa Ferreira Rodrigues Moreira, Tereza C. Carvalho, and Flávio de Oliveira Silva study noisy neighbours in beyond-5G networks. Virtual tools make mobile nets more modular and easy to scale. They also cut running costs and allow sliced nets for new uses.

In the data plane, one tenant's load can harm a neighbour's service. The team study that spill in 5G-style setups. Knowing its size helps operators set fair shares. The work links slice design to real service quality.  The study names where slice shares need firm caps.
arxiv-2601-12206:
Keng Hao Ooi sorts Sobolev multiplier spaces of Lorentz type and their preduals. Multiplier spaces hold functions that can multiply a Sobolev space into itself, or into a set target. Lorentz forms refine the scale by a second index.

He gives block forms and the Köthe dual of the preduals. As a use case, he shows the local Hardy-Littlewood maximal function is bounded on these spaces. Such bounds are core tools in harmonic analysis. The work gives a full map of this space family.  The dual work rounds out the full space map.
arxiv-2601-12406:
Keshab Chandra Bakshi studies a setup from operator algebra, where one algebra sits inside a larger one. The pair are simple unital C star algebras, and the step from small to large has finite index. Bakshi builds a canonical map on a key corner of this setup. That corner is the second relative commutant, a set of elements tied to both algebras.

The map he builds is completely positive and acts like a coproduct. With it, the corner gains the structure of a coalgebra. He calls objects of this kind weak quantum hypergroups. Such structures extend the math of symmetry past groups and quantum groups. The work gives a firm source for them from a plain inclusion of algebras.
arxiv-2601-12806:
Chih-Ting Lu and four co authors test whether a new particle could explain an excess seen at the CMS detector. The excess appears in top quark pair production data. Their candidate is a pseudoscalar particle with a mass of 365 GeV. It would live in a two Higgs doublet model, which adds a second Higgs field to the standard model.

They analyze four types of such models, labeled I, II, X, and Y. They use best fit parameters for the pseudoscalar, including its width and a key ratio called tan beta. The question is whether any conventional version of the model fits the excess. Their work was prepared for a nuclear physics journal. Such tests decide whether an anomaly needs new physics or fades away.
arxiv-2601-13106:
Vincenzo Lipardi, David Mestel, and Georgios Stamoulis study fast rough answers for a quantum magnet model. The model is the transverse field Ising model. It pairs pull or push links between qubits with a sideways field on each qubit. All weights are zero or plus.

Exact answers are hard, so the team builds classic rules that run in polynomial time. Such rules promise answers within a known gap of the best. Links may pull one way for some pairs and push for others. That mix makes the task hard yet rich. Good rough rules here help both maths and quantum staff judge what quantum tools must beat.
arxiv-2601-13206:
Neil Sehgal, Sharath Chandra Guntuku, and Lyle Ungar test if language models feel the clock in live talks. Such models write one token at a time, in set steps. Real talks, from care chats to trade deals, hinge on smooth time and hard stops. Yet most tests of such models skip time sense.

The team pairs agents in fake trade deals under strict time caps. They watch how the models shift tone and terms as the cap nears. Their finds point to flaws in time sense. A model may hold out too long or fold too late. For teams that put chat agents in live talks, the gaps flag a risk that plain text scores miss.
arxiv-2601-13906:
Andrzej Dudek and co-authors study uniform patterns in random ordered matchings in 2026. An ordered r-uniform matching is a set of disjoint r-element subsets of an ordered set. For the case of two edges, the pattern shows how the two sets intertwine. There are many such patterns, counted by a binomial formula.

The team looks for homogeneous substructures inside random matchings. Homogeneous means the small patterns inside all share one form. Random structures often hide such order at a large scale. Finding it helps combinatorics map the border of chaos and order.
arxiv-2601-14406:
Yixiong Chen, Zongwei Zhou, Wenxuan Li, and Alan Yuille tackle label quality in medical imaging in this 2026 paper. Large segmentation datasets mix manual labels with pseudo-labels of uneven quality. Bad labels can compromise both training and evaluation. They also make model training less robust.

The team built SegAE, a Segmentation Assessment Engine. It is a lightweight vision-language model that predicts label quality on its own. It covers 142 anatomical structures. Their method also uses synthetic data to teach the judge. Readers get a tool for checking label quality at a scale no human team could grade by hand.
arxiv-2601-14506:
Amogh Gupta, Niharika Patil, Sourojit Ghosh, and Snehalkumar Gaikwad study bias in AI tutoring in this 2026 paper, set for the ACM FAccT conference. AI chatbots are now popular worldwide, and students use them for coursework support. That spread creates a need to study their benefits and drawbacks. The authors ask one pointed question.

How do large language models perceive the intellectual capabilities of student profiles from intersecting marginalized identities, across distinct cultural contexts? The paper's title names its axes: language, caste, and context. It compares AI-generated explanations across Indian and American STEM educational systems. Readers get evidence on how demographic cues can shift the help students receive.
arxiv-2601-14706:
Chao Gao and a team at Gensmo.ai present a fashion search benchmark in this 2026 paper. LookBench is a live and holistic open benchmark for fashion image retrieval in real e-commerce settings. The authors use the word look in a shopper's sense. A look can mean finding the exact item, a close substitute, or a visually consistent alternative.

Most benchmarks test retrieval on clean catalog photos. Real shoppers search messy, real-world images. LookBench is built to mirror how people actually shop. It is live, so its data can refresh, and holistic, so it covers many search styles. Readers get a harder, more honest test for fashion retrieval systems.
arxiv-2601-14906:
Jan Dreier, Jakub Gajarský, and Michał Pilipczuk study ways to change a graph with logic. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with transductions, edits to a graph that first-order logic can state. The team asks how to undo such an edit, at least in rough form.

Running a transduction backwards is the hard part. The authors give a fast method that works when the source graph is sparse. Sparse here means the graph class has a bounded form of spread. The method gives an approximate reversal of the edit, not an exact one.
arxiv-2601-15106:
Giulio Bordieri, Giorgio Cartechini, and co-authors link radiation physics to cell survival with deep learning. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with proton and carbon ion beams used in therapy. How the beam's energy lands across scales helps decide the damage cells take.

Yet the link between those scales and the biological outcome is still not fully understood. The authors build a multi-scale deep learning model to predict cell survival. The model is made to stay interpretable, so its steps can be read. Their slogan is one scale to rule them all.
arxiv-2601-15406:
Hatef Otroshi Shahreza, Anjith George, and Sébastien Marcel test whether big multimodal models can match faces across sensors. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with heterogeneous face recognition. Enrollment and probe images come from different sensing modes, which makes matching hard.

The modes include visible light, near infrared, short-wave infrared, and thermal cameras. Multimodal large language models shine on many vision-language tasks. That raises hopes for biometric use. The authors run a systematic evaluation of the top models on this cross-sensor task, to see how far those high hopes truly hold up.
arxiv-2601-15606:
Jonghyeon Ahn studies barcode entropy in symplectic geometry in a 2026 arXiv paper. Barcodes come from persistence modules, which track features across scales. Barcode entropy measures how fast the count of long bars grows. Long bars signal lasting structure. Ahn's setting is the relative symplectic cohomology of a Liouville domain. That domain sits inside a larger symplectic manifold.

Symplectic cohomology is a tool for probing such spaces and their dynamics. Tying its barcodes to an entropy gives a new invariant to compute. Growth rates often reveal rigidity: some systems cannot grow past a bound. Results like this link algebra to the motion of Hamiltonian systems. The paper is aimed at specialists in symplectic topology. Its terms are technical, and the abstract states the setup with little gloss.
arxiv-2601-16306:
Emily Townsend, Joshua Pomeroy and Garnett Bryant draw a new Lindblad form for a driven spin dot. Their 2026 preprint deals with a quantum dot tied to a lead. The lead acts in a Markov way, with no long past. A wave field drives the spin state of the dot. Past Lindblad forms miss terms that the drive plus tie create.

The team draws the full form for that joint case. They show it keeps all states sound and sums to one. They also find the jump steps that the form holds. A sound form lets teams model driven dots with trust. Such dots sit at the heart of spin based quantum gear.
arxiv-2601-16606:
Antonio Bracale and three coauthors weigh flaws in base tone reads when volts waver. Their 2026 preprint deals with power grade on new grids. Base tone, the mains wave rate, is a key grade mark. True reads of it in short spans guide grid checks. New grids waver in volts far more than old grids did.

Waver bends tone reads in ways teams must count. The team tests read ways side by side in such terms. Each way is scored by its flaw size in short spans. Low flaw ways help grid teams spot faults fast. The work serves checks of grid health in real time.
arxiv-2601-16906:
Calarina Muslimani and a team of five co-authors help set reward scores for learning bots. A bot learns well when its score matches the true aim. Hand-set scores are slow to tune and oft off mark. Their 2026 preprint builds a score gauge called TAC. It rates how well a score path tracks the aim path.

The gauge first aids hand tuning of score weights. It shows which weights pull the bot off aim. Then it goes past tuning, to learn scores from data. Sound scores cut wasted runs in bot training. They also curb bots that game a poor score for gain.
arxiv-2601-17206:
Lars Andersson and Bernardo Araneda prove a result about Hermitian gravitational instantons. These are special curved spaces used in gravity theory. The authors look at the moduli space, the space of all such shapes. They show it is rigid at the small-change level. They also show small changes can be built up into full shapes.

Their result joins a recent proof by Biquard, Gauduchon, and LeBrun. That proof gave local rigidity for Hermitian instantons. Together, the two works complete the picture. The result holds for compact spaces and for open ones too. For geometers, it closes a clear gap. It tells them these rare spaces have no hidden flex.
arxiv-2601-17506:
Shohini Bhattacharya and four co-authors propose how to spot gluon GTMDs at the future Electron-Ion Collider. GTMDs are generalized transverse momentum distributions. They give a rich picture of gluons inside the proton. The team uses exclusive heavy vector meson production. Axial-vector mesons join the study too. The setting is lepton-proton collisions.

They work within collinear twist-3 factorization. In that frame, set azimuthal angle patterns mark GTMD presence. Clear signatures tell EIC teams what to measure. Gluon structure is a core EIC goal. A planned signature saves beam time and sharpens design. The work turns abstract distributions into detector targets.
arxiv-2601-18106:
Jiatan Huang and co-authors build a benchmark that joins food knowledge with health goals. Their 2026 preprint presents GLEN-Bench, a graph-language benchmark for nutritional health. Diet interventions are a main tool for managing chronic disease. Judging them needs both food facts and a patient's state. A graph can hold the links between foods, nutrients, and conditions, while language models supply the reasoning over that graph.

The benchmark tests how well systems handle such joined tasks. Nutrition advice is an area where wrong answers carry health costs. A shared test set helps compare tools on equal ground. It also shows where models still fail at diet reasoning. The work serves builders of health assistants.
arxiv-2601-18306:
Everlyn Asiko Chimoto, Mostafa Elhoushi, and Bruce Bassett argue that calibration data for shrinking models should span many languages. Their 2026 preprint deals with quantization, which cuts a model's storage and compute costs. Quantization often costs accuracy. The standard post-training methods calibrate on small English-only sets. What that choice does to multilingual models has been little studied. The authors test language diversity in calibration for quantized multilingual models.
