If diverse calibration guards non-English skill, the fix is cheap and broad. Most users of these models do not work in English alone. The study gives deployment teams a concrete lever to test. It also warns against English-only habits in model tooling.
arxiv-2601-18506:
Valentin Magro, Sébastien Garcia, and Alexei Ourjoumtsev study groups of atoms that act as one big atom when raised to high states. Such a group can hold a quantum bit and can give off lone bits of light. Those skills make groups of this kind strong picks for nodes in quantum nets. To grade a group, staff need a maths that is true to life yet cheap to run.

Real groups are large and messy, with atoms spread at chance. A cheap maths that skips the mess can give the wrong grade. The team build a maths that keeps the key facts of the mess while it stays cheap to run. It deals with a flaw in which the group fails to block a next rise as well as hoped. Firm grades help labs build nodes that link well in a net.
arxiv-2601-18606:
Yanhong Lai, Xianyu Tan, and Yubo Su study the winds of small far worlds that sit tipped far on their sides. With a new space scope in use, staff can now read the air of low-mass worlds, not just of big ones. In tight groups of worlds, pulls from mates can lock a world in a tipped pose for good. A tipped world also tends to spin out of step with its path.

That pose should drive odd winds. One side may bake while the next side freezes, in a beat set by the slow spin. The team model how air moves in that case. Their maps may help staff read the light of such worlds when the scope catches them. A good wind map is key to tell a world's heat tale from a few dots of light.
arxiv-2601-18706:
Health-SCORE sets out to make the grade sheets for health chat tools cheap to build and safe to trust. A grade sheet lists the traits a good reply must show, trait by trait. Such sheets are key for open asks, where no one right reply exists. In health work they count most of all, since a bad reply can harm. But good sheets take skill and time to build by hand.

The new frame builds sheets in a way that can scale to many health fields. It cuts the hand cost while it holds the worth of the grades. Trained and graded on such sheets, health tools could get both safer and more apt. The frame aims to make that loop cheap to run for each new use. That could lift the bar for health chat as a whole.
arxiv-2601-19206:
Min Namkung and five co-authors set privacy rules for quantum sensing spread across many clients. In such networks, clients share quantum resources to measure fields at many places, while servers they may not trust help run the work. Privacy is a basic need in that setup.

Past privacy rules leaned on ideal bounds that real measurements cannot reach. The team defines privacy in operational terms, tied to what real devices can do. Workable rules let engineers promise clients a level of privacy that a lab test could check, not just a theorem could state.
arxiv-2601-19306:
Sijia Li and five co-authors give phone agents a drive to go learn what they do not know. Mobile agents can run smartphone tasks, but in complex apps they stall on missing knowledge and new screens. The team adds curiosity driven knowledge retrieval, so the agent seeks facts when it feels a gap.

Curiosity here is a working rule: notice the gap, go fetch, then act. It was shown at the ACM Web Conference. Agents that fetch what they lack, at the moment they lack it, should handle unseen apps far better than agents frozen at training time.
arxiv-2601-19806:
Nuno Crokidakis and Lucas Sigaud model how racist content spreads through a population. They treat the spread like an epidemic, with three states for individuals. People can be susceptible, actively spreading, or opposed to the content. Transitions between states are driven by interactions, echoing how views pass between contacts, especially online.

The model shows phase transitions, sharp shifts between a society where the content dies out and one where it persists. Such thresholds depend on how strongly interactions push people between states. Online networks amplify the dynamics the model captures. Understanding the tipping points could inform moderation and education strategies. The work applies tools from statistical physics to a social harm.
arxiv-2601-20106:
Shamse Tasnim Cynthia, Joy Krishan Das, and Banani Roy ask whether all software developers use AI coding agents in the same way. Their 2026 study compares core developers, who sit near the center of a project, with peripheral developers, who contribute less often. Earlier work showed that the two groups adopt AI tools at different rates.

The authors study how that gap plays out now that coding agents can act on their own. The question matters because agents are changing how teams divide work and review code. If core and peripheral developers use agents in unlike ways, project leads may need unlike rules and support for each group.
arxiv-2601-20406:
S. Elgammal studies whether the High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider could reveal a torsion field, an extension of gravity in Einstein-Cartan theory. The analysis uses privately simulated data matched to the collider's planned setup, with proton collisions at high energy. It focuses on pairs of muons with large mass.

The key variable is an angular distribution measured in the Collins-Soper frame. A torsion field would distort that distribution in a characteristic way. Case studies of this kind tell experimenters which signals to hunt for when the upgraded collider turns on. They also show how strong a signal must be to stand out.
arxiv-2601-20606:
Xinyu Wang and five colleagues present WFR-MFM, a one-step inference method for dynamic unbalanced optimal transport. Reconstructing how a system evolves from limited observations is fundamental in single-cell biology. There, unbalanced optimal transport models transport and mass change together, since cells divide and die as they move through states.

Existing approaches simulate trajectories at inference time, which makes inference a bottleneck at scale. A one-step method removes that simulation loop. Faster reconstruction would let biologists trace how cell populations develop across far larger datasets. The point is speed. A one-step read can stand in for a long run that few labs can pay for. It turns a slow step into a fast one, and that is no small thing.
arxiv-2601-20806:
Jiangen He and Wen Lou map how library and information science schools organize their research. Their 2026 study is the first full empirical map of its kind, they report. It covers schools across the United States. The team analyzed more than fourteen thousand publications. They came from over twelve hundred faculty members at forty-four institutions, across the years 2013 to 2024.

The authors used word embeddings and topic modeling to sort the work. They found sixteen distinct research themes. Those themes group into three broad dimensions. They are Library and Knowledge Organization, Human-Centered Technology, and Computing Systems. The map shows how each school's structure and portfolio fit together. It gives the field a clear view of where its strengths now lie.
arxiv-2601-21006:
Michael Jones and five co-authors fuse simulation and experiment to read fusion shots. Their 2026 paper concerns inertial confinement fusion, or ICF. A mix of physics-based simulation and experiments was key to reaching ignition in ICF. Both sides produce mixed outputs: scalars and images. Only part of the simulated data is available in real shots. That gap makes inference about a shot hard.

The authors propose a joint diffusion approach to multi-modal inference. Diffusion models can fill in missing views in a principled way. Trained across both data worlds, the model can infer hidden values. Better inference helps physicists tune the next shot. The work joins plasma physics with machine learning.
arxiv-2601-21106:
Annesh Pal and three co-authors make a flexible clustering model scale to wide data. Their 2026 paper studies Dirichlet process mixture models, or DPMMs. These models estimate the number of clusters from the data itself. They draw that number from an infinite choice of partitions. That freedom makes them a robust alternative to parametric mixtures. The catch is cost: inference in high dimensions is heavy. Two key parameters are usually fixed by hand.

The authors let both the concentration parameter and the variance be unknown. Their adaptive model learns them from the data. Collapsed variational inference keeps the computation tractable. Scaling such models matters for modern datasets with many features. The paper targets clustering that adapts its own complexity. It serves analysts who cannot guess cluster counts in advance.
arxiv-2601-21206:
Yu Guo and Rong-Xin Miao study a web of linked theories in holography, the idea that a bulk world can be described by a theory on its edge. Their setup joins several such edge theories through branches of a curved gravity model. Each branch carries its own coupling strength.

Using a classic theorem recast for holography, the authors prove a junction rule on the joining surface. That rule leads to conservation laws at the nodes of the web. The work also links the setup to parallel worlds that a signal could pass through. It gives a cleaner picture of how linked holographic systems share energy and information.
arxiv-2601-21306:
Wei-Di Chang, Mikael Henaff, Brandon Amos, Gregory Dudek, and Scott Fujimoto question a basic belief about model-based reinforcement learning. The usual story blames weak long-term forecasts and piling errors for poor results. Planning by search, on that view, should fix a learned policy.

The authors find that search can hurt results even when the model is highly accurate. Swapping a learned policy for search is not a plug-and-play upgrade. Something about the search itself clashes with how the policy was trained. The finding urges care: a good world model does not guarantee that planning on top of it will help.
arxiv-2601-21506:
Joonhee Lee, Hyunseung Shin, and JeongGil Ko design a navigation system for indoor robots that pairs speed with understanding. Classic mapping methods locate a robot reliably but need detailed maps. They also cannot read the signs and room numbers that guide people indoors.

Vision-language models can read those cues but often react too slowly for a moving robot. The authors combine both strengths in a dual-process design. A fast process keeps the robot moving safely, while a slower one reads the scene for meaning. The pairing targets hospitals, offices, and malls, where robots must move quickly and still find the right door.
arxiv-2601-21706:
Nan Lin, Yanbo Wang, and Jacco Heres unify generative tasks for smart meter data under one flow-based model. Meter data underpin planning and running the distribution grid. Privacy rules often make the real data unavailable, and what is collected can be corrupted or too coarse.

A generative model can fill those gaps with realistic synthetic series. Flow matching gives one frame for tasks like imputation, upscaling, and scenario creation. Grid planners could then test plans against rich synthetic demand without touching private records. The unified design also cuts the need for a separate tool per task.
arxiv-2601-21806:
Walter Wreszinski revisits one of the oldest puzzles in quantum mechanics, the EPR paradox. The paradox was meant to show that quantum theory must be incomplete if it respects locality. Locality is the idea that distant objects cannot instantly affect each other. Generations of debate followed about what the theory really says.

In his 2026 preprint, Wreszinski draws out a principle he finds implicit in a 1935 paper by Schrödinger. Using it, he argues for a proof that the EPR-locality paradox does not arise within the Copenhagen interpretation. He shows the point already with the simplest case, an entangled pair of two spin one-half particles. The claim, if it holds, would settle a long conceptual dispute about where the paradox actually lives.
arxiv-2601-22006:
Vasily Bokov, Lisa Kohl, Sebastian Schmitt, and Vedran Dunjko ask how little quantum computing is enough. Quantum machine learning is often sold as a promising use for quantum computers, backed by proofs of possible advantage. The authors invert the usual question: how small a role can the quantum device play while the advantage survives?

Their 2026 preprint studies learning under quantum priors, where most of the work is classical and the quantum part is minimal. Proving advantages in that lean setting matters because near-term quantum hardware is scarce and error-prone. If a small quantum contribution still provably helps, useful quantum learning could arrive years earlier than designs that need a full quantum pipeline.
arxiv-2601-22206:
Shi Bo and AmirEmad Ghassami study imitation learning when the student cannot see the world cleanly. In offline imitation, an agent learns from recorded expert behavior. Trouble starts when part of the state that drove the expert's decisions is observed only through noisy measurements, and the distribution shifts before deployment.

Those flaws create spurious links between states and actions. Standard behavioral cloning then converges to systematically wrong behavior, whether it uses the raw measurements or ignores them. The authors' 2026 preprint develops causal imitation learning that corrects for measurement error and distribution shift. The problem is practical: robots and medical policies alike learn from sensors that never report the true state.
arxiv-2601-22506:
Kaili Sun and four co-authors show a surface that emits heat waves with a twist that flips by side. Metasurfaces are thin, patterned sheets that steer waves of many kinds. Their 2026 preprint reports Janus chirality: the emitted heat's spin turns one way on one face, the other way on the back.

Getting such coherent, two-faced emission from one device is a hard feat. The team show it in a real build, not just on paper. Control of heat glow's spin could serve sensing, signaling, and heat control. The work opens a new knob for thermal design.
arxiv-2601-22906:
P. H. Cezar and a team of astronomers report gas observations of six nearby quasars. These are type-2 quasars, bright galactic centers partly hidden from view, drawn from the QSOFEED sample. Using a near-infrared instrument on a large telescope in the Canary Islands, they took long-slit spectra of each one.

The spectra trace warm molecular gas plus atomic gas at low and high ionization. Such gas shows how quasar energy pushes back on its host galaxy, a process called feedback. Feedback helps explain how galaxies and their central black holes grow together.
arxiv-2601-23006:
Junyou Su and a team of co-authors pick better training data for fine-tuning language models. Training on full datasets is costly, and extra data often adds little. Existing selection methods are tied to one domain: what works for general instructions fails on reasoning, and the reverse also holds.

Their method, InstructDiff, uses differential entropy to judge data in a domain-adaptive way. Smarter selection could cut training bills while keeping quality high. It also makes fine-tuning feasible for smaller teams with narrow, specialized data. Domain-adaptive selection is the aim, since instruction data and reasoning data reward very different selection strategies.
arxiv-2601-23206:
Morten I. K. Munk, Arturo Valdivia, and Paolo Burelli generate dynamic game content with small language models. Large models promise rich, changing game worlds, but they suffer narrative incoherence and high running costs. Their size also forces cloud access, which offline games cannot assume.

The proof of concept shows small models can produce high-quality content locally. On-device generation keeps games playable without a connection and cuts server bills. It also keeps player data on the machine, a privacy plus for studios. Small models answer the offline problem directly, since they can run on the player's own machine without cloud access.
arxiv-2603-01506:
Jianqiang Ren, Lin Liu, and Steven Hoi build a way to turn one photo into a moving 3D head in this 2026 work. Fast, detailed head avatars matter for games, film, meetings, and virtual worlds. A single model should also serve both weak and strong hardware without losing key detail.

Their method, OMG-Avatar, stores the head as Gaussian blobs at several levels of detail. A transformer reads broad face traits, while sampled points add local detail, joined with depth cues to keep overlaps sane. Head and shoulders are built apart, then merged, which fixes a weak spot of older face models. The build takes a fraction of a second, and tests beat prior tools on rebuild quality, acting control, and speed.
arxiv-2603-01806:
Xiong Zhang, Hong Peng, Zhenli He, and colleagues spot anomalous nodes in networks without any labeled examples. Their 2026 work targets bad actors in social and review graphs, such as fake accounts and banned users. A recent method boosts links among normal nodes while cutting links of odd nodes, yet its fixed cutoff misfires.

Their model, GCTAM, splits the cutoff step into contextual and global parts that work together. Contextual truncation lowers the affinity of likely anomalous nodes based on local cues. Global truncation raises affinity among normal nodes, using high-order links the old method ignored. Wide tests on large real graphs show wins over peer methods on most tasks. Gains stand out on two famous review data sets, and the method still finishes on the largest sets where rivals fail.
arxiv-2603-02306:
Adrian Fraser simulates a mixing process inside stars in this 2026 paper. Fingering convection stirs chemicals in star zones where heavy material sits above light material. It matters in red giants and possibly in polluted white dwarfs. Past three-dimensional simulations could not reach the extreme settings found in real stars.

The gap is set by one ratio, comparing viscosity with heat spread, which is tiny in stars. Fraser runs simulations spanning old settings down to true stellar values. A standard mixing model stays consistent with simulations across that whole range. So clashes between that model and observations cannot be blamed on the old gap. Extra physics, not simulation limits, must explain the mismatch.
arxiv-2603-02806:
Jonas von Berg, Adalbert Fono, Massimiliano Datres, and colleagues prove that steady classifiers need to be much bigger than their data. Their 2026 paper defines stability as the average distance from a data point to the model's decision boundary. A larger margin means small input changes rarely flip the answer.

Their bound improves as stability grows, and it needs no smoothness assumptions, covering jagged classifiers too. A direct consequence follows: a model that merely fits its training points with about as many parameters as points must be unstable. Real robustness therefore demands heavy overparameterization. Experiments back the theory, with stability rising alongside model size and tracking test accuracy, while older norm-based measures said little.
arxiv-2603-03206:
Cullen Anderson, Narmeen Oozeer, Foad Namjoo, and colleagues test how poisoned examples can hijack an AI model's steering. Contrastive steering finds a trait direction by comparing the model's inner signals on paired examples. It then shifts those signals along that line at runtime. Safety teams use it a lot, yet nobody had checked how it holds up when the example set is rigged.

A modest share of rigged examples leaves steering mostly intact. Past a clear threshold, though, attackers can plant strong unwanted side effects on purpose. A look at the shapes of distinct attack types points to guards. The weak step is a plain average over many signals. Swapping in a robust form of that average cancels most of the harm.
arxiv-2603-03506:
A M Guzman and M C McDonald hunt for a pattern in detector noise that should exist across columns if it exists at all. Their hunt appears in an instrument report for Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Read noise in bias frames already grows with row number, because dark current builds during readout. Their report checks the column direction for the Wide Field Channel's four amplifiers, across different maintenance periods called anneal cycles.

No column dependence appears. Read noise in the physical prescan regions sits about half an electron lower than in the science arrays, exactly where no readout dark accumulates. Three follow-ups round out the study. Read noise shows no visible trend across an anneal period. Two amplifiers show a brief linear decline across their first science columns. And masking unstable hot pixels lowers the noise of their columns.
arxiv-2603-03606:
Satabdi Das and four colleagues ask blind and visually impaired people what would make photo sharing feel safe. A shared image can accidentally expose sensitive or embarrassing content its owner cannot see, risking privacy and relationships. Their 2026 study tests image obfuscation filters as a pre-sharing shield, with twenty blind and visually impaired participants judging filtered images of varying sensitivity.

Pixelation was the least preferred filter. Other preferences shifted with image type and with the audience, family, friends, or strangers, so no single filter wins everywhere. Across audiences, participants felt more comfortable sharing filtered images than unfiltered ones. The authors turn those patterns into design guidelines for sharing tools that warn and protect without taking control away from the person sharing.
arxiv-2603-03806:
Hanpeng Liu and four colleagues teach a vision model to read many images as one long book, with separators between chapters. Mamba, a state-space architecture, processes sequences causally and efficiently, which suits autoregressive pretraining, but vision versions were stuck with short sequences. Their 2026 method, STAR, inserts an identical separator token before each image, marking where one picture ends and the next begins.

That simple device quadruples the usable input sequence length while keeping every dataset image at its original size. Pretrained the long way, their STAR-B model scores competitively on the standard ImageNet classification benchmark, at the top of the Vision Mamba class. The authors argue the gain comes from finally exploiting the architecture's strength, long-range dependence across a genuinely long visual sequence, rather than from any added parameters.

William Walker Atkinson was a Chicago lawyer turned New Thought writer who filled magazines and cheap manuals with his teaching. His Thought Vibration, published in 1906, explains the law of attraction in the mental world. It became New Thought's most circulated manual.

His brisk, salesman-like tone helped the manual travel far beyond church circles.
