The memoir's own pages never start within the sample. Contents, therefore, cannot be stated from the evidence held for this entry.
moyle-institutes-justinian-1906:
Emperor Justinian ordered the Institutes in 533 as a first textbook for law students in the Roman Empire. J. B. Moyle's English translation, in the 1906 edition used here, made the short work a staple for students of Roman law. Justinian's compilers built it on older teaching books, chiefly the one by Gaius.

Four books lay out the law in order: persons and their status, property and wills, promises and wrongs, and how suits are brought. The style is brisk and plain, since new students had to grasp the whole map at once. Civil law systems across Europe and beyond grew from this frame, so the book still earns study.
mr-justice-raffles-pg9806:
E. W. Hornung's 1909 novel brings back Raffles, the gentleman thief, and his friend Bunny. The contents list nineteen chapters with names like Camilla Belsize and Corpus Delicti. Cricket, crime, and court all appear in the titles. Bunny narrates, as in the earlier Raffles books.

Raffles moves through London society as a sports hero. In secret he plans burglaries against the rich who host him. Bunny helps, doubts, and records each risk. The chapters mix matches, thefts, and narrow escapes. This Project Gutenberg text gives the full chapter list up front, so readers can see the shape of the plot at once.
my-novel-volume-06:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's sixth book opens with Mr. Caxton at his most abstract. Life, he says, comes whole or in fractions. A man's whole life is what he holds alone in his study. His shared life is sliced up by all who need him.

Captain Roland growls that he grasps not a word. Caxton explains with a locked door and a round sum of cash. Each friend dips a finger in the bag, he says. Some take much, some little, and some none at all. The chapter turns a family joke into a small philosophy of self, fame, and use.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
Volume six of The Ocean of Story, in the Penzer edition from 1924, presses Tawney's Kathasaritsagara past its midpoint. Penzer's comparative notes follow single motifs, like the life-token, through dozens of literatures. His learning can startle, yet the tales themselves stay brisk and bright in Tawney's English. The Sanskrit original ranks among the longest poems of India, and its scale is the point. An ocean is not read; it is sailed, story by story. Volume six keeps a fair wind for that voyage.

Admissions climbed steadily across the period, reaching their highest level in the first ten months of 2025. Men accounted for slightly more than half. Daniele Maria do Nascimento led a 2026 experiment on using microwave radiation to disinfect bean seeds against anthracnose, a fungal disease of common bean that travels in infected seed. Chemical fungicides are the usual control, but they risk resistant strains and environmental harm. The team exposed seeds infected in the lab to two microwave frequencies for thirty, forty-five, or sixty seconds and tracked both fungus and seed germination.

Longer exposure at the higher frequency cut infection to very low levels but killed the seeds outright, destroying germination. A shorter treatment at the lower one struck the better balance, cutting fungal incidence while keeping germination high. Microwave treatment can strongly suppress the fungus, the authors conclude. But parameters must be tuned with care so disinfection does not cost the seed its life, the condition for any practical use by growers.

paul-clifford-volume-06:
Volume 6 of Paul Clifford opens at chapter twenty-eight with the gang around a small fire. Pepper teases MacGrawler, the Scottish cook to the robbers, and Tomlinson and Long Ned trade insults about Scotland. MacGrawler's patriotism stings at every joke.

The comedy sits beside the danger, since these are highwaymen between expeditions. Lytton keeps the talk sharp and the thieves oddly likeable. Through the banter the book's question persists: whether men like these are villains by nature or by the making of the world that raised and now hunts them.
pelham-volume-06:
Volume 6 of Pelham turns from drawing rooms to a murder hunt. The country is in confusion, and the officers of justice search everywhere for the killers. Thornton and Dawson are examined at length and discharged, since no evidence touches them. A glove found in a shed seems to confirm their story.

Suspicion falls instead on a muffled horseman seen near Newmarket, whom witnesses describe as tall, short, and everything between. Pelham, whose own evidence pointed to that horseman, leaves Chester Park for London with a heavy heart. Reginald Glanville, his friend, stands at the centre of the mystery closing in.

plos-pbio-0020006:
Ajit Janardhan, Tomek Swigut, Brian Hill, and co-workers studied an HIV protein in PLOS Biology in 2004. The protein, Nef, helps HIV spread and weaken the immune system. The team found that Nef grabs a pair of host proteins, DOCK2 and ELMO1, inside immune cells.

That grip switches on a protein called Rac and changes how the cell moves. Infected T cells then fail to move toward chemical signals as they should. A virus that slows the movement of immune cells gains room to spread. The finding maps one exact contact HIV makes with its host. Contacts like that are possible drug targets, since blocking them might restore normal immune cell behavior.
plos-pbio-0020106:
Robert M. Sapolsky and Lisa J. Share reported a case of animal culture in PLOS Biology in 2004. A troop of wild baboons in Kenya changed its social style after many of its most aggressive males died. The troop stayed calmer than baboon troops usually are, and the calm lasted for years.

Young males who later joined the troop picked up the relaxed style, which shows the behavior was passed on socially, not by genes. Low-ranking males faced less stress, and grooming replaced much of the fighting. The study became a touchstone for debates on animal culture. It shows that even a famously rough primate society can shift, and stay shifted, through learning.
plos-pone-0000006:
Qizhou Lian and co-authors reported in 2006 on a search for cells that could seed new blood vessels. Working with mouse embryonic stem cells, they grew embryoid bodies, small clumps that mimic early development. Inside them they hunted for a rare cell type marked by high CD9 and no SSEA-1.

From single cells of that type, the team raised clonal lines, families of identical cells. Those lines showed endothelial-like potential, meaning they could act like the cells that line blood vessels. A clean, copyable source of such cells matters for studying vessel growth and, one day, for repair work in damaged tissue. The study maps how to find and grow them.
plos-pone-0000106:
Chi Zhang, Timothy F. Carl, Evan D. Trudeau, and their team traced a signal loop in early embryos in PLOS ONE in 2006. The mesoderm is the middle germ layer that forms muscle, bone, and blood. A switch called NF-κB and a factor called Slug reinforce each other in a loop as the mesoderm forms in vertebrate embryos.

Loops like this lock in a cell's fate once it starts down a path. NF-κB is famous for immune roles, so its early embryo job widens its story. Slug helps cells change shape and move, skills the young mesoderm needs. The study shows how old tools get reused in development, and it gives embryo research a defined circuit to test.
plos-pone-0000206:
Gonghua Huang, Xiaojin Xie, Yan Han, and colleagues published this immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Amphioxus is a small sea animal often used to study the ancestors of vertebrates. The authors report finding lymphocyte-like cells and lymphoid-related genes in it, signs of the raw material of the adaptive immune system.

Adaptive immunity, with its targeted antibodies and memory cells, was thought to appear with vertebrates. Hints of its parts in amphioxus suggest a twilight zone before the full system emerged, as the title puts it. The paper helps trace how one of biology's most complex systems was assembled over evolution.
plos-pone-0000306:
Chozhavendan Rathinam and Christoph Klein published this immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gfi1 is a transcriptional repressor, a protein that switches genes off. The authors show Gfi1 integrates signals from cytokine receptors, the antennas for immune messages. In doing so it controls how B cells differentiate, the making of the cells that produce antibodies.

B cell development must balance growth signals against maturation cues. A single repressor that sums those signals is a control point worth knowing. The paper clarifies Gfi1's place in that wiring, relevant to immune deficiencies and blood cancers where B cell development breaks.
plos-pone-0000406:
Caroline Besson and colleagues looked for inherited immune genes behind Hodgkin's lymphoma within families, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The genes in focus are KIR genes, which tune the activity of natural killer cells, part of the immune system's first line of defense. Some families see this lymphoma more than chance would predict.

Studying families with the disease concentrates any inherited signal, making associations easier to spot. The team tested whether particular KIR gene patterns run with the lymphoma in such families. A confirmed link would suggest that the way killer cells are set by birth influences who develops this cancer, and might eventually help gauge risk.
plos-pone-0000506:
Onur Sakarya and colleagues found a piece of animal scaffolding older than animals themselves, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The post-synaptic scaffold is the protein framework that organizes a synapse's receiving side. The team described such a scaffold at the origin of the animal kingdom, in animals like sponges that lack true nervous systems.

If the scaffold predates synapses, evolution built the synapse partly from parts already on hand. Sponges use related proteins for other cell jobs, and nervous systems later recruited them. Studies of this kind rewrite the synapse's origin story. Sudden invention gives way to gradual assembly. The evidence rests on genomes of simple animals sequenced in this era.
plos-pone-0000606:
Jenni E. Pettay and colleagues mined historical records for natural selection acting on women's lives, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. They studied natural selection on female life-history traits in pre-industrial human populations. They asked how social and economic class changed the picture. Did traits like age at first birth relate to reproductive success in the same way across classes?

Old records, from church registers, capture human life before modern medicine flattened its pressures. Finding selection gradients that differ by class shows evolution responding to social structure, not just to climate or disease. Human life-history evolution is hard to observe directly, so archival populations like these are prized evidence.
plos-pone-0000706:
Emmanuel Coudeyre, Florence Tubach, François Rannou and colleagues tested whether a simple booklet changes the course of back pain. Their 2007 PLOS ONE trial gave standardized written information about low back pain to patients with an acute episode. Mass-media campaigns were already known to modify back pain outcomes, which suggested beliefs shape recovery.

The design was a three-month, multicenter controlled trial in primary care, grouped by geography rather than randomized. The outcome of interest was pain persistence. If paper information alone reduces lingering pain, a cheap intervention beats many costly ones. Trials like this speak directly to everyday clinical practice and to how doctors talk about backs.
plos-pone-0000806:
Akihiro Asai, Nita Sahani, Masao Kaneki and colleagues tested a two-hit account of muscle damage in muscular dystrophy, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Duchenne muscular dystrophy features increased muscle damage and abnormal blood flow after contraction, a state called functional ischemia, where working muscle starves itself of blood. The cause-effect relationship between the disease process and that ischemia was unclear.

The title asserts a primary role for functional ischemia, with quantitative evidence for the two-hit mechanism. The team also tested phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor therapy in the mouse model, a drug class that improves blood flow. If faulty flow is one hit, restoring it could soften the disease's second blow to muscle fibers.
plos-pone-0000906:
Fabienne Lesueur, Tiphaine Oudot, Simon Heath and colleagues named ADAM33 as a fresh candidate gene for psoriasis, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Psoriasis is a long lasting skin disorder with many causes, genes among them. An earlier genome scan in forty-six French families with plaque psoriasis had already pinned down one major risk region.

Building on that scan, the team point to ADAM33 as another possible contributor. A candidate is not proof, and the authors present it as a lead to test. Each solid lead matters because psoriasis treatment still relies heavily on broad immune calming. A gene based lead could one day point to a narrower target.
plos-pone-0001006:
Daniel Compagno, Carole Merle, Aurelie Morin and colleagues silenced a hormone receptor to slow resistant prostate cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Prostate tumors first need male hormones to grow, and hormone blocking treatment shrinks them. In time, most return in a castration resistant form with a poor outlook, yet they often keep a working androgen receptor.

The team used small interfering RNA, delivered in living animals, to silence that receptor. Blocking the receptor directly tests whether resistant tumors still depend on it. If they do, the receptor stays a drug target even late in disease. The in vivo step moves the idea beyond cell dishes.
plos-pone-0001106:
Miriam Liedvogel and co-authors tested the light chemistry of a bird magnetic sense protein, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cryptochromes are proposed as the basis of the light dependent magnetic compass in migratory birds. To work as compass sensors, these proteins must show specific physical traits.

Chief among them: being excited by blue light, and forming long lived radical pairs. Those are unstable molecule pairs whose behavior a magnetic field can sway. The team report bird cryptochrome 1a shows both. Each required trait confirmed makes the radical pair theory harder to dismiss. The compass remains one of biology's strangest senses.
plos-pone-0001206:
Why do harmful gene variants linked to late-life diseases persist? Samuel Pavard and C. Jessica Metcalf take up that question for BRCA1, a gene whose variants raise breast and ovarian cancer risk, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their framework is the evolutionary theory of aging.

Natural selection weakens with age, so alleles that kill late in life are selected against only feebly. The authors model negative selection on BRCA1 susceptibility alleles against that background. Their analysis clarifies the population genetics of late-onset diseases. It also tests a classic theory of why organisms age.
plos-pone-0001306:
Analyzing the genome of a single cell requires amplifying its DNA first, and that copying step distorts the result. Kazuya Iwamoto and colleagues systematically surveyed that distortion, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Whole-genome amplification from single cells suffers from allele dropout and preferential amplification, which hamper the quality of results.

Using an oligonucleotide SNP array, the authors measured amplification bias and present an optimized workflow for detecting chromosomal structural alterations in single cells. Single-cell analysis matters for embryos, tumors, and rare cells. Their survey tells users how far the method can be trusted.
plos-pone-0001406:
Philippa Wiggins wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE paper that puts forth a bold claim about water in cells. Many basic cell steps still lack a clear account at the level of molecules. Among them are how cells do work, build proteins, and cut bonds. Wiggins argues that two kinds of water in cells may hold the key.

She sets out how these two water states could drive steps that now seem hard to explain. The paper is a theory piece, not a lab report, and it invites tests. Bold frames like this can spur fresh work, even when parts prove wrong. Readers get a new lens for old puzzles in cell chemistry.
plos-pone-0001506:
Anna Rose Childress and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on brain replies to cues too faint to note. The brain lights up its reward zones for clear signs of sex or of drugs. The team asked whether the same zones react when such cues flash too fast to be seen in a knowing way. Volunteers viewed masked cues during brain scans.

Even unseen, the drug and sex cues lit the reward zones. That means craving circuits can be sparked below full awareness. The finding helps explain relapse when users swear they felt no urge. It also urges care in how cue based therapies are built and timed.
plos-pone-0001606:
Christopher Guest and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a kinase in human white blood cells. These cells, called monocytes, can take on many states to meet threats in the body. What sets their state was still partly unknown. The team found a calcium linked kinase is made by these cells and shapes their state.

When the kinase is active, the cells lean to one profile of replies. When it is curbed, the profile shifts. That makes the kinase a dial for immune tone. Dials like this are prize targets for drugs that calm or rouse immunity as the case demands.
plos-pone-0001706:
Vijayakrishna K. Gadi, Kathleen E. Malone, Katherine A. Guthrie, and their co-authors ran a case-control study of pregnancy cells and breast cancer in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Having been pregnant is known to lower breast cancer risk. Pregnancy also leaves small numbers of fetal cells living in the mother, a state called fetal microchimerism, and those cells stay immunologically active.

The team compared women with breast cancer and women without, measuring fetal cells in their blood. The full text gives the cell counts and the risk comparison. If fetal cells patrol the mother and help destroy early tumors, that would explain part of pregnancy's protective effect, and cell-based prevention ideas could follow.
plos-pone-0001806:
Sergio Rojas-Galeano and co-authors presented a math method for biology data with thousands of factors in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Protein and genomic profiles contain hundreds or thousands of variables, and finding the key markers among them is a many-factor problem. Noise, redundancy, and cross effects among factors make the search harder.

Their method, iterated weighted kernel functions, estimates which factors are relevant for a pattern. The full text gives the method, the test data, and its success rate against other methods. Reliable marker choice is the bottleneck in turning omics data into medical tests, since most measured factors are noise.
plos-pone-0001906:
Fanny Lanternier and colleagues compared a rare immune illness in adults and children in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In mastocytosis, the body makes too many mast cells, the cells that drive allergic reactions. In adults the illness tends to spread through the body and last, and often links to a gene fault called c-kit 816.

In children the illness mostly stays in the skin and often fades on its own. The team enrolled one hundred forty-two adults with proven cases and set their traits beside those known in children. Clear contrasts in gene faults and spread help doctors judge risk and pick care that fits the age group.
plos-pone-0002006:
Tero Harkonen and co-authors tracked Baltic ringed seals across the seasons, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Ringed seals are key parts of cold sea and lake ecosystems at high latitudes. Yet how they use those harsh waters through the year was little known. The team fitted satellite tags to nineteen adult seals in the Baltic Sea.

The tags logged where each seal went and how it dove, season by season, building an activity budget for the year. Such budgets show when seals feed, rest, and haul out, and which waters matter most at each time. That guides protection of a species pressed by ice loss and human use.
plos-pone-0002106:
Anthony Little and co-authors asked whether face symmetry tracks how male or female a face looks, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Many animals display and assess multiple signals at once. Two traits widely studied are symmetry and sexual dimorphism, the gap between male and female form. Both have been proposed as cues to heritable fitness benefits, such as fertility.

The team gathered data across cultures in humans and across species in other animals. As the title states, symmetry is related to sexual dimorphism in faces. Linked cues complicate mate choice science: a face can signal quality in several channels at once.
plos-pone-0002206:
Elisabet Josefsson and co-authors pinpointed two building blocks that a staph protein needs to cause disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Staphylococcus aureus is a common bacterium that can turn dangerous. Its surface protein clumping factor A grabs fibrinogen, a blood protein, and earlier work had shown this protein matters in septic arthritis.

The team changed two amino acids in the protein, at positions 336 and 338, to other amino acids. Those small changes broke its role in disease. Pinpointing the exact spots tells drug designers where the protein's grip lies, and where a blocking drug might take hold.
plos-pone-0002306:
David Fouchet and Roland Regoes modeled the dance between two cell types, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. One type is regulatory T cells. The other presents antigens to them. Regulatory T cells keep the immune system tolerant of the body's own tissues and allergens. They also set how strong a response to infection should be, so their control loops matter in health and in autoimmune disease.

The authors built a population dynamics model of adaptive regulatory T cells meeting antigen presenting cells. Feedback between the two decides whether a response grows or is held down. A mathematical account like this can predict behavior that single experiments on one cell type cannot reveal.
plos-pone-0002406:
In 2008, Bonevski and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Billie Bonevski, Amanda Wilson, David A. Henry, and others. Its subject is an Analysis of News Media Coverage of Complementary and Alternative Medicine. To examine the accuracy and adequacy of lay media news stories about complementary and alternative medicines and therapies.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002506:
A research team led by Timinszky reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Gyula Timinszky, Miriam Bortfeld, Andreas G. Ladurner, and others. Its subject is repression of RNA Polymerase II Transcription by a Drosophila Oligopeptide. Germline progenitors resist signals that promote differentiation into somatic cells.

This occurs through the transient repression in primordial germ cells of RNA polymerase II, specifically by disrupting Ser2 phosphorylation on its C-terminal domain. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002606:
Work from Davey and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Victoria J. Davey, Robert J. Glass, H. Jason Min, and others. Its subject is effective, Robust Design of Community Mitigation for Pandemic Influenza: A Systematic Examination of Proposed US Guidance. United States guidance for a flu pandemic includes isolation and antiviral treatment of ill persons.

It also includes voluntary quarantine of household members, social distancing, and school closure. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002706:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Dorine W. Swinkels and colleagues addresses advances in quantitative hepcidin measurements by Time-of-Flight mass spectrometry. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Dorine W. Swinkels, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Assays for the detection of the iron regulatory hormone hepcidin in plasma or urine have not yet been widely available. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002806:
Liang Chen led a team whose 2008 PLOS ONE article deals with identify alternative splicing events based on Position-Specific evolutionary conservation. The catalog record names Liang Chen first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The evolution of eukaryotes is accompanied by the increased complexity of alternative splicing which greatly expands genome information. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002906:
Mehrdad Alirezaei, William Kiosses, Claudia Flynn and co-authors linked infected microglia to neuron harm in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Autophagy is the cell's self-cleaning system, and evidence suggests it protects neurons. Damage to neurons is well documented in the brains of people infected with HIV.

The team reports that infected microglia, the brain's immune cells, disrupt neuronal autophagy, and that this leads to neurodegeneration. Inflammation and oxidative stress form part of the backdrop. The work points to protecting the cleanup system as one way future HIV brain treatments might help. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003006:
Debora Arlt, Pär Forslund, Tobias Jeppsson and co-authors estimated habitat-specific growth of a farmland bird population in 2008. Judging whether a species will persist in patchy landscapes needs the effects of habitat on both reproduction and survival. Averages across habitats can hide sinks where numbers fall.

The team used a matrix population model for northern wheatears living on farmland. That yields separate growth rates by habitat type. Published in PLOS ONE, the approach shows conservationists which patches truly support the population and which only look suitable. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003106:
Xiaowei Sylvia Chen, W. Timothy White, Lesley Collins and co-authors found spliceosomal RNAs in Giardia intestinalis by computer search in 2008. RNA processing other RNAs is general in eukaryotes, but how ancestral it is was unclear. Pre-messenger RNA splicing is one of the most important such mechanisms, catalyzed in most eukaryotes by the spliceosome.

Giardia branches deep in the eukaryote tree. Identifying four spliceosomal small nuclear RNAs there pushes splicing's origin further back. Published in PLOS ONE, computational finds in a gut parasite inform the early evolution of all complex cells. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003206:
Satoshi Naganawa, Masaru Yokoyama, Teiichiro Shiino and colleagues study a variable loop of HIV-1 in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The third variable region, V3, of the HIV-1 envelope gp120 subunit helps determine which coreceptor the virus uses and how the host antibody response sees it. Positive charge in V3 plays a key role in that coreceptor choice.

The team test how the net positive charge of the V3 sequence in strain CRF01_AE regulates viral sensitivity to humoral immunity. Readers learn how a small charge change can alter antibody attack. That matters for vaccine design, since envelope traits decide what antibodies must overcome.
plos-pone-0003306:
María Berdasco and co-authors study gene shutdown in young plant cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Plants must keep some cells undifferentiated, able to regrow tissue or make new plants from cuttings. Marks on histones, the spools DNA wraps around, help hold that flexible state. The team used genetic and drug tests on the model plant Arabidopsis.

The title reports heavy DNA methylation at gene promoters and gene repression in these undifferentiated cells. Readers see methylation lock genes off while cells stay able to regrow. Those controls matter for plant cloning and crop work.
plos-pone-0003406:
Yu Sun, Huai Li, and Ying Liu compared gene activity in stem cells across species in 2008. Embryonic stem cells can turn into many cell types as an embryo grows. Genes do not switch on one by one; they move in groups. The authors looked for gene groups whose joint activity stayed the same across species.

Those shared groups point to old, conserved rules for cell change. They guide stem cells as they pick a final cell type. Finding the shared rules could steady efforts to grow tissues in the lab. The paper treats evolution as a filter for what truly matters.
plos-pone-0003506:
Björn Friedrich and co-authors linked a gene variant to insulin release in this 2008 study. The gene, SGK1, makes a kinase switched on by serum and stress hormones. That kinase also plays roles in salt balance. Three European study groups took part in the work.

Variation in SGK1 tracked with differences in insulin secretion. The pattern appeared across the TUEF, EUGENE2, and METSIM studies. Consistent results across groups strengthen the claim. SGK1 now stands as a candidate gene for type 2 diabetes risk. Three groups agreeing makes a gene claim far harder to dismiss.
plos-pone-0003606:
Catherine J. Auger and Robin M. Forbes-Lorman studied a hormone's calming effect in male rats in this 2008 paper. Progesterone can reduce anxiety-like behavior in many animal tests. It acts by binding classic progestin receptors inside cells. Whether that route explains the calming effect was the question.

Their work tied the reduction in anxiety-like behavior to the progestin receptor. Blocking that receptor pathway changed the hormone's effect. A reproductive hormone thus steadies behavior through a named molecular route. The result clarifies how progesterone reaches the anxious brain. Anxiety disorders are very common. Calm without sedation is a long-sought goal for drug makers who study hormone routes like this one in male rats.
plos-pone-0003706:
Marybeth Langer, Alexander Malykhin, Kenichiro Maeda, and colleagues published this anthrax study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Inhaled anthrax can kill through runaway inflammation as much as through the germ itself. The authors suspected peptidoglycan, a mesh in the wall of Bacillus anthracis, of driving that response.

They purified the wall component and exposed human monocytes, a type of immune cell, to it. The peptidoglycan set off an inflammatory response through the p38 MAP kinase pathway. The finding names a bacterial building block behind the deadly inflammation of inhalation anthrax. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008.
plos-pone-0003806:
Mark B. Bain, Nuanchan Singkran, and Katherine E. Mills published this environmental study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Managing a great lake means juggling public interests, living ecosystems, and changing water conditions at a large scale. Lake Ontario's water levels are regulated, and each plan helps some users while hurting others.

The authors compared the impacts of seven water level management plans for the lake. Their integrated ecosystem assessment projects effects across ecological and human measures together. The framework shows how to run a great lake for people and nature at the same time.
plos-pone-0003906:
Soohyun Lee, Simon Kasif, Zhiping Weng, and co-authors examined gene data inside variable DNA regions in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns single-letter DNA changes called SNPs. Such markers are used widely in genetics and health studies. By habit, markers failing a balance test were thrown out of analyses.

The authors focus on regions where DNA copy counts differ between people. Extra or missing copies can make good markers look unbalanced. Their analysis warns against discarding markers in those regions too fast. The guidance helps genetics studies keep real signals they once dropped. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004006:
Xavier Gigandet, Patric Hagmann, Maciej Kurant, and co-authors weighed trust in MRI brain wiring maps in 2008. Diffusion MRI tractography draws the brain's white matter connections. Checking whether those drawn fibers are real remains hard. False connections could mislead both research and surgery.

Their PLOS ONE article proposes ways to estimate confidence in each connection. A confidence level tells users which links to trust most. That honesty makes tractography safer for clinical planning. It also helps brain network studies weigh strong and weak links. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004106:
Yuchuan Zhou, Min Zheng, Qixian Shi, and co-authors described a sperm protein from the epididymis in 2008. Sperm must mature in the epididymis before they can fertilize eggs. That final readiness step is called capacitation. Roles of epididymal proteins in the process were little known.

Their PLOS ONE article reports a secreted protein named HongrES1. It is made specifically in the epididymis of their study animals. The protein critically regulates capacitation and male fertility. Losing it impairs the sperm's ability to fertilize. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004206:
Valentina Mangano and colleagues published this malaria genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Interferon regulatory factor 1 is a transcription factor with wide roles in the immune system's gene networks. It is a critical mediator of interferon gamma signalling and a major player in the response to infection.

Because of that record, the gene was a candidate for influencing severe malaria. The team tested it in child-parent trio studies across three African populations. They report a lack of association: the gene did not track with severe malaria. A clear negative result like this steers the search for malaria's genetic factors elsewhere.
plos-pone-0004306:
Anton Nikolaev and colleagues published this vision study in PLOS ONE in 2009, the second of a pair. Retinal networks must adapt constantly to present the changing visual world to the brain at its best. In the companion paper, the team showed that adaptation improves how the fly eye represents naturalistic stimuli over time.

Here they test the hypothesis that this adaptation results from different mechanisms at several synaptic connections within the network. Working in the Drosophila eye, they separate the contributions of those connection points. The pair of papers shows a small eye solving a big problem: keeping vision sharp as light changes.
plos-pone-0004406:
Malaria parasites make a vitamin cofactor they cannot live without. Ingrid Müller, Fang Wu, Bärbel Bergmann, and co-authors target that pathway in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. The parasite Plasmodium falciparum synthesizes pyridoxal 5-phosphate during its blood stage.

The parasite also has an enzyme to activate B6 vitamins salvaged from the host. The authors propose poisoning PLP-dependent enzymes as a new strategy against the parasite. Hitting a cofactor the parasite must make or activate could yield new drugs. Fresh targets matter as resistance spreads. Enzymes that need PLP span many pathways, widening the strategy's possible reach.
plos-pone-0004506:
Geometric patterns in cancer tissue are presented as a window on a biological magnetic field by Jairo Diaz, Mauricio Murillo, and Natalia Jaramillo in PLOS ONE in 2009. In earlier work the team described crystal-like structures in diseased human tissue. They call them geometric triangular chiral hexagon crystal-like complex organizations.

Here they gather those observations into a framework built from collagen type I, a structural protein, and blood vessels. They propose that these parts form an invariant geometric attractor, a stable pattern, in cancer tissues. The claim is unusual and the framing is the authors' own. Readers get a record of the patterns the team reports, and their attempt to link tissue geometry to magnetic effects in tumors.
plos-pone-0004606:
Green tea compounds rescued mouse brains from the effects of an extra gene linked to Down syndrome, report Faycal Guedj, Catherine Sebrie, Isabelle Rivals, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene is DYRK1A. People and mice carrying an extra copy of it show altered brain development. They also show learning impairments that model those seen in Down syndrome.

The team gave green tea polyphenols, plant compounds from tea, to mice with the extra gene. The treatment rescued brain defects induced by the gene's overexpression, as the title reports. Earlier brain scans and tissue studies had mapped those defects in detail. A safe dietary compound that offsets a single gene's overdose is a promising lead for Down syndrome research.
plos-pone-0004706:
Panagiota Foteinou and colleagues used a computer model to test how steroid drugs calm whole body inflammation, in PLOS ONE in 2009. When inflammation starts, cell signals switch on a master factor that drives the response. If that drive is too weak or too strong, the body can fail to fight germs or harm itself.

The team built a math model of the master switch and its control loops. They then tested steroid effects inside the model rather than in patients. Models like this can screen dose ideas before trials. They also show where a drug may help or backfire.
plos-pone-0004806:
Elizabeth Machado and colleagues reported emergence of primary NNRTI resistance mutations without antiretroviral pressure in a treated child, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Use of antiretrovirals during pregnancy drastically reduced perinatal HIV transmission rates worldwide. As a consequence of widespread use, transmission of drug resistant strains from mothers to babies is increasing. Complicating early treatment choices for infected infants in many medical settings.

Ultra sensitive methods detected resistance in the studied child case. Primary resistance arose without direct drug pressure on the child virus. Such hidden resistance can cause first regimen failure. Baseline testing matters even for young children. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004906:
William Hennah and David Porteous showed the DISC1 pathway modulates neurodevelopmental, synaptogenic, and sensory genes, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genetic and biological evidence supports DISC1 roles across major mental illnesses including schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Evidence for interplay between DISC1 variants and interacting loci prompted output review of pathway effects on genes governing brain growth. Synapse formation, and sensory perception in cellular models.

One risk gene influences broad working programs. Network effects explain pleiotropic psychiatric outcomes. Pathway thinking supersedes single gene thinking. Drug targets may lie downstream. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0005006:
Saliva carries a natural antiviral protein called SLPI. At normal levels in saliva, it blocks HIV-1. How it shields cells was unclear. Bénédicte Py and colleagues found its landing sites in PLOS ONE in 2009. They identified two cell-surface proteins as its receptors. They are the phospholipid scramblases 1 and 4.

The scramblases sit in the cell membrane. They also interact with CD4, the doorway HIV uses to enter cells. SLPI docking there may explain its antiviral punch. The study maps a natural defense in fine detail. It could inspire new ways to block HIV at the cell surface.
plos-pone-0005106:
The tongue's sweet sensor also lives in the pancreas. There it may taste sugar in the blood. Yuko Nakagawa and colleagues studied it in PLOS ONE in 2009. They worked in MIN6 cells and mouse islets. The receptor's expression was checked first. Then its function was tested in insulin-making beta cells.

The sweet taste receptor activated calcium signaling. It also activated cyclic AMP signaling. Together those systems stimulated insulin secretion. The pancreas can, in effect, taste sweetness. That adds a sensor to blood-sugar control. It may respond to sweeteners as well as sugar. The finding links taste machinery to metabolism. It opens questions about artificial sweeteners and insulin.
plos-pone-0005206:
Spotting one marked protein in a single cell is routine, but reading many marks at once is hard. Fluorescent tags have broad, overlapping colors, which limits how many can be read together. Shachaf and colleagues offered a new tag system in PLOS ONE in 2009 based on Raman scattering.

Their composite nanoparticles boost a scattered light signal that carries a sharp fingerprint. The method detects protein phosphorylation, a key on-off tag, inside single cells. Narrow fingerprints could let labs read far more cell marks at once than fluorescence allows. Tags like these could one day let a lab read a whole panel of cell marks from a single drop of sample at once.
plos-pone-0005306:
Ribosomal protein L22 helps build the large subunit of the ribosome, the cell's protein factory. It also binds RNA and gathers in the nucleolus, the factory's workshop inside the nucleus. Houmani and Ruf mapped what drives both traits in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Clusters of basic amino acids, the positively charged building blocks, contribute to L22's RNA binding. The same clusters help send the protein to the nucleolus. Shared targeting codes like this show how one small protein region can serve two jobs at once. Small marks of this kind, just a few charged parts in a row. Turn up again and again in cell life as address tags that send proteins to the right room.
plos-pone-0005406:
Angiotensin II drives damaging changes in the kidney, but a shorter relative, angiotensin-(1-7), may counter it. That peptide acts through a receptor called Mas. Esteban and colleagues studied the pair's role in renal inflammation in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Kidneys deficient in Mas showed diminished damage in models of renal insufficiency, placing the axis among the key players in kidney inflammation. The counter-regulatory arm of the angiotensin system is a drug target in its own right. Balancing the system may protect kidneys better than blocking one side alone. Kidney harm creeps up on many men and women with high blood pressure. Diabetes, so a built-in brake in the same system that drives the harm is a lead of great worth for new drugs.
plos-pone-0005506:
Morgan Goulding traced cell fates in a snail embryo for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Snails and their kin divide in a spiral pattern, and each early cell is fated to form set parts of the body. In the mud snail Ilyanassa, that map was known only for the first day of divisions.

Goulding extended the map much further, cell by cell. The fuller map shows that some body regions form faster than in related animals. Comparing maps across species shows how development speeds up or slows down as animals evolve new forms.
plos-pone-0005606:
Francisco Álvarez-Blasco and co-authors studied a blood protein gene in women with polycystic ovary syndrome in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The syndrome affects hormone balance, weight, and blood sugar in women before menopause. The protein haptoglobin mops up free haemoglobin, and its forms differ in how well they fight oxidation.

The team asked whether the weaker form of the gene adds to the oxidation and inflammation seen in the syndrome. They compared women with the syndrome across gene forms and measures of sugar control. A gene effect would help sort patients by risk.
plos-pone-0005706:
Chenyu Zhang and Adam Kuspa watched in 2009 how a bacterial invader rewires the power plants of a soil amoeba. The amoeba Dictyostelium serves as a stand-in host for Legionella, the germ behind Legionnaires' disease. The germ survives inside cells that would normally digest it.

During infection, the amoeba's mitochondria cut back on gene activity and even chop up their own ribosomal RNA. Those changes may help the germ feed or hide. Studying them in a simple host reveals tricks the germ likely uses in human lung cells too. Each trick is a possible weak point for future drugs.
plos-pone-0005806:
Carla Ribeiro and co-authors studied in 2009 how a common antibiotic resets gene activity in human airway cells. Azithromycin, taken long-term at low doses, helps patients with certain chronic lung diseases. The benefit seems to come from calming inflammation, not just killing germs.

The team profiled gene changes in well-differentiated airway epithelia after treatment. Pathways for inflammation, fat metabolism, and cell cycling all shifted. Those shifts sketch how the drug soothes airways over months. Knowing the pathways may let doctors mimic the benefit with fewer antibiotic side effects, like resistance.
plos-pone-0005906:
Maria Swanberg and co-authors narrowed in 2009 the gene regions that decide how much nerve damage a strain suffers. When axons are cut, some animals lose far more neurons than others, and genes set that susceptibility. Two regions, Vra1 and Vra2, were known to be involved.

Fine mapping shrank those regions toward the actual causal genes. Knowing them could explain why neurodegeneration varies so much between patients. It also offers targets for protecting axons in diseases from glaucoma to multiple sclerosis. The study is patient genetics: each narrowed interval makes the final gene hunt cheaper.
plos-pone-0006006:
A memory chemical in the brain also answers to immune signals. Virginie Labrousse, Laurence Costes, Agnès Aubert and colleagues explored that link in 2009 in mice lacking the P2X7 receptor, a sensor on immune and brain cells. Their PLOS ONE paper looks at the hippocampus, a brain area vital for place memory, and at two molecules tied to learning.

Mice without the receptor showed weaker spatial memory, matched by low levels of both IL-1beta and c-Fos in the hippocampus. An immune signal thus seems required for normal remembering. The work ties inflammation's tools to memory's machinery and hints that some memory loss may start in the immune system, not in neurons alone.
plos-pone-0006106:
A protein that rises in asthma patients' blood may be written in their genes. Camilla Rathcke, Johan Holmkvist, Lise Husmoen and colleagues checked that link in a large Danish group in 2009. Their PLOS ONE study tests polymorphisms in CHI3L1, the gene for the protein YKL-40, against asthma and atopy in six thousand five hundred fourteen adults.

YKL-40 levels already serve as a marker for asthma and poor lung function. If common variants in its gene also track the disease, the marker gains a causal hint, not just a correlation. A population study of this size can settle modest effects, and its results feed the search for asthma's inherited share.
plos-pone-0006206:
Glioblastoma is among the most common and worst-treated primary brain tumors. Francesca Pistollato and colleagues studied cells grown from such tumors in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They examined a factor called HIF-1 alpha, which responds to low oxygen. They also studied BMP2, a signal that can push tumor cells toward a star-like brain cell fate.

Oxygen levels and BMP2 together reshape how HIF-1 alpha is tuned in these cells. Low oxygen had earlier cast doubt on using BMP signals as therapy. Understanding the tug of war helps judge when such treatment might work. The work adds detail to the search for better brain tumor care.
plos-pone-0006306:
Tuberculosis urgently needs new drugs as resistant strains spread worldwide. Alistair Brown and colleagues tested platensimycin, an antibiotic from soil bacteria, against TB enzymes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The enzymes, called beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthases, build the fatty acids of the bacterium's waxy cell wall.

Blocking wall building is a proven strategy against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The study measures how well platensimycin hits those mycobacterial targets. A natural compound with a fresh target profile is valuable against multi-drug resistant strains. The work is an early step, from enzyme tests toward possible treatments.
plos-pone-0006406:
Electronic noses try to copy animal smell, but they rarely match the original. Amalia Berna, Alisha Anderson, and Stephen Trowell benchmarked e-nose sensors against biology in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The instruments have had limited utility because their discriminating power lags behind living noses and antennae.

The manner in which odour space is sampled explains part of that gap. Bio-benchmarking sets the biological original as the standard to beat. Honest benchmarks steer engineers toward designs that close the gap. Applications from food quality to security depend on better artificial smell.
plos-pone-0006506:
Zuben Sauna, Chinyere Okunji, Ryan Hunt, and colleagues characterized antibodies against a clotting enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. ADAMTS13 is a zinc metalloprotease that cleaves von Willebrand Factor, a protein that helps blood clot. Problems with ADAMTS13 are implicated in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, a serious clotting disorder. The team studied antibodies that are sensitive to the enzyme's conformation, its folded shape.

Shape-sensitive antibodies can reveal when the enzyme changes form. They can also become diagnostic tools for the disorder. Characterizing them is a step toward better tests for patients. The work sits where protein structure meets clinical medicine.
plos-pone-0006606:
Tandis Vazin and co-authors combined factors to grow dopamine nerve cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. One strong way to make these cells from embryonic stem cells uses signals from stromal cells. But defined factors are safer and more clean for medical use. The team present a new mix of factors, which they term SPIE. It drives stem cells toward the dopamine nerve cell fate.

Their title says SPIE promotes this cell fate from human embryonic stem cells. Steady, safe growth of dopamine cells is a key goal for Parkinson's disease cell therapy. People with that disease lose just these cells. A defined mix is a step toward cells that clinics could one day use.
plos-pone-0006706:
Sasan R. Fereidouni and colleagues infected mallard ducks with bird flu viruses in PLOS ONE in 2009. Wild birds may carry the dangerous H5N1 form of avian influenza. Whether they spread it widely is still debated. Ducks commonly catch milder flu subtypes, sometimes several at once. Earlier mild infections might change how a later dangerous infection plays out.

The team gave mallards immunity from low-pathogenic viruses first. Some immunity matched the later virus, and some came from other subtypes. They then exposed the ducks to highly pathogenic avian influenza. Comparing groups showed how prior immunity blunted or failed to blunt disease. The results inform how outbreaks may move through wild duck populations.
plos-pone-0006806:
Suja S. Rajan and David C. Sokal checked old HIV forecasts against what truly hit Malawi in PLOS ONE in 2009. In 1992, a team had charted the epidemic for the years ahead. They used data from the past decade and the standard models of the day. High and low paths framed the forecast. This report sets those paths next to real counts through the year 2000.

Such checks are rare, and they teach a lot. Where the forecast missed, the miss shows modelers what to fix. Malawi's epidemic was watched as closely as any in Africa. Which path came close tells planners how much to trust the next forecast. The check closes the loop on ten years of plans.
plos-pone-0006906:
Tiago F. Outeiro and his team watched dopamine bend the shape of a Parkinson's protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is alpha-synuclein. When its units clump, nerve cells sicken and die in Parkinson's disease. Clumps had most often been caught by round-about means in cells. Soap-based pulls can warp the very thing they aim to gauge.

Dopamine changed the protein's shape on its own. A bent shape may seed the bad clumps. The cells that die first in Parkinson's are the ones that make dopamine. A straight hit of dopamine on the protein could help solve that riddle. The find ties brain chemistry to the disease's mark protein.
plos-pone-0007006:
Roberto Danovaro, Serena Fonda Umani, and Antonio Pusceddu warned about warming seas in PLOS ONE in 2009. All oceans carry marine snow, small clumps of organic matter. Warming surface water can make the water column more stable. That stability can let marine snow merge into huge mucilage aggregates.

The authors link that process to the spread of microbial pathogens. Their focus was the Mediterranean Sea. Mucilage events foul beaches, nets, and marine life. If warming makes them more common, coastal health and tourism both suffer. The paper frames mucilage as a climate change problem, not just a nuisance.
plos-pone-0007106:
Lauren Solomon, Jennifer Li, Nathalie Bérubé, and colleagues tested a chromatin protein in mouse cartilage in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mutations in the human ATRX gene cause developmental defects. These include skeletal deformities and dwarfism. ATRX remodels chromatin, the packaging of DNA. Its actual job in building skeletons was unknown.

The team deleted Atrx in mouse cartilage using a targeted genetic switch. Skeletal development was barely disturbed, as their title reports. A minimal effect is still an answer. It suggests other tissues or partners carry ATRX's developmental weight, steering future work elsewhere.
plos-pone-0007206:
Anette P. Gjesing, Thomas Sparsø, Knut Borch-Johnsen, and colleagues tested gene links to obesity and blood pressure in 2009. Their PLOS ONE study covers 6,514 adult Danes, named in the title in words as more than six thousand adults. Earlier evidence on the ADRB2 gene was unusually unclear and mixed.

ADRB2 makes the beta-2 adrenergic receptor, which affects body fat and blood pressure. Some reports linked single variants to real effects, while others found none. The authors test haplotypes, or inherited variant groups. They find no consistent effect on obesity, hypertension, or related body measures.
plos-pone-0007306:
Masato Abe, Yuka Setoguchi, Tsubasa Tanaka, and colleagues studied membrane traffic control in fruit fly wing cells in 2009. A lipid-making enzyme called class III PI3K regulates vesicular transport at many steps. It produces a lipid signal that marks membranes for sorting inside cells as cargo moves through.

Protein location at distinct membrane domains needs tight regulation. The authors examine a partner protein, Rabenosyn-5, alongside PI3K. They report location-dependent regulation of membrane proteins in Drosophila wing cells. Their work shows the same transport machinery can act differently depending on where a protein sits.
plos-pone-0007406:
Aoife T. Heaslip, Stephanie C. Ems-McClung, and Ke Hu characterized a microtubule-binding protein in a parasite in 2009. The microtubule cytoskeleton gives essential structural support to all eukaryotic cells. These assemblies are built in a spatially and temporally controlled manner to perform very different functions, from cell division to maintaining cell shape.

The parasite is Toxoplasma gondii, which infects many animals and some humans. The authors identify a novel microtubule binding protein, TgICMAP1, in this parasite. Their PLOS ONE characterization adds a part to the parasite's internal skeleton. Such parasite-specific parts can become drug targets.
plos-pone-0007506:
Kevin Gobeske and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on why exercise sharpens the mind. Running and enriched surroundings are known to grow new neurons in the adult hippocampus, the brain's memory hub. They also improve some kinds of learning. The signals that connect exercise to new neurons were unclear. The team tested one pathway, called BMP signaling, in mice.

BMP signaling mediated the effects of exercise on both new neuron birth and cognition. When the pathway's influence changed, the benefits of exercise changed with it. That places a defined molecular chain between behavior and brain growth. A known pathway is something medicine can work with. The study moves the exercise-brain link from folklore toward mechanism. It also suggests new ways to mimic exercise's gains for people who cannot run.
plos-pone-0007606:
Jordi Viñas and Sergi Tudela published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on identifying tuna by their genes. Tunas of the genus Thunnus include the bluefins, among the most valuable and most endangered trade fish in the world. Once a fish is cut into steaks or sushi, sight identification fails. That gap lets protected species slip into trade. The authors set out to validate a genetic identification method for these species.

A validated DNA method gives regulators a firm tool. Samples taken at markets or ports can be assigned to species with confidence. Enforcement of protections for threatened tunas depends on exactly that confidence. Without it, quotas and bans are hard to police. The study is methodological, but its stakes are conservation stakes. Naming the fish correctly is the first step to saving it.
plos-pone-0007706:
Gentaro Kumagai and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests stem cell transplants as a treatment for spinal cord injury. Grafts of neural stem cells after injury have improved movement in rodents. Which cell types help most was still unclear.

The team derived gliogenic stem cells from embryonic stem cells. These cells are primed to become glia, the support cells of the nervous system. After transplant, the cells aided functional recovery in injured animals. The study helps sort which graft cells suit spinal repair, a step toward future human trials.
plos-pone-0007806:
Gangwei Ou and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It studies a toxin made by the cholera bacterium, Vibrio cholerae. Cholera causes severe diarrhea through the gut. One of its weapons is cytolysin, which attacks intestinal cells.

The authors show that cytolysin provokes an inflammatory response in human intestinal cells. A second bacterial product, the protease PrtV, modulates that response. PrtV normally shields the bacterium from tiny predators in water. Inside the gut, it also dials the toxin-driven alarm up or down. The interplay helps explain how cholera symptoms unfold.
plos-pone-0007906:
Yevgeniy Grigoryev and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It maps how immune activation reshapes gene splicing in human T and B cells. Alternative splicing lets one gene yield several proteins. Parts called exons are included or skipped during processing.

Splicing shifts were known to occur when lymphocytes activate. Which genes change, and in what classes, was little known. The genome-wide analysis found distinct classes of alternatively spliced genes. The catalogue helps immunologists see activation as a splicing program, not just a volume change. It may expose new control points in immune responses.
plos-pone-0008006:
Ney Leite and colleagues solved the shape of a mosquito scent carrier in PLOS ONE in 2009. Aedes aegypti spreads yellow fever and dengue by finding people to bite. Carrier proteins in its antennae grab scent molecules and ferry them to sensors.

The shape showed a pocket where scents sit, capped by a lid that opens or shuts with acidity. That lid may time the grab and release of each scent. A lid that can be jammed is a tempting target for sprays or traps that blind the mosquito to its hosts.
plos-pone-0008106:
Kara Bischoff and colleagues solved the case of a fly wing mutant in PLOS ONE in 2009. The mutant, called xenicid, grows blistered wings. Wing building needs many gene systems in step: pattern, cell fate, cell size, and cell grip all play a part.

The fault lay in a gene called Additional sex combs, cut short at its tail end. Cloned patches of mutant tissue in otherwise normal wings proved the link. That gene is a chromatin regulator, a shaper of gene access, so the case ties wing form to how DNA is packed.
plos-pone-0008206:
Jian Huang and colleagues cataloged small RNAs in a parasite in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Schistosoma japonicum causes schistosomiasis, a serious parasitic disease found worldwide. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that do not code for proteins. They help control gene activity in many living things. Little was known about them in this parasite.

Using deep sequencing, the team searched the whole genome for these microRNAs. A full catalog shows which regulators the parasite carries. Those regulators may shape its growth and its life inside hosts. The list gives future studies a starting point for new control ideas.
plos-pone-0008306:
Koen Nelissen and colleagues mapped shape perception in the monkey brain in PLOS ONE in 2009. The brain extracts three-dimensional shape from flat images. Shading and texture are two monocular cues to depth. The team used contrast-enhanced fMRI in alert monkeys. They mapped which cortical regions respond to each cue.

A parallel human imaging study allowed direct cross-species comparison of the results. Shared regions would point to a common primate system for shape. Knowing where depth structure is computed guides models of vision. The work links single-cue processing to the wider visual system.
plos-pone-0008406:
Rajaie Namas and colleagues studied trauma and shock responses in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Trauma with hemorrhagic shock triggers cytokine-driven acute inflammation. That inflammation is generally considered detrimental to patients. Paradoxically, blood levels of the early cytokine TNF-alpha were elevated in survivors. Other signals such as IL-6 and IL-10 did not show the same pattern.

An adequately robust early TNF-alpha response proved a hallmark of survival. The first hours after admission carried the key signal. A strong early response may organize later healing rather than harm. That flips a common assumption in trauma care.
plos-pone-0008506:
Joao Cordeiro and co-authors study how vaccinia virus spreads in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Vaccinia is a virus related to smallpox. To exit an infected cell, it must cross the actin cortex. That cortex is a mesh under the cell membrane that acts as a barrier. Past work hinted the virus boosts its own spread. A viral protein called F11 plays a part in that process.

F11 blocks RhoA signaling, a system that tightens the actin mesh. Blocking it loosens the barrier and enhances viral spread. The team show this both in lab cells and in a mouse nasal infection. The find clarifies a key exit step for the virus.
plos-pone-0008606:
Mathias Kolliker and co-authors examine parent-offspring conflict in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Across many species, offspring have means to influence parental investment. Young can beg, signal, or compete for food and care. Parental investment thus evolves as an interacting trait. Indirect genetic effects may strongly affect how offspring and parent behaviors coevolve. Theory had focused mainly on offspring demands or parent supply alone.

The authors model antagonistic parent-offspring co-adaptation. Each side adapts in ways that oppose the other's interests. Their dynamics differ from models where only one side evolves. The work refines evolutionary theory of family conflict and care.
plos-pone-0008706:
Prabhakar Putheti, Amit Awasthi, Joyce Popoola, and colleagues showed that human memory T cells can change jobs. Their immunology study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. IL-9 is a growth signal for T cells and mast cells. In mice, certain signals push helper T cells to make IL-9. Whether adult human memory cells could do the same was open.

The team cultured human CD4 memory cells under guiding conditions. The cells began making IL-9, a new identity for them. Flexible memory cells could feed allergies or fight parasites, depending on setting. The finding adds a branch to how doctors picture immune memory.
plos-pone-0008806:
Christopher Williams and Eric Kramer used physics to prize the tapered shape of whiskers. Their analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Whiskers help land mammals feel their way in the dark. Each whisker carries touch forces down to sensors at its base. Real whiskers thin toward the tip rather than staying uniform. Whether that taper improves sensing was the question.

Their mechanical analysis compared tapered and straight shafts. A taper spreads signals in ways that sharpen touch information. The geometry acts like a built-in signal processor. Engineers designing artificial touch sensors can borrow the same trick.
plos-pone-0008906:
Karan Mangla, David Dill, and Mark Horowitz stress-tested computer models of the yeast cell cycle. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Living cells must keep division timing steady despite noise. Modelers often update every signal in a model at once. That tidy choice hides real timing variation between steps. Asynchronous updating, where steps fire at varied times, is more realistic. Budding and fission yeasts offered two classic models to compare.

Both cycles kept working under sloppy, varied timing in their tests. Robust timing may be a built-in feature of cell cycle design. Modelers can trust these models further than feared. The result also suggests real cells tolerate noisy clocks well.
plos-pone-0009006:
Michael Suits and co-authors took the portrait of a sugar-cutting enzyme from a strep bacterium, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The bacterium, Streptococcus pyogenes, causes strep throat and worse infections. Its enzyme, an alpha-mannosidase, snips mannose sugars off larger molecules. The enzyme belongs to the GH38 family, versions of which work in human cells too.

The team solved the enzyme's three-dimensional structure. They also measured how fast it cuts its sugar targets. The structure shows the shape of the cutting site in fine detail. Comparing bacterial and human versions may help design drugs that hit only the germ's copy.
plos-pone-0009106:
Robert Friesen and co-authors tested a new class of antibodies against severe flu in ferrets, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Circulating H1N1 viruses had grown resistant to oseltamivir, the leading flu drug of the time. Highly dangerous bird flu strains added a second, pandemic threat. Fresh ways to control influenza were urgently needed by health officials.

The antibodies were given before infection and again after it had started. Ferrets were protected by the dose given ahead and helped by treatment after. Antibodies that can both prevent and treat flu are rare and valuable. They could be stockpiled as backup for a pandemic when vaccines lag behind.
plos-pone-0009206:
Ian Stevenson and Konrad Körding published this neuroscience methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neuroscientists want maps of how neurons influence each other. Different recording tools capture that activity at very different speeds. Spike records resolve far less than a millisecond, while other methods blur time much more.

The authors asked whether maps built at one time scale agree with maps built at another. If the maps match, results from slow and fast tools can be compared fairly. If they differ, each method may be telling a different story. Their analysis of functional connectivity across time scales helps researchers know how much trust to place in each kind of map.
plos-pone-0009306:
Guillaume Calmettes and co-authors published this heart study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Low oxygen, or hypoxia, strains the heart and underlies many common diseases. Bodies can adapt to long-term low oxygen, gaining a measure of resistance. Understanding that adaptation could help doctors protect hearts during sudden oxygen loss.

The team studied mice kept in chronic low oxygen. Their hearts regulated energy supply better than unadapted hearts. That improved control countered the disturbed energy balance that hypoxia usually causes. The work shows adaptation is not just endurance; it rewires how the heart manages fuel.
plos-pone-0009406:
Jeffrey Brown and C. James McKnight published this cell structure study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The brush border lines the gut's absorbing surface. It is built from microvilli, finger-like projections about one micrometer long. Thousands of them stand in neat hexagonal arrays on each cell.

The authors present a molecular model of the skeleton inside those fingers. The model also explains how the whole border is organized. A working model of this tiny machinery clarifies how the gut maximizes its absorbing area. It also helps explain what fails in diseases where the brush border breaks down.
plos-pone-0009506:
Nisha Yadav and co-authors applied statistics to an ancient script in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Indus script comes from a Bronze Age culture in South Asia. No one has yet read it. Some scholars doubt the signs form true writing at all. The team used n-gram methods, which count how often symbol pairs and chains occur.

Patterns in those counts can be compared with known writing systems and with non writing sign sets. Their analysis probes whether the Indus signs behave like language. Results of this kind cannot yet translate the script. They can, though, test claims about its basic nature with numbers instead of opinion.
plos-pone-0009606:
Ronnaug Solberg and co-authors profiled blood chemistry in pigs in PLOS ONE in 2010. When the body is starved of oxygen, doctors have few good tests to track the damage. That gap matters most for newborns after a hard birth. The team used pigs, whose bodies respond much like ours. They measured hundreds of small molecules in blood during oxygen loss and revival.

The pattern of molecules shifted in clear ways as oxygen fell and returned. Some molecules tracked cell injury and recovery closely. Those are candidates for early warning tests. Better tests could guide the first critical minutes of resuscitation, in pig studies now and perhaps in care later.
plos-pone-0009706:
Fragile X syndrome is a genetic condition tied to autism and social difficulties. Marjelo Mines and colleagues studied a mouse model of the syndrome for PLOS ONE in 2010. They focused on GSK3, an enzyme that acts like a switch inside cells.

The enzyme shaped how the mice behaved with other mice. It influenced which companions they preferred and how anxious they acted during meetings. Social symptoms are central to both fragile X and autism. Tying one enzyme to those behaviors offers a target for future treatments. The work adds a molecular clue to a behavioral puzzle.
plos-pone-0009906:
A protein that helps cells take in fats also shapes how cholesterol leaves the body. Pin Yue and colleagues studied mice that lack that protein entirely. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The missing protein is CD36, and the mice are called CD36 null. Without it, the liver secreted more apoA-I, a building block of good cholesterol particles. ApoA-I is the main protein in HDL, the good cholesterol carrier. The mice also showed enhanced peripheral efflux of cholesterol and phospholipid. The findings redraw the map of how cholesterol exits tissues.
plos-pone-0010006:
Kylie Swisher and Roy Parker studied yeast cell structures in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. When cells face stress, they gather loose RNA and proteins into clumps called stress granules and P-bodies. These clumps help control which messages get translated into protein and which get broken down.

The authors located five proteins, Pbp1, Pbp4, Lsm12, Dhh1, and Pab1, in the common yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. They tested where each protein sits and what each one does to stress granules. One of them, Pbp1, links to a human protein tied to nerve disease, so yeast findings may carry wider lessons.
plos-pone-0010206:
The authors were Burkhard Poeggeler, Kumar Sambamurti, Sandra Siedlak, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested a natural compound against aging damage. Aging has many drivers, but reactive oxygen species are widely seen as major contributors. Mitochondria, the cell's power plants, make most of those harsh molecules, so they sit at the center of aging theories.

The team found a novel endogenous indole, a compound the body itself makes. It protected rodent mitochondria from damage in their tests. It also extended lifespan in rotifers, tiny aquatic animals used in aging research.
plos-pone-0010406:
Cees van den Wijngaard and colleagues asked whether symptom tracking can spot local outbreaks, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Health agencies increasingly watch patterns of illness reports to catch unusual events early. Critics doubt such watching helps at the small, local scale. The team tested it on outbreaks of lower airway infections. They checked whether alarms fired for real outbreaks without drowning staff in false ones.

A system that cries wolf loses trust fast in practice. Balancing early warning against noise is the core design problem. Their evaluation speaks to towns deciding whether to invest in such systems. It also clarifies what syndromic data can and cannot do. Watching symptoms is cheap, but only useful if the signal beats the noise.
plos-pone-0010506:
Swaminathan Sethu, Peter Pushparaj and Alirio Melendez linked an enzyme to inflammation in a mouse model of peritonitis in PLOS ONE in 2010. The signal TNF-alpha drives many inflammatory diseases. The team had shown in dishes that TNF-alpha uses an enzyme, PLD1, to switch on an inflammatory master control. They now tested that link in living mice. The model inflamed the abdominal lining, mimicking a serious human condition.

PLD1 proved necessary for the full inflammatory response in the animals. Confirming a dish result in a body is a key step toward drug development. Enzymes like PLD1 are druggable, unlike some signaling proteins. This study supports PLD1 as a target in TNF-driven diseases. It also maps one route from signal to inflammation.
plos-pone-0010606:
Brigitte Bollag and colleagues studied a small protein made by JC virus, in PLOS ONE in 2010. JC virus lives quietly in many people and rarely causes harm. Its small t protein was known to matter, but its role in copying viral DNA was vague.

The team showed the small protein grabs two host control systems, PP2A and the Rb family. Viruses missing a working small t copied their DNA poorly. Those grabs push infected cells toward a state that favors virus growth. The details help explain how a mostly silent virus can turn dangerous when immunity fails.
plos-pone-0010706:
Steven Jackson and colleagues mapped the brief windows when stem cells heed growth signals, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Embryonic stem cells can be guided toward gut and other inner tissues by timed doses of signals. Three signal families, BMP, Wnt, and activin, do much of that guiding in the early embryo.

Each signal worked only during its own time window in the dish. Too early or too late, and the same dose did little. The windows overlapped in a set order. Recipes for growing replacement tissues depend on such timing charts, since the right signal at the wrong hour makes the wrong cell type.
plos-pone-0010806:
Olga Alekseyenko, Carol Lee, and Edward Kravitz manipulated serotonin neurons in fighting fruit flies, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Male flies fight over food and mates, and their fights escalate in set patterns. Serotonin, a brain chemical tied to mood in people, shapes aggression across many species. Older drug studies in flies could not target serotonin cells precisely.

Genetic tools switched specific serotonin neurons up or down during fights. The changes altered how fast aggression escalated. Fly fights are simple, but their control circuits can be taken apart gene by gene. What those circuits teach may explain why the same chemical steadies some tempers and not others.
plos-pone-0010906:
Birgit Fogal, Carolyn McClaskey, Sha Yan and co-authors published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Premature babies can suffer white matter injury, where the cells that coat nerve fibers with insulation, called oligodendrocytes, are lost or fail to mature. No drug existed to push those cells to grow and wrap fibers, so the team tested diazoxide, a drug that opens potassium channels.

Because calming a cell's electric state seems to favor these cells' growth, diazoxide was a logical candidate. In rat precursor cell cultures and in brain slice cultures, the drug encouraged the precursor cells to multiply and supported the formation of insulation. Fogal and colleagues offer early evidence that a known, approved drug might be repurposed to help repair the injured preterm brain.
plos-pone-0011006:
Sarah Bennett, John Mercer and Mohamed Noor published this fruit fly genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The human BRCA2 gene guards against breast cancer, and its fly counterpart carries a repeating array of segments that bind a DNA repair partner. Their group had found that array apparently expanded in the ancestor of one fly species, Drosophila yakuba, and now examined variation within that species and its relatives.

They found short, typical arrays also circulating in the very species thought to carry the expansion, alongside the long form. Those short forms do not look inherited from a single common source, suggesting independent contractions produced look-alike arrays, a phenomenon called homoplasy. Bennett and colleagues caution that repeat counts can mislead family trees, since the same number can evolve twice. The lesson applies wherever repetitive DNA is used to trace evolution.
plos-pone-0011106:
Rotman, Amado and Kuzminov described a viral stowaway in PLOS ONE in 2010. A bacterial virus called Lula can live quietly inside gut bacteria grown in labs. The authors found it could also spread sideways between cultures without anyone moving it on purpose.

The study details the tactics the virus uses to travel and persist in the lab setting. Unnoticed spread can spoil experiments and confuse results in many labs. Knowing how Lula moves helps labs guard their cultures against it. The work is a practical warning for anyone who grows bacteria for research.
plos-pone-0011206:
Melo, Reyes-Lecca, Vitor-Silva and colleagues studied schoolchildren with two infections in PLOS ONE in 2010. In their study area, many children carry both gut worms and a relapsing form of malaria. Anemia, a shortage of red blood cells, is a common harm of malaria in children.

Children carrying both infections suffered less anemia than expected. That odd partnership complicates policy, since removing worms is normally a clear good. Programs must weigh competing harms before changing deworming plans in malaria zones. The finding urges joined up thinking about children who rarely carry just one infection.
plos-pone-0011306:
Boye, Boye, Pang and colleagues restored vision in mice by gene therapy for PLOS ONE in 2010. The mice lacked an enzyme needed in the retina's light sensing cells, causing blindness from birth. The team delivered a working copy of the gene to the eye and then tested sight in several ways.
