Both functional measures and behavior showed vision was restored in the treated mice. That proof of concept supports gene therapy for inherited blindness of this type. Eye doctors gain a model showing what success should look like before human trials. The work moves inherited retinal disease care toward actual cures.
plos-pone-0011406:
José Nájera and co-authors tested in 2010 whether adding one viral gene could strengthen an experimental HIV vaccine. The vaccine uses a harmless carrier virus, NYVAC-B, to deliver HIV pieces that train the immune system. The team inserted a host-range gene from a related virus, hoping the carrier would persist longer and teach more strongly.

In animal tests, the modified carrier raised stronger immune responses against the HIV pieces than the original carrier did. A small genetic tweak improving the carrier itself is a practical path forward, since the HIV pieces need not change. The result matters for the long search for an HIV vaccine, where many candidates fail for being too weak. Strengthening trusted carriers may be as important as choosing which viral pieces to deliver.
plos-pone-0011506:
Xiaowei Zhang and co-authors mapped in 2010 how brain wiring changes in mice born without the dopamine transporter. The transporter normally mops up dopamine after it signals, so without it dopamine lingers and floods the gaps between brain cells from birth. Such mice are used to model conditions involving dopamine excess, including aspects of ADHD and addiction.

The team found altered neurocircuitry across the knockout mouse brain, showing that lifelong dopamine excess reshapes the wiring itself, not just moment-to-moment signaling. Structure and chemistry thus grow up together, each bending the other. The altered circuits caution model users: behavior in these mice reflects a differently built brain. They also show what sustained dopamine imbalance can do during development, a lesson for any condition or drug that raises dopamine for years.
plos-pone-0011606:
Timothy Sweeney and co-authors studied sepsis in mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sepsis is a severe whole-body reaction to infection, here caused by Staphylococcus aureus bacteria. The team focused on the PGC gene family, which switches on production of mitochondria, the cell's energy factories, and responds when those factories are damaged.

They tracked how each of the three family members behaved during infection. The members were not regulated alike, moving in different directions rather than as one unit. That split response matters because restoring energy supply is a hoped-for route to helping patients survive sepsis.
plos-pone-0011706:
Mohsin Yakub and Mohammad Iqbal surveyed adults in Karachi, Pakistan, for PLOS ONE in 2010. Both high blood lead and high levels of homocysteine, a blood amino acid, have been tied to cardiovascular disease. Average levels of both have been reported as high in the Pakistani population.

The survey measured blood lead and plasma homocysteine in the same people and tested how the two relate. Their cross-sectional results examine whether lead exposure travels with this heart-risk marker. The link, if confirmed, would flag a double burden for communities already exposed to lead pollution.
plos-pone-0011806:
Inna Ovsyannikova and co-authors studied genetic influences on rubella vaccine response, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Recent work suggested HLA genes help determine how strongly people respond to the vaccine. The class III region of that complex holds several immune genes, including those for lymphotoxin alpha, tumour necrosis factor and a leukocyte transcript.

The team examined extended gene combinations, or haplotypes, spanning these genes and their association with vaccine-induced immunity. Their results help explain why the same shot protects people unequally. Genetic prediction of weak responders could guide booster policy for rubella.
plos-pone-0011906:
Clive Rosenthal, Christopher Kennard, and David Soto asked in 2010 whether people can learn a visual sequence without seeing its parts properly. Learning links between items that sit near each other in space and time is a basic feature of memory. Higher-order patterns, where items are separated, can be picked up with or without awareness.

Their study concerns visuospatial sequence learning when the visual input itself is unavailable to awareness. If the brain still registers the pattern, then sequence learning runs deeper than conscious sight. Findings of this kind speak to patients with damaged vision, whose brains may keep learning from material they cannot report seeing.
plos-pone-0012006:
Phillip Gienapp and Juha Merilä tested in 2010 whether Siberian jays are as faithful as their reputation claims. Extra-pair paternity, chicks fathered outside the pair, is common in birds and varies with ecology and social life. Group-living species often show high rates, which made the group-living jays an interesting case.

Genetic testing found no evidence of extra-pair paternity in the Siberian jays studied. A species that truly keeps pair bonds, with fathers investing in their own young, is a valuable exception for testing theories about why cheating evolves elsewhere. The jays' fidelity also fits their cooperative family life, where trust inside the group is the working currency.
plos-pone-0012106:
Sarah Pendergrass, Everett Hayes, Giuseppina Farina, and colleagues studied blood markers in people with a limited form of scleroderma, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In this illness the skin and organs slowly harden, and some patients go on to develop dangerous high pressure in the lung arteries. Checking for that lung problem now needs invasive tests, so a blood signal would be a real advance.

Patients who had the lung complication carried blood signs of inflammation and blood vessel injury that set them apart. Markers like these could lead to simple screening tests that flag risk early. They also hint at how the lung damage starts, which may guide future treatment.
plos-pone-0012206:
Wai-Kin Mat, Hong Xue, and J Tze-Fei Wong reported changes in the genetic code itself, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The code that translates DNA into proteins has kept the same set of building blocks for roughly three billion years, in every known organism. That frozen pattern makes the rare exceptions, where a lab-made or unusual code assigns a new building block, scientifically precious.

The authors describe code mutations in which a bacterium encodes a fluorine-bearing variant in place of a standard one. Each such case tests which parts of the code are truly fixed by chemistry and which are historical accident. That question touches the origin of life and the design of engineered organisms with expanded chemistry.
plos-pone-0012306:
Julia Lee, Puthigae Sathish, Daniel Donaghy, and co-authors studied how pasture grass survives running out of carbon, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A plant cannot move to better conditions, so when drought or cold cuts its photosynthesis, it must ration the sugars it has stored. Using ryegrass, the backbone of temperate pasture farming, they tracked which biological processes the plant adjusts first when carbon runs short.

The grass actively remodels its metabolism to stretch its reserves rather than simply starving. Knowing the survival program helps breeders select grasses that bounce back after drought or hard grazing. For livestock regions, that resilience is the difference between a paddock recovering and a farm buying feed.
plos-pone-0012406:
Jason Noel, Nabil Arrach, Ali Alagely and colleagues tracked how Salmonella bacteria respond to tomatoes, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Outbreaks traced to raw vegetables showed that gut germs can live on and in plants for long stretches before infecting people. The team used a gene-fishing method to see which Salmonella genes switch on inside tomato fruit.

The bacteria answered differently depending on tomato variety and on how ripe the fruit was. Ripeness and breed thus shape how well the germ persists on produce. Food safety rules that treat all tomatoes alike may miss real risk differences, and growers could use variety choice as one more defense.
plos-pone-0012506:
Shengli Zhao, Yang Zhou, Jimmy Gross and colleagues created a mouse line that lights up newborn brain cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Adult brains grow new neurons in the hippocampus, a region for memory, and those newborns may help learning and mood. Studying them has been hard because they blend into mature neighbors.

In the GAD67-GFP mice, young dentate granule cells glow green, so researchers can find and follow them live. A reliable label turns guesswork into direct observation. The tool should speed studies of how exercise, stress, and drugs change adult brain growth, with relevance to depression and memory loss.
plos-pone-0012606:
Raz and co-authors studied brain damage after a stroke-like event in rats. After blood flow to the brain is cut and restored, harmful oxygen radicals surge and kill nerve cells. An enzyme called NADPH oxidase helps make those radicals, yet what switches it on in the brain was poorly known.

Their 2010 paper points to Rac1, a small switch protein, as a key controller of that enzyme after ischemia. When Rac1's role was blocked, damage and memory problems were reduced in their tests. The finding names a possible drug target for limiting harm after stroke.
plos-pone-0012706:
Wu, Zhou, Lan and co-authors followed the signals that let a goat egg cell finish dividing. When an egg divides, a ring of actin and myosin squeezes it into two unequal parts. Their 2010 study used a chemical trigger to start this division in goat oocytes outside the body.

They show the master factor MPF turns on two partners, RhoA and MAPK, to build and tighten the ring. Egg division underpins fertility in farm animals and people alike. Mapping its controls helps explain failed fertilisation and guides breeding work.  Timing of each signal was measured during the division.
plos-pone-0012806:
Wang, Huang and Hsu asked whether stunted growth explains the lasting brain effects of a steroid given to newborns. Dexamethasone is used to help the lungs of babies born too early. Worry has grown that it also harms the hippocampus, the brain's memory centre, over the long term.

Their 2010 rat study separated the drug's growth-slowing effect from its direct effect on synapses, the links between neurons. Untangling the two matters for judging how risky the drug really is. Neonatal care needs that balance to be evidence based.  Synapse strength was measured in brain slices from treated pups.
plos-pone-0335006:
Oluwasegun Akinyemi and co-authors asked what happened to hospital bills for women treated for major depression after Medicaid expanded under the Affordable Care Act. They compared Maryland and New Jersey, two states that expanded coverage, with Florida, which did not. The records covered more than a decade of inpatient stays by women with depression as the main diagnosis.

The two expanding states moved in opposite directions. In Maryland, charges fell compared with Florida, and the drop reached every racial group and insurance type, with the biggest falls for uninsured and Medicaid patients. In New Jersey, charges rose instead. The split suggests that how a state pays hospitals can matter as much as whether it expands coverage at all.
plos-pone-0342806:
Tatiana Maroilley and co-authors describe a Calgary course that gives health science undergraduates real research instead of canned laboratory exercises. Bioinformatics needs fluency in both biology and computing, and few degrees teach the blend. Their 2026 report covers a course-based research experience run across three winter terms at the Cumming School of Medicine.

Student teams investigated how large genetic rearrangements change gene activity in a tiny roundworm, a standard model animal. Students detected the variants, traced their effects in expression data, and presented findings like working researchers. Maroilley and colleagues argue the format scales research training beyond the few students who win laboratory placements, while teaching applied computing on a live question.
plos-pone-0343606:
Iqramul Haq, Md Yusuf Hossain Ador, and Diego Nobrega test whether machine learning can flag unsafe drinking water in Bangladesh, in this 2026 study. The bacterium E. coli signals fecal contamination, but lab testing every household supply is slow and costly. The team used a national survey covering more than six thousand household water samples and trained ten different algorithms to predict contamination from survey information.

About two in five households had contaminated drinking water, with one hill district standing out as the worst hotspot. After the data were balanced to handle the uneven classes, ensemble methods performed best; one boosting model edged out the rest on overall accuracy and caught nearly all contaminated samples. The authors argue such models could let authorities target scarce lab testing where risk is highest.
plos-pone-0344506:
Chongchao Zhang and colleagues propose a login method for electric car charging that keeps checking who is plugged in, rather than checking once at the start. Their scheme, PufCB-Auth, builds a fingerprint from two sources: the unique electrical quirks of the charger's hardware, which cannot be cloned, and the driver's own charging habits. Together these factors guard against stolen passwords and copied credentials.

Habits drift and hardware signals wobble, so an enhanced version refreshes the stored fingerprint over time instead of locking users out. Simulations showed the method verified users accurately with little computing cost, suiting busy public chargers with modest hardware. The authors tested the design against a modern fast-charging standard and present it as ready for real-world trials.
plos-pone-0346606:
Osman Darici, Chanel Cabak, and Jeremy D Wong built a low cost camera system in 2026 that grades walking function without body markers. Standard gait labs are dear and slow, so formal walking assessments happen rarely for older adults.

Three ordinary cameras feed open source tracking software and custom analysis. Against a laboratory marker system in a small test group, step length, step width, and head speed matched very closely. Reports on older volunteers resembled published norms, with room to add extra gait measures. A cheap, automatic setup could bring regular walking checks into ordinary clinics and homes.
plos-pone-0347206:
Seth M. Gibbons and a team of colleagues tested whether DNA floating in river water can track river herring, once-abundant fish now in decline in North Carolina. The murky Neuse and Tar-Pamlico rivers defeat easy counting. Weekly water samples at eight sites during spawning season were checked for herring genetic traces, alongside traditional electric-shock fishing counts at two places.

DNA levels and fish counts rose together during the first three weeks of spawning. Later, DNA stayed high even as adult fish left, likely lingering from eggs, young fish, and the water itself. Upriver sites gave the most consistent signals. The authors say the method suits long-term monitoring of these hard-to-watch rivers.
plos-pone-0347606:
Hanane Abbou and her team read eleven genes in one hundred nine people from Morocco. The genes run the body's own cannabis-like signal web. This web steers pain, mood, and more. The team found one hundred seventy gene forms never seen in print. They then zoomed in on one shift in the chief gene of the web.

In cell models, that shift shook the build of the web's key lock. The lock lost some of its twist and sat less snug. It took a higher-energy, less firm shape. The team says such shifts may change how folk react to drugs based on this plant.
plos-pone-0348206:
Courtney Bir, Jinho Jung, and Nicole Olynk Widmar asked American workers not whether they like remote work, but why. Using a nationally representative survey from late 2021, during the pandemic, respondents repeatedly picked their most and least valued reasons for working from home. The 2026 study then grouped workers by what they prized most.

Balancing the job with caregiving topped the list, followed by saving commute time and money, avoiding illness, and simply liking home. Four camps emerged, centred variously on caregiving, productivity and comfort, multitasking and safety, or no single motive. Remote workers also changed grooming and dress habits. The authors warn employers that one flexibility policy will not fit all.
plos-pone-0348506:
Yuanxiang Peng surveyed five hundred visitors at a major international music festival to test whether going green wins loyalty. The study separates festival green efforts into environmental, social, and economic practices. Then it traces how those practices shape whether visitors praise, return to, and support an event. It looks for the mental steps in between.

All three kinds of practice directly strengthened visitors' supportive intentions, with environmental action carrying the strongest pull. The effect also travelled along chains: green practices raised environmental awareness, awareness raised the value visitors felt they got. That sense of value fed satisfaction, which in turn fed loyalty. Peng advises organisers to treat these practices as a strategic asset that improves the experience itself, not a compliance chore to hide backstage.
plos-pone-0348606:
Qian Yang, Yun Wang, and Mingjun Wu evaluated a staffing change in their hospital's sterile supply department, the unit that cleans and packs surgical instruments. Under the new model, supply staff are posted forward in the operating suite itself rather than serving it from a distance. The team compared a year of the new model against the previous year under the traditional setup.

Instruments needing a second cleaning fell by about two-thirds, packing quality rose, and clinical staff reported higher satisfaction. The first scheduled surgery of the day also started on time far more often. Small logistics changes rarely make headlines, yet in surgery a missing or dirty instrument delays care, so a forward-posted team shows measurable value.
plos-pone-0348806:
Qin Lai and co-workers rate the front faces of old Catholic churches in China's Sichuan and Chongqing region. Built between eighteen forty and nineteen forty-nine, these churches blend Chinese and Western building traditions. Their 2026 study scores sixty-two surviving churches on how their fronts meet their surroundings, their outlines, styles, decoration, and religious expression.

About a fifth of the churches are mainly Chinese in style. Chinese-style fronts still borrowed Western vertical layouts, while Western fronts often added Chinese touches and plain folk decoration. Style, decoration, and religious expression rose and fell together closely. Grading heritage fronts with numbers gives protectors a shared language for deciding what to save and how.
plos-pone-0348906:
Ying Lu and co-authors built a system that watches and listens to miners, then judges whether their emotions have turned unsafe. Tired, angry, or frightened miners judge risks poorly, and mistakes underground can kill. Their model reads two channels at once: the sound of speech, handled by networks that catch both tone patterns and how they unfold over time. It also reads facial expressions, using a compact vision network.

Trained on recordings sorted into five unsafe emotional states, the combined system recognised them with accuracy in the mid-eighties percent range. Small field trials in a working mine suggested the approach can function outside the lab. The authors offer the system as an early warning layer, flagging struggling miners before a poor decision becomes an accident.
plos-pone-0349106:
Palanisamy Angappan and co-workers tackle a shop-floor problem: a tough heat-proof metal alloy that is hard to cut cleanly. The alloy is used in hot settings but hardens fast while being cut and holds heat poorly. In their 2026 study, they test cutting tools marked with tiny laser-made grooves, paired with a semi-solid lubricant, on a computer-run lathe.

Tools with grooves running in straight parallel lines did the best cutting work. They left the smoothest surface, needed the least force, and stayed the coolest of the four tool types tried. The grooves shortened contact with flying metal chips and helped the lubricant work better. Wear checks under a microscope showed rubbing and material spread as the main damage.
plos-pone-0349206:
Antonina Kaczorowska and colleagues asked more than eleven hundred people aged sixty to ninety in southwestern Poland how good their lives feel, using a standard World Health Organization quality of life questionnaire. Scores cover body, mind, relationships, and surroundings. The team then looked for the social traits that separate people thriving in old age from those merely getting by.

Just over half the group rated their quality of life as good. Men scored higher than women on mental and environmental measures, people in relationships scored higher across most areas, and more schooling lifted nearly every score. Good self-rated health and fewer chronic illnesses mattered most of all. The authors urge policy that widens access to education and protects health across the whole lifespan, not only in old age.
plos-pone-0349406:
Mariam Ahmed, Sharon Owino, and co-authors studied a little-known brain receptor, GPR37, to see whether dialing it down changes body weight and blood sugar control. With obesity affecting about forty percent of American adults, fresh drug targets are in demand, and this receptor family supplies many existing medicines. Their 2026 study used mice carrying only one working copy of the gene and measured weight, glucose tolerance, and insulin response.

Male mice with reduced gene dosage weighed less, handled fasting better, and responded more sensitively to insulin than normal males. The effect was sex-biased, showing clearly in males. The authors read this as a previously unrecognized role for the receptor in whole-body energy balance and nominate it for deeper, tissue-specific follow-up as a possible metabolic drug target.
plos-pone-0349506:
Damilola Onietan and colleagues lay out a protocol for mapping research on psychosocial help for teenagers uprooted by war and persecution. Adolescents make up forty percent of the world's forcibly displaced people and carry heavy mental health burdens, yet support programs for them are scattered and unevenly studied. A scoping review will chart what exists before anyone judges what works.

The review will gather studies of refugees, asylum seekers, and internally displaced youth aged ten to nineteen. It will span qualitative, quantitative, and mixed designs, where the intervention aims at psychological well-being or social functioning. The finished map is meant to steer policy and practice toward the gaps, showing which groups and which kinds of help researchers have ignored.
plos-pone-0349606:
Lotte J S Fleurkens-Ewals and co-authors ran a reader study in 2026 on scoring cancer spread inside the abdomen from CT scans. The score guides treatment for cancers that seed the belly lining, and pre-drawn region outlines might help readers agree.

Eighty-two clinicians from nineteen countries scored nine scans, with and without colour overlays marking the regions. Agreement, closeness to the surgical score, confidence, and user experience were compared. The overlays did not significantly improve agreement, the headline the authors report plainly. Negative results like this save hospitals from buying decision aids that feel helpful but do not measurably help.
plos-pone-0350006:
Karina Patasova, Marie Holmqvist, and co-authors hunted for hidden genetic links between systemic sclerosis, a rare autoimmune disease, and the cancers its patients develop at elevated rates. Whole-genome comparisons had found no overall relationship, but averaging can hide local links where effects point in opposite directions. Their 2026 study applied finer methods that test genetic correlation region by region against breast and lung cancers and blood malignancies.

Again, no overall genetic correlation appeared. Zooming in, though, they found twenty-three local regions where the diseases' genetics correlated significantly, some positively and some negatively, exactly the pattern global methods miss. Follow-up analyses probed genes in those regions for shared biology. The authors argue the sclerosis-cancer connection may live in specific genomic neighborhoods rather than across the whole genome.
plos-pone-0350106:
Hye Young Hong and Young Ae Kang led a review of lung patients in Korea. The illness is a slow lung infection from a germ kin to the TB germ. Care takes a year or more of drugs. Many patients quit too soon. The team followed four hundred twenty patients treated from 2010 to 2023. They split those who quit early from those who finished.

Thirty in a hundred quit early. Bad drug side effects raised the odds of quitting a lot. Poor diet did too. Quitters then died at near three times the rate of finishers. Low diet scores also tracked with death. The team urges close watch for side effects and food support from day one.
plos-pone-0350506:
Donrawee Waeyeng and Soisungwan Satarug led a study of diet and kidney health in southern Thailand. People there face long-term contact with two toxic metals, cadmium and lead. Both metals can harm the kidneys. The team asked if eating more plant foods might help. They signed up ninety-six adults aged fifty and over in late 2024.

People who ate more plant foods showed less of a urine sign of kidney cell harm. Those who ate more nuts and seeds did best of all. High metal contact, by contrast, came with signs of kidney stress. The team says plant-rich diets may soften metal harm. They also back the urine test as an early warning tool.
plos-pone-0350806:
Felix A Andong and colleagues studied breeding male village weaver birds in Amurum Forest Reserve, Nigeria, during the costly season when males breed, moult, and fight infection at once. One hundred and forty eight males were grouped by worm infection and moult status. Blood stress balance, blood sugar, and feather colour quality were measured within minutes of capture.

About half the males carried the worms. Infected birds showed strained stress chemistry. Males facing both infection and moult scored worst on sugar control and feather quality by far, beyond either burden alone in direct contrasts. Bright honest signals, the work shows, collapse first when body budgets are doubly drained.
plos-pone-0351106:
Akram Hasanov and four colleagues study the wildest days in energy stock markets — the rare crashes and spikes that standard risk models handle badly, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Using two decades of daily data to early 2025, they estimated how quickly the chance of extreme returns decays for renewable and conventional energy share indices. The method asks, in effect, how many statistical moments of the return distribution even exist.

Both kinds of index showed heavy tails following a power law. Average returns and volatility appear finite and usable, but higher shape measures may be mathematically infinite, which quietly breaks tools built on them. A rolling analysis showed tail risk swelling around major market stresses. Investors in green energy, the authors warn, should plan for extremes that history understates.
plos-pone-0351306:
Markku Kallio and colleagues pooled data on close to sixteen hundred children with confirmed bacterial meningitis in six countries across Latin America, Angola, and Finland. Simple spinal fluid tests at admission, sugar, protein, and white cell counts, were checked against death in hospital and brain outcome at discharge. Such cheap tests could help triage where intensive care is scarce.

Death rose step by step as spinal fluid sugar fell and as protein rose. Children with both very low sugar and very high protein died at a rate near twenty seven percent, versus one percent when both values looked normal. Low white cell counts also warned of danger. Two routine numbers together, the authors show, flag high risk children early.
plos-pone-0351406:
Bian and colleagues audited urine leakage prevention for intensive care patients with catheters in a Chinese hospital in a 2026 study. The team first built audit standards from the best available evidence, then checked real practice with dozens of nurses and patients. Gaps between standards and bedside care were then analyzed for causes.

Audits of this kind sort which failures come from knowledge, staffing, supplies, or habit. That sorting shapes training and workflow fixes in the next phase of the project. Catheter leakage harms skin, comfort, and infection risk, so even small compliance gains matter in units where patients stay for weeks. The baseline review gives the unit a clear starting measure.
plos-pone-0351506:
Long COVID symptoms vary wildly between people, so Su-jin Kim and Jinhee Kim sorted Korean adults with lasting symptoms into natural groups. Their 2026 PLOS One survey covered about six hundred thirty adults whose symptoms had run at least twelve weeks, scoring twenty-six complaints and overall quality of life.

Four profiles fit best. About a quarter had light symptoms overall; the largest group, over two fifths, had moderate problems across many body systems; another group centered on exhaustion that worsens after effort. Quality of life fell as symptom load rose. The authors say clinics should treat these profiles differently rather than handing everyone the same plan.
plos-pone-0351606:
Editorial Note: PLOS One flags an overlap concern between a published study of DNA sequences in ice from Antarctica's subglacial Lake Vostok and a companion paper by the same group. This 2026 note explains that both articles analyze the same two ice cores, which the authors had declared before publication.

The authors say the papers differ in focus: one on the lake's likely living conditions, the other on which species and body processes the sequences suggest. An independent editorial board member reviewed the overlap question. Readers should keep the shared dataset in mind when weighing the two papers' conclusions about life beneath the Antarctic ice.
plos-pone-0351706:
Dinh Thi Nguyen and Loan Thi Ho catalogued the leaf beetles of Cat Ba Island, a limestone island off northern Vietnam, pairing old-fashioned specimen work with DNA barcoding. Shelf islands in Southeast Asia are biological crossroads and among the least surveyed places for insects. Field collecting found thirty-six species-level units across thirty genera, dominated by one large subfamily.

Barcoding sorted the catch into thirty-one genetic clusters, most of them new to the global barcode library, proof of how much diversity sits undocumented on one island. Clock estimates place the main lineages' origins in the Miocene, before the island itself took shape, so the beetles are heirs of mainland forests later stranded by rising seas. For conservation, Cat Ba is not a depauperate offshoot but an archive, and its beetles deserve the archive's protection.
plos-pone-0352206:
Lismaryin Muñoz-Requene, Pedro Sánchez-Zamora, and Rosa Gallardo-Cobos measured how exposed Nicaragua's North Caribbean Coast is to tropical cyclones, town by town. The region is among the country's most storm-hit and poorest, and climate change is loading the dice further. They built a vulnerability index from twelve indicators covering exposure, the fragility of people and housing, and each municipality's capacity to adapt.

The map that emerged is uneven. Bonanza combined high exposure and fragility with weak adaptive capacity, while Waslala showed sturdier structure. Three clusters of towns shared similar risk profiles. A single regional plan would fit none of them well. For disaster agencies, the index names where shelters, drainage, and income support buy the most safety before the next storm season, not after the damage is photographed.
plos-pone-0352506:
Isabel von Känel-Cordoba and seven colleagues gather everything known about the half-distance Ironman triathlon, in this 2026 PLOS ONE systematic review. The event — a swim, a long bike ride, and a half marathon — has boomed worldwide, yet research has trailed the full-distance race. Searching five databases, the team assembled eighty-six studies covering training, nutrition, body measures, weather, and medical issues.

Cycling emerged as the strongest single predictor of finish time. Professional men peaked around age twenty-eight, women around thirty-two, and participation is growing fastest among women and older athletes. Racing temporarily dents immunity and muscles, then recovers. The authors note the field's blind spots: small samples and too few women studied.
plos-pone-0352906:
Rafael Flores and co-authors designed a family of lipoic-acid-derived molecules aimed at a brain receptor tied to neurodegeneration. The sigma-1 receptor is implicated in Alzheimer's disease and related disorders, and diverse, easy-to-make activators are wanted. Their 2026 design follows a three-part recipe: a sulphur-bearing hydrophobic head, a flexible amide linker, and a greasy tail.

Twenty-one molecules were designed, docked in the computer, synthesised, and tested for binding at both sigma receptor types. Three stood out for selective sigma-1 binding in the nanomolar range, though a standard comparison ligand bound far tighter still. Flores and colleagues keep the three as starting leads for a follow-up round of structure tuning.
plos-pone-0353106:
Yinchun Wang and four co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One language study of Chinese scholars speaking academic English. Their focus is hedging, the words speakers use to soften claims. Hedging is a known stumbling block at conferences and defenses. The team built a large corpus of Chinese scholars' spoken English. They compared it with an American academic speech corpus. Verb-based hedges were the focus.

Chinese scholars used far fewer personal stance markers like 'I think.' They used far more shared markers like 'we see.' The authors read this as a strategy that favors group harmony and shared duty. The study does not stop at diagnosis. It builds a classroom module with worksheets to train these forms. The aim is fewer communication failures in high-stakes settings.
plos-pone-0353206:
Limin Tang and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One experiment on licorice stem and leaf silage as cattle feed, tested in laboratory rumen fluid rather than live animals. The team prepared silage at four dry matter levels and followed fermentation over seventy-two hours, measuring gas output, acidity, nutrient breakdown, and the microbes involved. A licorice feed additive was included in the silage.

The batch at fifty-five percent dry matter performed best overall, producing the most gas and microbial protein, breaking down nutrients fastest, and supporting the richest microbial community. Helpful fermentation products also peaked earlier in that batch. Statistical rankings placed it first among the four, and the authors recommend that moisture level for turning licorice stems and leaves into useful dairy feed.
plos-pone-0353306:
Wieland and colleagues compared two advanced methods for fitting random epidemic models in a 2026 study. Epidemic models that include chance events help forecast outbreaks, but working out their settings from data is mathematically hard. The team tested both methods on three standard disease models of rising complexity.

Each method had to recover known settings from data produced by the models themselves. Their strengths differed by model and data richness, giving modelers a practical guide on which to pick. Fast, reliable fitting matters during real outbreaks, when officials need quick forecasts that honestly reflect uncertainty. The comparison saves future teams from choosing a fitting tool blind.
plos-pone-0353506:
Sabah and Alaa presented a self-tuning method for grouping texts by topic in a 2026 study. Modern language models turn text into rich numeric codes, but each model shines in different fields. Older blending methods fix how much each model counts ahead of time, wasting their complementary strengths.

Their framework lets a search algorithm adjust the blend weights as grouping proceeds, with no labels needed. Better blends should give cleaner clusters for tasks like news sorting and routing technical questions. The work targets a quiet but costly step in text systems, where poor grouping early on degrades every later answer. Dynamic weighting offers a path to clusters that fit each collection's own character.
plos-pone-0353606:
Hattan Abutarboush and colleagues report in 2026 on a thin microwave absorber built from printed rings. Their design uses two nested rings on a common circuit board material, with four small stubs placed evenly around the outer ring and a solid metal backing. Keeping the build to one layer was the central aim.

Tests of a made sample matched computer models and showed strong uptake in six separate frequency bands, each above nine tenths of the incoming energy. Lower bands linked mainly to magnetic responses, while higher bands mixed electric effects as well. A simple flat design that handles several bands at once could help with shielding, sensing, and reducing unwanted radar reflections.
plos-pone-0353706:
Natthapon Inta, Annmarie Grealish, and Mary Leamy explore what recovery from mental illness means in Thailand, in this 2026 PLOS ONE interview study. Recovery is a guiding idea in modern mental health care, but its meaning shifts between cultures. They spoke with service users, family carers, and health professionals in primary and community services, then tested the themes in feedback workshops.

Participants described recovery as moving from symptom relief toward hope, meaning, and social connection. Family backing, community acceptance, and trusting relationships with staff were central, while obstacles appeared at personal, family, service, and community levels. From this, the authors propose a recovery support model fitted to Thai culture.
plos-pone-0353906:
Niu and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask whether immune system genes raise the risk of clogged heart arteries in people from Northeast China. The HLA genes help the immune system tell self from invader, and they vary a lot between people. The team compared two HLA genes in about two hundred people, split between those prone to artery clogging and controls.

Dozens of gene variants were counted. Two single variants appeared more often in the disease-prone group, but neither survived strict correction for the many tests run. A paired combination of the two variants, inherited together, was more than twice as common in the disease-prone group. That signal also faded under the strictest correction, though its size was too large, the authors argue, to dismiss as pure noise. They label the pair a candidate risk marker and call for much larger studies to confirm or refute it.
plos-pone-0354206:
Lyu and colleagues, in a 2026 review, work out how much exercise helps depression among middle-aged and older people with Parkinson's disease, and which kinds help most. Earlier trials tested exercise one dose at a time, which hid the shape of the benefit. The team pooled twenty-five trials and modeled dose on a continuous scale, counting weekly energy spent.

Benefit followed a curve, not a straight climb. Gains held across a broad middle band of weekly dose and peaked near its center; at the highest doses the effect turned unstable. Two kinds of exercise stood out: exercise paired with mental training, and mind-body exercise such as tai chi styles, both peaking at the same middle dose. Walking helped only at higher doses, and several other types showed no dependable range. The authors say dose and kind must be prescribed together, like a drug and its amount.
plos-pone-0354606:
Nnaemeka Iriemenam and co-authors tested front-line health staff at seven Nigerian sites for coronavirus antibodies late in the pandemic. Health staff faced the worst exposure, and counts of past infection guide safety plans. Their 2026 study enrolled more than twelve hundred nurses, lab staff, doctors, and pharmacists for blood tests and a habits survey.

Antibodies were near universal: about ninety-eight in one hundred staff tested as past-exposed. Most hits bore the mark of the virus's inner protein, a sign of true past infection, not shots alone. Nurses were three times as apt to test as past-exposed as lab staff. Half the staff still lacked shots at the time. The team urges stronger shots and ward safety for front-line staff.
plos-pone-0354706:
Fei Chen and co-authors propose in 2026 a better way to estimate the health of lithium ion batteries from electrical response tests. Single response measures miss how ageing parts of a battery interact, giving weak predictions. Their method picks several response features that track capacity loss, then feeds them to a neural network tuned by three search methods borrowed from nature.

Across test conditions with plenty of data and with noisy, scarce data, tuned networks kept errors low and stable. Two of the tuning methods stood out in the hardest cases. Reliable health estimates matter for safe use of batteries in vehicles and portable devices.
plos-pone-0355106:
Issiaka Sare and co-authors tested a locally isolated fungus as a malaria mosquito killer and traced its effects across generations. Fungi offer an eco-friendlier alternative to chemical insecticides, but their full life-history costs to mosquitoes were unclear. Their 2026 study exposed a major malaria vector to two strains of the fungus at larval and adult stages.

Larvae were reared in spore-dosed water, and survivors were followed for lifespan, wing size, egg laying, and blood feeding. Separately, sprayed adult females were followed through their offspring's survival. Survival analysis used standard hazard models, with other traits compared across treatments. Sare and colleagues frame the results for biocontrol planners weighing fungal sprays against resistance-prone chemicals.
plos-pone-0355406:
Amit Hasan and co-authors report in 2026 the first known case in Bangladesh of a fungus causing leaf spot on quinoa, a nutritious grain like crop with growing local promise. Sick plants at a university farm in Dhaka yielded one fungus again and again from spotted leaves. Shape study, gene sequencing, and family tree analysis named the culprit, and infection tests on healthy plants reproduced the spots.

The fungus was reisolated from the newly sick plants, completing the classic proof of cause. Colonies grew grey to black with curved, thick walled spores. The authors warn growers to watch for this emerging threat and urge resistance screening and joined up disease control.
plos-pone-0355506:
Benedicto Mgala and colleagues explore in 2026 daily life for patients in Tanzania who must take warfarin for life after receiving an artificial heart valve. The drug prevents dangerous clots but needs tight dose control, a strict diet, and regular blood checks. Twelve patients at the national heart institute gave in depth interviews about their routines.

Many felt better after surgery, yet diet limits, side effects, low mood, and lost work weighed heavily. Keeping blood levels in range was hard amid money strain, uneven drug use, mixed advice, and scarce testing away from the centre. The authors call for a clearer, joined up path of care.
plos-pone-0355606: Cervical cancers resist immunotherapy through epigenetic trickery involving HDAC2. This paper showed HDAC2 restrains IGF2BP1-associated m6A dysregulation driving that resistance. The mechanistic chain reveals a druggable target that could re-sensitize tumors to immune attack.
plos-pone-0356006:
Vicente Lopez-Chavarrias, Irene Aldea, and Jovita Fernández-Pinero published a 2026 software paper in PLOS ONE introducing PePApipe, a tool that automates genome analysis for African swine fever virus. The virus devastates pig farming and triggers trade bans, and tracing outbreaks needs full genomes, yet the analysis steps were scattered across separate programs. The pipeline chains thirteen tools into one workflow, from raw sequencing reads through quality checks, genome assembly, and variant listing.

PePApipe was built for laboratory professionals with little computing background, needing only basic command-line skills, and it can run on a single machine or a computing cluster for batches. Outputs arrive in structured folders: a consensus genome plus a file of differences from a chosen reference, with intermediate files kept and steps switchable. The authors say one automated path cuts user error and makes results reproducible, easing the step from sequencer to outbreak report.
plos-pone-0356206:
Daisuke Sudo and Daisuke Toyoda ran a pilot trial testing whether eye exercise training adds anything to leg strengthening for thirty community-dwelling older adults. The bid was to cut falls by sharpening vision. Their 2026 randomized study trained both groups' legs for eight weeks. Half also drilled six visual skills on a dedicated training system. The skills ran from eye-hand coordination to peripheral perception.

No clear advantage appeared. Adjusted comparisons showed no confirmed differences in visual or physical outcomes. Several estimates leaned toward the vision group on exactly the skills practiced, though with wide uncertainty. The authors are candid: thirty people cannot settle the question. The pilot's real product is a blueprint for a properly powered trial with fairer controls and meaningful endpoints.
plos-pone-0356806:
Irina Elena Ionescu and colleagues compared two standard recipes for growing dendritic cells, the immune system's teaching cells, from mouse bone marrow, because the recipe quietly changes what the cells become. Their 2026 laboratory study grew cells with one growth factor alone or with a second added, then compared surface markers, cytokine output, and the ability to coach naive T cells.

Cells grown with the single factor looked mature yet still answered bacterial stimuli with cytokines and primed T cells in an antigen-specific way. Adding the second factor kept cells less mature but introduced nonspecific T cell signaling that could muddy experiments. The message for immunologists is to choose, and re-check, the recipe against the exact question being asked.
plos-pone-0356906:
Guillaume Bouguéon and colleagues test how long prepared bags of idarubicin, a workhorse drug against blood cancers, stay safe to use. Hospital pharmacies would like to prepare doses ahead, but shelf life in modern plastic bags lacked solid data. The team filled bags at two strengths in two common fluids. Some bags were stored cold. Others sat at room temperature. Samples were assayed across a full month, alongside checks for particles, acidity, and salt balance.

Drug levels stayed above ninety-five percent of the starting strength through day thirty in every condition, with no breakdown products detected. Bags showed no color change or precipitate, particle counts stayed within limits, and acidity and salt balance did not drift. Bouguéon and colleagues say pharmacies can safely prepare a month ahead under either storage style.
plos-pone-0357006:
Nayana Gunathilaka, Deshaka Jayakody, and Iranga Dilshan mapped fifteen years of rickettsioses in Sri Lanka. These are tick- and mite-borne fevers that are often missed. Their 2026 analysis used weekly national case reports from all twenty-five districts between 2009 and 2023. Satellite weather data was paired with the reports. The aim was to find where and when the diseases strike, and which climate conditions travel with them.

More than eighteen thousand cases were reported. They were heavily concentrated in Jaffna in the north, with the central highlands next. The modeling linked incidence patterns to local climate and geography. Knowing the hotspots and seasons lets health officials aim fever testing, public warnings, and vector control. They can target the districts and months where these under-recognized illnesses actually cluster.
plos-pone-0357106:
Julia Ruß and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article in veterinary medicine. It measures serum reverse triiodothyronine, a thyroid-related hormone in blood, in three groups of dogs: those with hypothyroidism, those whose illness is not thyroidal, and healthy dogs. Thyroid tests in dogs are notoriously muddied by other illnesses.

Nonthyroidal illness can make a healthy thyroid look underactive, leading to wrong treatment. Comparing this hormone across the three groups tests whether it separates true thyroid failure from the shadow of other disease. Veterinarians diagnosing sluggish, gaining dogs are the readers who need cleaner thyroid markers.
plos-pone-0357206:
Ruy Felipe Melo Viegas led a team of eight authors who compared blood and saliva tests in heart failure patients, in a PLOS ONE study from 2026. Checking a failing heart now means drawing blood to measure stress and injury markers. The team asked whether saliva could carry the same signals in useful amounts.

Viegas and his co-authors measured three markers in both fluids: one linked to heart strain, one to heart muscle injury, and one to inflammation. Setting the saliva values beside the blood values shows how close a spit test could come to the standard. A simple saliva check would make repeat testing easier for patients who need close tracking.
plos-pone-0357406:
Huawei Wang led a team of five authors improving crane scheduling in railway freight yards, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rail-mounted gantry cranes move containers between trains and trucks, and poor scheduling jams the whole yard. The team built a flexible scheduling method that balances several goals at once.

Wang's model weighs speed against energy use and fairness across jobs, instead of chasing one target. Yards must make that trade-off daily as trains arrive off schedule. A model that bends without breaking helps dispatchers keep freight moving. Faster, steadier yards lower the cost of rail freight, which matters for shifting goods off roads and cutting transport emissions at the same time.
plos-pone-0357706:
Aysegul Erinc and colleagues ask whether a simple blood score predicts survival in people with scarring lung disease who do not have diabetes. The score combines fasting sugar and blood fat values and is often read as a sign of insulin resistance. Records covered well over a hundred patients on anti-scarring therapy, followed for close to three years on median, with lung tests and survival tracked.

The abstract reports the cohort's profile and the study design in detail, linking the score with lung function and death from any cause. Because patients here stayed within the non-diabetic range, the work tests whether small shifts in the score still carry meaning. Erinc and colleagues frame the score as a cheap add-on to scans and lung tests when judging outlook.
plos-pone-0357806:
Katie L Kowalski led a team of eight authors measuring rehabilitation science across Canada, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. They asked who produces rehabilitation research, how much they publish, and what impact it has. Their data mixed public records with a survey of faculty across the country.

Kowalski's faculty-wide picture shows where the field is strong, where it is thin, and who shapes its future. Universities and funders can use that picture to spot gaps, such as regions or topics with few active researchers. Rehabilitation serves an aging population with growing needs, so the health of its research base matters beyond academia. The study offers a baseline for judging future growth.
plos-pone-0357906:
J. Richard T. Korecki and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for project FIERCE, a trial testing a meditation program built for stressed doctors. Most healthcare providers report burnout, poor sleep, and low mood from workplace strain, and mindfulness courses help but rarely target positive emotion. Their six-week program, BEST, delivered online, adapts the Buddhist Four Immeasurables practice to cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.

Ninety full-time doctors will be randomized to the program or a waitlist, completing surveys and giving blood samples at the start, middle, and end. Perceived stress is the main outcome, with burnout, depression, well-being, and sleep also tracked, with blood inflammation markers adding a hard-data layer. The design also tests what carries any benefit, measuring compassion, positive affect, equanimity, and mindfulness as candidate carriers. A positive-emotion focus, they hope, proves stronger medicine than attention training alone.
plos-pone-0359206:
Kathryn Date and eight colleagues published this study protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It describes the CONIFAS2 study, a feasibility test of a nature-based intervention for children with ADHD. The intervention was co-produced, designed together with the people who would use it.

A feasibility study asks whether a bigger trial can work at all: will families join, stay, and accept the activities? Nature-based activities are a low-drug option many families welcome, but they still need proper testing. Researchers planning the full trial, and clinicians who advise families with ADHD, are the readers for this groundwork.
plos-pone-0359306:
Monique Bussmann, Marieke Groot, Chris Kuiper, and Mieke Cardol published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is an ethnographic multi-case study of musical encounters in healthcare, moments when music is brought to patients. The authors call these encounters precarious, valuable yet fragile, and explore why.

Perspectives come from both care professionals and the musicians themselves, whose views of the same visit can differ sharply. Ethnographic observation across several cases shows how setting, timing, and expectations make or break a musical visit. Arts-in-health organizers and hospital staff hosting musicians are the readers for this account.
pmc-13217206:
Patil, Khan, and Mahyavanshi chart infections of the brain and spinal cord in children from rural western India. Such infections remain a leading cause of death and disability for children in poorer countries. Local patterns shift with vaccine uptake, environment, and how easily families can reach care, yet rural data from this region were scarce.

The study tracks which infections appeared, how their frequency changed, and what neurological outcomes children were left with. Findings like these help hospitals plan beds, tests, and follow-up for survivors with lasting damage. They also show where prevention, above all vaccination and earlier referral, could cut the toll most.
pmc-13235706:
Perin and colleagues estimate what killed newborns and young children worldwide between 2000 and 2024. Their secondary analysis covers 195 countries. It uses a Bayesian statistical model to split deaths by cause, drawing on journal studies, health surveys, and World Health Organization mortality records, among many other sources.

Cause splits matter because the big killers of the first month differ from those of ages one to four. Fresh estimates show where past gains came from and where deaths still cluster. Governments and aid groups use such numbers to aim vaccines, newborn care, and nutrition money. The authors update an earlier round of estimates with data through the pandemic years.
pmc-13235906:
Reginato and Brandl build a new tool for naming the small, hidden fishes of coral reefs. Reefs hold more than a third of all marine species, yet many reef fishes are tiny, shy, and easy to confuse. Specialists who can tell them apart are few, so much reef life goes unrecorded in surveys.

Their tool joins deep learning with the branching structure of biological classification and very detailed images. Teaching the model the family tree, not just the final name, helps it sort look-alike species. Better identification from photos could widen reef monitoring sharply, letting cameras and computers do work that now waits on a handful of experts.
pmc-13240906:
Nguyen at Vietnam's National Economics University weighed land use efficiency and urban form across three Indochina capitals. Hanoi, Vientiane, and Phnom Penh were tracked from 2017 to 2024. The assessment paired the UN land-consumption indicator with spatial clustering statistics. A shape index gauged how compact each capital's footprint stayed.

Land expansion outran population growth in all three cities. Phnom Penh showed the most compact, strongly grouped growth despite the fastest land uptake. Hanoi sprawled with weaker clustering, while Vientiane expanded in loose, fragmented patches. Nguyen urges tighter spatial planning before these trajectories harden.
pmc-13241206:
Singh and colleagues at Royal Darwin Hospital charted chronic melioidosis across Australia's Northern Territory over thirty-four years. Cases with symptoms lasting two months or more came to one hundred twenty-six. That was under a tenth of all melioidosis recorded since 1989. Chronic cases were set head-to-head with acute presentations.

Pneumonia and skin infections dominated, and scans were often first read as cancer or tuberculosis. Chronic patients carried fewer classic risk factors like diabetes. Their blood tests turned positive far less often, and death was much rarer. Antibody tests, notably, flagged eighty-seven percent of chronic cases at diagnosis.
pmc-13241506:
Galectins, a family of proteins that bind sugar chains on other molecules, take center stage in a review by Popatia and colleagues at the University of Ottawa. The authors map how these proteins steer signaling inside and outside cells. Sixteen mammalian galectins fall into three structural types, each with its own binding habits. Their influence reaches growth, blood vessel formation, and immune control.

Across diseases, the review links galectins to cancer spread, heart and vessel damage, brain degeneration, metabolic problems, and autoimmunity. Some family members push in opposite directions depending on tissue, which complicates drug design. Trials already test blockers ranging from modified carbohydrates and pectins to antibodies. New tools such as single-cell glyco-RNA sequencing and CRISPR glycoengineering may sharpen future galectin drugs.
pmc-13241606:
Phimha and colleagues at Khon Kaen University measured what a denture visit really costs elderly Thai patients and their caretakers. The team surveyed three hundred forty-six patient-caretaker pairs at three tertiary hospitals. Data came from structured questionnaires collected over six months. Costs were split into direct payments and lost income.

Each visit drained about one hundred forty-eight purchasing-power-adjusted dollars from the household. Patients carried the largest share through medical payments and their own lost earnings. Caretakers absorbed well over a third of the burden, almost entirely as forgone wages. Visits averaged more than six hours, and the authors urge policies that cut both household costs and clinic time.
pmc-13241706:
Draidi's team in Doha chased a bleeding source that hid from every camera and scan. Their patient, 69, kept returning with black stools and severe anemia needing transfusions. His blood pressure swung wildly between spells. Standard upper and lower scope exams found nothing at all. CT vessel scans also failed to find the elusive leak.

A swallowed camera capsule hinted at far small-bowel bleeding without pinpointing it. Sepsis tangled the transfusion-dependent course. Keyhole surgery finally exposed two jejunal pouches with engorged vessels. Cutting out that bowel segment stopped the bleeding for good.
pmc-13242106:
Güner's team at Hacettepe fix a naming slip in their 2023 study of swallowing problems and frailty in Alzheimer's disease. The Methods named the thinking test the Mini-Mental State Examination. The team in fact used the test's standard form. Rights and trademark claims forced the fix. The study first appeared in BMC Geriatrics.

Every mention now reads Standardized Mini-Mental State Examination, shortened to SMMSE. The mark rests with the test's creator and its licensed seller. The authors state plainly that the data, results, and takeaways stand untouched. The journal amended the article in full.
pmc-13242506:
Mahmoud Abdel-Nasser and colleagues studied how to protect a badly decayed old manuscript without harsh chemicals. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. The eleventh-century manuscript, paper pages and leather binding alike, suffered stains, acidity, weakened fibers, and missing pieces. Imaging and chemical tests documented the damage, and the team cultured the fungi living on it, finding thirteen strains, led by Aspergillus species that secrete fiber-eating enzymes.

Their proposed remedy pairs an extract from bacterial probiotics with nanoparticles made by green methods. The goal is a treatment that suppresses the manuscript's own fungi while sparing the artifact, the conservator, and the environment. Traditional synthetic fungicides can endanger all three. The study first proves how much of the decay is biological, driven by enzymes the fungi release. It then argues this gentler mix deserves a place in museum practice.
pmc-13242906:
Deepika Beereddy and co-authors describe a severe immune complication of cancer immunotherapy that resisted standard treatment. Their case report appeared in Cureus in 2026. A seventy-seven-year-old woman with advanced endometrial cancer developed weakness, drooping eyelids, double vision, and breathing trouble twenty-four days after one combined dose of chemotherapy and pembrolizumab. Tests showed inflammation of heart muscle, skeletal muscle, and the nerve-muscle junction, plus an overactive thyroid.

Under the escalated regimen her symptoms and blood markers finally improved, and she went home on a tapering plan. The authors urge doctors who spot one part of the triad to screen for the others.
pmc-13243106:
Ying Lei and colleagues wrote this 2026 review on Crohn's disease, a long-term gut illness that often leads to disability. Watching the disease closely matters, but common checks can be invasive, slow to show change, or unable to see through the full bowel wall.

The review centres on blood fats and on creeping fat, a layer of belly fat that wraps around the inflamed bowel in this disease. During active illness, patients show a typical pattern of disturbed blood fats tied to body-wide inflammation. Creeping fat itself feeds inflammation and scarring, and scans can use it to predict surgery risk and return of disease after an operation.
pmc-13244506:
Muhammed Hassan Nasr and co-authors ran a placebo-controlled trial of high-dose vitamin D in men with type 2 diabetes. Their study appeared in the Journal of Pharmaceutical Policy and Practice in 2026. Sixty men at Taibah University in Saudi Arabia took either fifty thousand units of vitamin D3 weekly or a dummy pill for twenty-four weeks. Blood tests tracked vitamin levels, insulin resistance, fasting sugar, and glucose control.

The supplement did its first job well: vitamin D levels climbed in the treated group and deficiency was corrected, while the placebo group barely moved. But the hoped-for metabolic payoff never came. Insulin resistance, fasting glucose, and glycated hemoglobin all failed to improve beyond placebo. Weight and lipids likewise showed no shift. The authors conclude vitamin D should be prescribed to fix deficiency, not marketed as a glucose treatment. Their negative result matters because hopes were high.
pmc-13246506:
Nguyen and colleagues measured what marine plastic costs small-scale fishers in Viet Nam, in this 2026 Communications Earth and Environment study. Working in the Mekong and Red River deltas, the team interviewed nearly two hundred nearshore fishers, ran follow-up verification interviews, and audited the debris hauled up in hundreds of fishing nets.

Plastic cost each vessel roughly thirty-four hundred dollars a year, about an eighth of vessel revenue and a quarter of the owner's income, through lost time, damaged gear, and reduced catches. Fishers also reported injuries, and even deaths, from entanglement incidents at sea. The burden fell hardest on lower-income Mekong fishers. Paying fishers to collect plastic at priority spots, the authors suggest, could cut pollution and support livelihoods together.
pmc-13246806:
Jander, Bergner, Schönwald, and co-authors examined whether a newer Parkinson's infusion therapy also eases non-motor symptoms, in this 2026 Journal of Neurology study. Foslevodopa/foscarbidopa delivers Parkinson's medication continuously under the skin and is approved for motor swings in advanced disease, but its effects on sleep, pain, mood, and gut problems were poorly documented. The team followed twenty-one day-clinic patients for nine weeks.

Standard non-motor scores improved by roughly a third, a change past the threshold patients can feel, with the largest gains in sleep disturbance, pain, and constipation. Questionnaire scores for gut symptoms, sleep quality, and depression also improved early on. Four patients developed psychotic symptoms, a known risk. The authors call the results encouraging but exploratory, needing controlled trials.
pmc-13247306:
Liu and co-authors tested a plant extract against hair graying in this 2026 Dermatology Research and Practice study. Graying is driven largely by oxidative stress killing or disabling the melanocytes that pigment hair, and no effective treatment exists. The team tested Gynostemma pentaphyllum extract, from a vine used in Asian herbal medicine, on pigment cells and mice stressed with hydrogen peroxide.

In cell culture the extract kept melanocytes alive, cut their death rate and internal reactive oxygen, and raised melanin production and the activity of two protective enzymes. In mice it visibly protected hair follicles from peroxide damage. The authors link the effect partly to the Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway and propose the extract as a candidate anti-graying treatment, pending human testing.
pmc-13248106:
Okura and co-authors report a genetic kidney-tubule disorder hiding until old age, in this 2026 Case Reports in Endocrinology article. Bartter syndrome type 3, a defect in salt handling in the kidney's loop of Henle, normally declares itself in childhood. Their patient was a sixty-six-year-old woman whose only clue was severe, stubborn low blood potassium found without symptoms, alongside the syndrome's typical alkaline blood and overactive hormone signals.

Ordinary potassium replacement, even at high doses, failed to fix her levels. Careful diuretic challenge tests separated Bartter physiology from its mimic, Gitelman syndrome, and gene sequencing confirmed a homozygous stop variant in the CLCNKB gene. A low-dose combination of an ACE inhibitor and spironolactone then normalized her potassium safely. The authors urge keeping Bartter syndrome in mind for unexplained low potassium at any age.
pmc-13248306:
Hao and a large team searched eye scans for warning signs of abnormal blood vessel growth, in a 2026 study. Their patients had chronic central serous chorioretinopathy, a fluid disorder under the retina that sometimes develops a harmful vessel membrane. Using widefield dye imaging, they compared eyes with and without that complication.

The study covered two hundred ninety-three eyes from two hundred twelve patients, and about a third had the vessel growth. A dominant drainage vein in one corner, vessel links near the macula, and pale scattered spots each stood out in the affected group. The authors propose these features as markers that flag eyes needing closer watching.
pmc-13248906:
Belongia and a large Vaccine Safety Datalink team checked whether COVID-19 vaccines ever made the disease worse, reported in 2026. Enhanced disease after vaccination was a theoretical worry when the shots were authorized. The team estimated vaccine protection against hospitalization and severe illness across variant waves from 2021 to 2023, watching for any negative protection.

Two original doses protected against hospitalization at over ninety percent during the pre-Delta and Delta periods. Protection dipped under Omicron but stayed clearly positive, and booster or bivalent doses restored much of it. At no point, for any dose or variant, did the numbers suggest enhanced disease. The authors close a long-standing safety question with real-world data.
pmc-13249606:
Srivastava and an Indian team profiled immune signals in spinal fluid from patients with autoimmune encephalitis, in a 2026 study. In this condition the immune system attacks the brain, and antibody tests are slow or sometimes come back negative. The researchers measured six signaling proteins in fluid from forty-three patients and thirty-four comparison patients.

Every measured signal ran higher in the encephalitis group. Two attractant proteins, CXCL10 and CXCL13, stood out and rose together with a third, interleukin-6. Patients without detectable antibodies showed the same pattern as those with them. The authors propose the panel as a supporting test that can speed recognition, while stressing it cannot diagnose the condition alone.
pmc-13249706:
Huizenga and colleagues asked teenagers directly how they cope with mental health struggles, in a 2026 pair of Dutch studies. An online tool let adolescents describe, in their own words, what they do about attention problems, behavior problems, or emotional problems, and rate how much each tactic helps. The first study ran during the pandemic with two hundred eighteen participants.

Fifty-one distinct strategies surfaced, some familiar from coping research and others invented by teenagers themselves, and tactics differed by symptom type. The strategies used most were also rated most helpful. A second study after the pandemic, with one hundred eighteen fresh participants, reproduced the picture closely. Helpfulness did not depend on whether a tactic aimed at solving the problem or avoiding it.
pmc-13251306:
Qianwen Ding and a large team test a gut bacteria protein against fatty liver in fish in this 2026 study. The protein, Amuc_1100, comes from a gut microbe linked to metabolic health, and earlier work showed it eases fat build-up in the liver on a fatty diet.

Zebrafish fed the protein with a high-fat diet gained less weight and stored less liver fat than fish on the diet alone. Moving gut microbes from treated fish into germ-free fish copied the benefit, while wiping microbes out with antibiotics erased it. The protein was found to bind a partner in the gut wall, and blocking that partner stopped the effect.
pmc-13252706:
JunYoung Seo and co-authors simplify patient leaflets with a chatbot in this 2026 study. Digital therapeutics are software treatments with real evidence behind them, but their explanation sheets are often too hard to read, which holds back uptake.

The team built a rewriting tool on GPT-4o and tested it in two online experiments with 500 people each, covering insomnia and nicotine dependence treatments. Readers were picked for relevance, such as smokers or poor sleepers. Those given the simplified sheets improved their felt understanding more than readers of the originals, and rated the text easier and clearer. Effects were small to moderate, the authors note.
pmc-13252806:
Adanze Cynthia and colleagues map health care access for Sub-Saharan African migrants in Europe in this 2026 scoping review. This growing population faces heavy barriers to care, and the review gathers what is known as these communities age.

Fourteen studies met the bar across five databases. Three themes stood out. Structural blocks included insurance gaps, legal insecurity, and tangled administration. Undocumented migrants, women, and people with HIV faced sharper vulnerability. Language and culture often clashed with health systems. Only one study looked at ageing and long-term care choices. The authors urge migrant-sensitive services and long-term research following people across their lives.
pmc-13252906:
Loai Albinsaad and colleagues describe a one-sided thyroid in this 2026 case report. A 34-year-old Saudi man came in with swelling on the right side of his neck that pressed on his throat, causing trouble swallowing and breathing.

Examination confirmed an enlarged right thyroid lobe, while hormone levels stayed normal. Ultrasound found several solid lumps inside it, and a needle sample raised suspicion of a follicular growth. Surgeons removed the right half of the gland and confirmed a non-invasive growth of that type. The surprise was the left side: he had been born with no left thyroid lobe at all, a rare defect usually found only by chance.
pmc-13253706:
Ashok Aspatwar reviews carbonic anhydrase VIII, called CA VIII, in a 2026 paper on cell signaling. Most proteins in this family help balance acid in the body, but CA VIII lacks a key part and cannot do that job. Yet it is kept across species and is rich in nerve tissue, hinting at a new role.

Evidence cited shows CA VIII binds a channel that releases calcium inside cells, shaping nerve firing and brain growth. Gene faults in families from Iraq and Saudi Arabia link its loss to ataxia, meaning poor balance, and slow brain growth. The author casts CA VIII as a repurposed signal regulator.
pmc-13254206:
Mona Nabil and colleagues set out greener lab methods to measure a cold and flu medicine in a 2026 study. The product mixes phenylephrine, chlorpheniramine, and ibuprofen to ease congestion, allergy, and fever. Two chromatography methods, which separate and measure ingredients, were built with ecology in mind.

One method used thin-layer plates and the other a liquid system that finished in about six minutes. Both separated the three drugs cleanly and hit very low detection limits, as stated in the paper. The liquid method could also track how fast tablets dissolve, and both passed standard validation checks.
pmc-13255206:
Somayeh Momenyan and co-authors trace PTSD paths after road crashes in a 2026 cohort study. They followed 1,042 survivors recruited from Canadian emergency departments between 2018 and 2020. Symptoms were checked at 2, 4, 6, and 12 months, along with life quality and return to work and daily activities.

Three paths emerged: Chronic, Delayed-Recovery, and Resilient. The first two groups started with high life quality, then fell sharply and stayed low on full recovery and return to work. They were more often female and had more pain and distress before injury. The authors urge early care that treats PTSD and pain together.
pmc-13257406:

Chen and colleagues state that the fix leaves their scientific conclusions unchanged. An academic editor approved the correction, and the original publication has also been updated.
pmc-13260106:
Zhangfan Ding and colleagues publish a recipe for imaging whole organs in three dimensions within about two days. Seeing cells and molecules across an intact organ beats slicing it thin, but antibody staining of big tissues is slow. Their 2026 protocol compresses every stage.

Steps run from bleaching and antigen retrieval through enzyme digestion that lets antibodies soak deep. The team then details whole-tissue labeling, dehydration, and optical clearing for light-sheet microscopy. Human tissues and soft organs both fit the workflow. Labs chasing tumor and tissue microenvironments get a fast, start-to-finish playbook, building on the group's earlier method paper.
pmc-13260206:
Tahra ElObeid and co-authors turn beet sugar waste into an ice cream ingredient. Factories extracting red beet pigment discard a sugary liquid that still holds value. Their 2026 study cleans and concentrates that stream to stand in for glucose syrup.

Fourteen ice cream mixes, planned by statistical design, swapped the upcycled syrup against glucose syrup and salep stabilizer. Color, texture, melting, and flow all modeled predictably across recipes.Usable ice cream resulted, proving colorant waste can rejoin the food chain under a circular economy.
pmc-13263506:
Weili Bao and co-authors present a 2026 case report of two elderly patients who developed a serious eye infection after cataract surgery. The infection, endophthalmitis, is inflammation inside the eye that can destroy vision. Both patients, aged 69 and 87, received emergency surgery to remove the eye's gel, washing of the front chamber, and vancomycin injected into the eye.

Cultures from the eye gel confirmed Enterococcus faecalis, a gut bacterium, which was sensitive to several antibiotics including vancomycin. Both patients needed repeat washing because cloudiness persisted. Vision later improved clearly in both cases. The authors suggest early gel-removal surgery plus vancomycin works well, while warning that two cases are a small base for conclusions.
pmc-13265006:

The drug is used in general anesthesia, and failing kidneys can alter drug handling, so dosing for transplant patients needs proof. They compared kidney transplant patients on dialysis with matched patients whose kidneys worked normally.

Drug use during surgery, waking times, and blood pressure and heart stability also matched. Side effects like low blood pressure, slow heart rate, and slowed breathing occurred at like rates. The authors conclude that kidney failure does not meaningfully change this drug's sedative effect or safety.

Dipak Paudel had been left off the author list. The notice records his contributions: he ran the HPLC analysis of samples and standards, processed the data, and curated the study data set. The corrected list names Nim Bahadur Dangi, Hemraj Sharma, Dipak Paudel, and Hari Prasad Sapkota, with their Nepali university affiliations. The notice closes with an apology for the error.
pmc-13267806:
Xiaohan Wang and Zhiping Wang wrote a 2026 letter about a trial of the sedative remimazolam during painless colonoscopy. pmc-13268706:

The approved product is grown in hamster ovary cells; growing it in E. coli bacteria could be cheaper. The team screened four bacterial-made versions in cell tests, picked the strongest, and compared it with the hamster-cell product in 15 rats. Sponges carrying the protein were placed in muscle pouches for four weeks.

The winning bacterial version beat the standard in cell tests and formed roughly ten times more bone in rats, with more mature structure under the microscope. The authors warn that potency cannot be assumed from protein weight alone: each supplier's product needs its own testing before clinical trust.
pmc-13269606:

The fused model beat either single-source model, with accuracy scores of 0.90, 0.80, and 0.73 across the sets. In a separate group on immune therapy, patients with high model scores lived longer without disease growth. The score stayed predictive when combined with clinical factors.
pmc-13269806:

Their mineral content was higher, but the mineral particles were thinner and more disorganized, and collagen fibers looked like barbed wire. pmc-13270106:

Paper samples were tested before and after cleaning for structure, chemistry, look, and water behavior. The version using agarose, a seaweed gel, performed best, removing most glue layers while keeping the paper intact. Agarose gave a stiff, porous gel that holds water and stops the paper getting soaked. The synthetic part added flexibility, letting the gel peel off in one piece.
pmc-13271106:
